Severe drought conditions, declared for the northern half of Caswell County at the end of November, persisted through January 4th due to precipitation that was significantly below normal during this period. At the beginning of January, NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm was below the 2nd percentile. Local streamflows were below normal per the USGS WaterWatch website. There were few impacts to agriculture and livestock given the winter time of the year, affecting both winter wheat as well as cover crops designed to reduce soil erosion with only miniscule growth. It is not known if the poor growth resulted in any financial impact. Severe drought conditions were improved to moderate drought on the January 4th edition of the U.S. Drought Monitor after 2 to locally 3.5 inches of rain fell across Caswell County during January 1st to the 3rd.

Entering January 2022, Severe drought conditions had been in effect for the southwestern corner of Yadkin County since December 7th due to several weeks of precipitation that was significantly below normal. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm soil at the start of January was below the 2nd percentile. Local streamflows remained below normal through the month per the USGS WaterWatch website. Severe drought conditions were improved to Moderate drought on the January 4th edition of the U.S. Drought Monitor after 2.5 to locally 3 inches of rain fell across southwest Yadkin County during January 1st to the 3rd.

A personal weather station near Baldwin measured a wind gust of 71 MPH at 10:20 AM EST. In addition, the AWOS site at Jefferson (GEV) measured a 66 MPH wind gust at 03:15 AM EST and a 58 MPH wind gust at 10:35 AM EST.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KVAGALAX92) near the City of Galax observed a 75-minute rainfall total of 1.39 inches. This amount is estimated to be between a 2- and 5-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration.

An employee of a country store/gas station reported that a clogged drainage ditch across the road caused water to overflow across the gas station parking lot and into the store up to 3 inches deep.  The water receded quickly after the rain ended, however some merchandise was damaged by the water and could not be sold.

The Smyth County 911 Center reported minor flooding of small creeks and streams at various locations across the county during the afternoon and evening of the 24th due to prolonged rainfall atop saturated soils.  A few roads had several inches of standing water on them, causing lanes of traffic to be closed for brief periods of time.  No damage was reported.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVASALTV6) recorded 2.36 inches of rainfall during the morning and afternoon of the 24th, which is in addition to 1.53 inches that fell on the 22nd and 23rd, for a 3-day total of 3.89 inches.  Rainfall rates on the 24th at times approached an inch per hour.  These rainfall totals have average recurrence intervals generally between 2-year and 5-year events per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

The COOP observer at Saltville 1 N, VA (SLTV2) recorded a 3-day rainfall total of 4.08 inches of rain, which is about a 5-year average recurrence interval per a NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimate.  This rainfall total occurred in at least three rounds spaced over the 3-day period.
A CoCoRaHS observer (VA-SM-9) observed a 3-day rainfall total of 4.20 inches.

A tornado touched down along Kinzer Road four miles east-southeast of Gladesboro, VA. The tornado traveled northeast along Gladesboro Road toward Football Lane before lifting south of U.S. Highway 58. Numerous trees were snapped and two structures were damaged along the tornado path. The one structure was a two story family home that was shifted off its foundation and had its roof torn off along Gladesboro Road. Additionally, a modular home along Football Lane had its roof partially blown off. Damage values are estimated. There was $255,000 in damage to the two damage structures, $45,000 in roof damages and approximately $100,000 in replacement costs for outbuilding structures.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Bluefield, WV (BLFW2) observed a 24-hour (ending 11Z on May 24th) precipitation amount of 2.73 inches. This was the 5th-highest 24-hour total for this station all-time, and 2nd highest during the month of May. This 24-hour amount is about a 5-year ARI event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation estimates. Records date back to December 1998.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCMOUNT12) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 3.13 inches, most of which fell in a little over 12 hours.  Rainfall rates remained mostly below 0.5 per hour, but at times were near 1 per hour.  This amount is almost a 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration.  Runoff from this rainfall eventually flows into the East River.

The East River at Willowton, WV (ERVW2, USGS:03177120) crested at 9.83 feet, less than a foot above the flood stage of 9.0 feet.  This caused portions of WV Highway 291/8 upstream of the gauge to become inundated with water.  No damage was reported after the water receded.

The Watauga River at Sugar Grove crested at 7.11 feet at 5:15 am EDT on May 27th, causing the river to overflow its banks across portions of Watauga River Road.  A few low water bridges along the river were also flooded and impassible.  No damage was reported however.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCSEVEN25) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 3.28 inches. Rainfall rates remained mostly below 0.5 per hour. This amount is almost a 2-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration. Runoff from this rainfall eventually flows into the Watauga River.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCBOONE156) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 3.00 inches. Rainfall rates remained mostly below 0.5 per hour. This amount is about an 1-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration. Runoff from this rainfall eventually flows into the Watauga River.

The stream gauge located along Wolf Creek at Narrows (WOLV2, USGS:03175500) crested at 10.07 feet, less than a foot above the flood stage of 10.0 feet. The creek flowed out of its banks in spots, covering portions of Old Wolf Creek Road a few inches deep, with a couple homes about one half mile downstream of the gauge becoming surrounded by water. No damage was reported after the water receded.  This event resulted in an updated Flood-Impact statement for this gauge in NWS AHPS website.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Burkes Garden, VA (BURV2) recorded at 24-hour rainfall total of 3.58 inches, which is the highest 1-day total ever for this station during the month of May, and the 6th-highest 1-day total all-time.  This 24-hour rainfall total is between a 5- and a 10-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  Runoff from this rainfall flows into the headwaters of Wolf Creek.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KVANARRO14) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 3.99 inches. Rainfall rates remained mostly below 0.5 per hour but, at times, were as high as 1 per hour. This amount is between a 10- and 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration. Runoff from this rainfall eventually flows into the Wolf Creek.

The stream gauge located along Wolf Creek at Narrows (BRVV2, USGS:03177710) crested at 7.41 feet, less than a foot above the flood stage of 7.0 feet.  Minor lowland flooding was observed, with no damage reported.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KVABLUEF10) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 3.40 inches. Rainfall rates remained mostly below 0.5 per hour, though at times increased to nearly 1 per hour. This amount is around a 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration.

An EF-2 tornado with max winds of 135 mph touchdown 0.4 miles southeast of Norwood before heading north northeast toward U.S Highway 221. The tornado crossed Bethany Church Road and Langford Lane where two mobile homes were destroyed. The tornado then continued northeast snapping and uprooting trees just west of the Ivy Hill Golf Course. Additional tree damage was noted on the western slopes of Fleming Mountain along Rocky Mountain Road. In total, 15 homes were damaged along with 35 structures including sheds, outbuildings, and garages. Three injuries were reported with zero fatalities. The length of the tornado track was estimated at 6.25 miles, and the maximum width was approximately 330 yards.

Rough Creek was observed well out of its banks, flowing over Old Evergreen Road at least 6 inches deep at around 3:00 pm EDT.  No damage was noted to the road, which became passable again once the flooding receded.

A National Weather Service survey team inspected storm damage along the western end of Green View Road approximately 1.6 miles south southwest of Chandlers Fork and 3.8 miles north of Randolph. Significant roof damage along with glass doors and windows were broken on the home. A few trees and power lines were also damaged along Green View Road before the tornado lifted.

A trained weather spotter observed Big Clear Creek out of its banks and flowing across U.S. Highway 60.  The highway was temporarily closed until flooding of Big Clear Creek receded.  No damage to the highway was reported.

Heavy rain caused Little Town Hill Creek to overflow its banks, flooding across Hillcreek Road, as well as U.S. Highway 460 to a depth of up to 4 feet.  One car was caught in the floodwater and the occupant had to be rescued by emergency responders.  Flooding across Highway 460 lasted for around two hours before flooding receded and the highway was reopened.  No damage to the road was reported, but with some damage to the flooded vehicle.
Minor flooding was reported along Burnette Street when a tributary of the Clinch River was observed overflowing its banks onto Burnette Street.  No damage was reported.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVARICHL6) recorded 2.63 inches of rainfall from a thunderstorm within a nearly 2 hour period.  Rainfall rates were observed as high as 2.5 inches per hour.  This was a 25-year rainfall event for this location per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in the Town of Richlands observed a 24-hour rainfall amount of 2.07 inches, caused by a thunderstorm.  This was a new daily record for this station and the 2nd-highest 24-hour total during the month of August.
Minor street flooding was observed on South Main Street due to heavy rain from a thunderstorm.  No damage was reported.

Heavy rain from a series of training thunderstorms caused Gochenhour Branch to flood out of its bank and across Brattons Run Road up to 3 feet deep.  No damage was reported and the road was reopened after flooding receded.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVADUGSP7) recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 4.84 inches, most of which fell between 2 pm and 9 pm on the 21st.  Rainfall rates were observed at 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the event.  This total was about a 50-year rainfall event at the 6-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAHILLS48) recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 4.97 inches, which fell between 3 pm and 9 pm on the 21st.  Rainfall rates were observed at 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the event.  This total was about a 100-year rainfall event at the 6-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

Lovills Creek was observed overflowing its banks and flooding several inches deep across Wards Gap Road.  The road was impassible until the flood waters receded.  No damage was reported to the road and it was reopened after flooding ended.
Little Spoon Creek was observed overflowing its banks and flooding several inches deep across Highway 58.  The highway was reopened after flooding receded and no damage was reported.

Campbell Branch was observed overflowing its banks and flooding several inches deep across Commerce Street near the town of Stuart.  No damage was reported and the road was open after the flooding receded.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAFAIRF60) recorded a 3-hour rainfall total of 3.33 inches, most of which fell between 8 am and 10 am EST on the 21st. Rainfall rates were observed in excess of 3 inches per hour during the event. This total was about a 50-year rainfall event at the 3-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

Heavy rain caused a tributary of Mill Creek to overflow its banks and flood across Old Chapel Road near the intersection with Kennel Hill Lane.  The road was reopened after flooding receded, with no damage reported.
Heavy rain caused Marlbrook Creek to overflow its banks and flood across Sterrett Road.  The road was reopened after flooding receded, with no damage reported.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVALEXIN46) recorded a 3-hour rainfall total of 3.94 inches. Rainfall rates peaked at nearly 3 inches per hour during the storm. This total was about a 200-year rainfall event at the 3-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.
Blacks Run was flooded by up to 3 feet of water flowing across the roadway due to heavy rain.  The road was reopened after flood water receded and no damage was reported.

Three to four inches of rain from a slow moving thunderstorm caused several roads within the Hillsville area to become flooded and impassible. Some of the roads were flooded 1 to 2 feet deep where they intersected small flooded streams. Some of the streams overflowed their banks across U.S. Highway 52, making the highway impassible at some locations. The roads were passible again once the flooding receded, with no damage reported.

Three to four inches of rain fell along the crest of the Blue Ridge between the communities of Fancy Gap and Meadows of Dan, resulting in flooding of several small streams along the Blue Ridge Parkway.  Some of these streams flooded across the parkway several inches deep, making the road impassible until the flood waters receded.  No damage was reported.  CREST (Coupled Routing and Excess Storage) Unit Streamflow estimated as much as 600 cfs per mi^2 in this area.
Gravel from a roadway was washed away by heavy rainfall.

A passing thunderstorm produced rainfall rates ranging from 4 to 5 inches per hour, which inundated Powder Mill Creek.  The creek was observed flowing over 6 inches deep across School Board Road, making the road impassible.  The road reopened after flood waters receded, with no damage reported.

Numerous trees and power lines were downed by non-thunderstorm winds from the remnants of Ian throughout Henry County. At least 12 roads were blocked by downed trees and eight power lines were blown down. There were and estimated 2,248 reported power outages in the county. Non-thunderstorm winds from the remnants of Ian continued to impact the area overnight through the morning hours of October 1, 2022.

Several trees were blown down across Pittsylvania County and the City of Danville from the remnants of Ian. In Danville, at least nine trees were blown down, including Audubon Drive, Guerrant Street, Lanier Avenue, Lexington Avenue, Mountain Hill Road, North Main Street, Schoolfield Drive and Updike Place.  Other known locations were trees were blown down include Chalk Level Road and the intersection of Chestnut Level Lane and Spring Garden Road. 17,000 residents, or about 42% of the county, were without power during the peak of the storm. A peak wind gust of 51 MPH was measured at the Danville Regional Airport.

Several large trees were downed by non-thunderstorm winds from the remnants of Ian throughout Carroll County, including near Cana, Lamsburg, and Fancy Gap.  A peak wind gust of 60 MPH was measured on Interstate 77 near mile marker 1.8. Approximately 3,494 residents lost power.

The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 13.01 feet 5:15 pm EST on Nov 11th due to prolonged moderate to heavy rain associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Nicole.  This is the 20th-highest crest in the history of this gage, and is the highest crest since June 2019. This crest (8,630 cfs) ranks between a 2-year and a 5-year event (0.5-0.2 ARI) per USGS StreamStats.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCBANNE130) recorded a 48-hour storm rainfall total of 8.97 inches.  8.45 inches fell in a 24 hour period between 3 pm on 11/10 and 3 pm on 11/11, which is between a 25- and 50-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates for this duration.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCSEVEN24) recorded a 48-hour storm rainfall total of 7.31 inches. 6.06 inches fell in a 24 hour period between 3 pm on 11/10 and 3 pm on 11/11, which is between a 5- and 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates for this duration.

The East Fork South Fork of the New River at Deerfield Road crested at 7.94 feet at 4 pm on the 11th.  This stream overflowed its banks several inches deep across both Deerfield Road and Bamboo Road further upstream.  Remediation consisted of only minor debris removal.
The South Fork of the New River at M.L.K. Jr. Street in the Town of Boone crested at 12.07 feet.

The Middle Fork South Fork of the New River at Deerfield Road crested at 6.92 feet at 11 am on the 11th and remained above 6.5 feet into late afternoon. This stream overflowed its banks across Deerfield Road.

The South Fork New River at Jefferson (JFRN7) crested at 8.31 feet 11 pm EST on Nov 11th due to prolonged moderate to heavy rain associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Nicole. The heaviest rain fell in the headwaters of the New River in Watauga County. This is the highest crest since May 2020. This crest (7,300 cfs) ranks between a 2-year and a 5-year event (0.5-0.2 ARI) per USGS StreamStats.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCBLOWI104) recorded a 48-hour storm rainfall total of 5.42 inches. 5 inches fell in a 24 hour period between 4 pm on 11/10 and 4 pm on 11/11, which is between a 2- and 5-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates for this duration.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCBLOWI92) recorded a 48-hour storm rainfall total of 4.90 inches. 4.50 inches fell in a 24 hour period between 4 pm on 11/10 and 4 pm on 11/11, which is between a 2- and 5-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates for this duration.

A cell phone video showed the Watauga River flowing over a foot deep across Guy Ford Road in western Watauga County during the afternoon of November 11th. Large debris was caught on the bridge that would require equipment for removal.

A cell phone video from a motorist in the Valle Crusis area showed Dutch Creek and a smaller creek (name unknown) that runs along Frank Mast Road both out of their banks.  Water from these flooded creeks was observed up against the Valle Crucis United Methodist Church, the Valle Crucis Log Cabin Rentals, and the Mast General Store.  Portions of the Valle Crusis Community Park was flooded over a foot deep.  Water was observed flowing across Broadstone Road.  Reported damage was minor and consisted mainly of cleanup of debris.

Flooding from Dutch Creek flooded the property of Valle Crucis Elementary School all the way up to the school building. Water did enter portions of the building, but cleanup was quick and no damage was reported in the building.  Cleanup of the school grounds consisted mainly of debris removal.
The Dewitt Barnett Road bridge crossing the Watauga River was submerged at least 2 feet deep by flooding.  No damage was reported and the bridge reopened after flooding subsided.

The combination of sleet and freezing rain resulted in slick road surfaces on Interstate-64 near White Sulphur Springs. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closure.

The stream gage at Anthony Creek near Anthony (ANYW2) crested at 15.87 feet (7,865 cfs) at 1:20 pm EST on 2/17/23.  This is roughly a 2-year event (50% AEP) per USGS Streamstats for this location and the highest crest on record since 2014.  The Anthony Creek basin received between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rainfall in about a 24-hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/23, falling over ground that was moistened by widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  There was no snow cover prior to this event.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KWVWHITE7) recorded 2.35 inches of rainfall during at 24 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. This was across ground already highly moistened from periods of heavy rain during the 12th & 13th a few days before.  Rainfall rates at times were observed between 0.5 inch per hour to nearly an inch per hour. This amount is only a 1-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates.  Runoff from this location flows into Anthony Creek.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KWVCRAWL8) recorded 2.89 inches of rainfall during at 24 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. This was across ground already highly moistened from periods of heavy rain during the 12th & 13th a few days before. Rainfall rates at times were observed up to 0.5 inch per hour. This amount was between a 2-year and a 5-year event (50%-20% AEP) per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the Meadow River.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KWVCHARM1) recorded 3.44 inches of rainfall during at 25 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. This was across ground already highly moistened from periods of heavy rain during the 12th & 13th a few days before. Rainfall rates at times were observed up to 1.5 inch per hour. This amount was between a 5-year and a 10-year event (20%-10% AEP) per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the Meadow River.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KWVRAINE18) recorded 2.52 inches of rainfall during at 25 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. This was across ground already highly moistened from periods of heavy rain during the 12th & 13th a few days before. Rainfall rates at times were observed up to 0.5 inch per hour. This amount was between a 5-year and a 10-year event (20%-10% AEP) per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into Sewell Creek.

The Meadow River at Hines, WV crested at 14.15 feet (Flood stage is 14 feet).  This was caused by between 2.5 and 3.5 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  Water was observed creeping up to Highway 60 in the Hines and McRoss areas, but it is unknown if the highway was actually closed.

The Bluestone River at Spanishburg, WV (SPNW2) crested at 12.10 feet (Flood stage is 12 feet). This was caused by between 2.5 and 3.5 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior. Water was observed creeping up to Highway 19 in the Spanishburg area, but there were no reports that the highway was actually closed.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KWVBLUEF24) recorded 2.39 inches of rainfall during a little more than 24 hours ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. This was across ground already highly moistened from periods of heavy rain during the 12th & 13th a few days before. Rainfall rates at times were observed up to 0.5 inch per hour. This amount was about a 2-year event (50%-10% AEP) per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the Bluestone River.

Brad Paisley community park was flooded up to the foundation of a pavilion there from water rising out of Wades Creek.  The park is located at the confluence of Wades Creek and Howard Creek.  No damage to the park was reported.

The tunnel under the railroad tracks on Old Bramwell Road was flooded.  One car became stranded in the floodwater trying to drive through the tunnel. Water eventually rose up to the hood of the car.  Flooding was most likely caused due to poor drainage within the tunnel.  The nearby Bluestone River was several feet below flood stage at the onset of flooding within the tunnel.  A nearby personal weather station indicated that rainfall rates since midnight on the 17th never exceeded 0.5 inch per hour with a storm total amount of 1.7 inches, not an unusual event.  The damage estimate is for flooding to the car.

The James River and Kanawha Turnpike was closed due to flooding of small creeks between the communities of Rainelle and Meadow Bluff.  The road was reopened after flooding receded, with no damage reported.

A National Weather Service employee reported signs that Anthony Creek, as well as multiple tributaries of the creek were out of their banks and covering Highway 92 near the community of Neola, WV during the 17th.  No damage was reported, though removal of debris was likely necessary.
Portions of Germany Road were closed due to heavy runoff from prolonged rainfall.  No damage to the road was reported.
Portions of Highway 43 were reported to have standing water on them up to a foot deep.  The road was closed briefly to allow the water to run off.  No damage was reported.

This amount was around a 2-year event (50% AEP) per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the Clinch River.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KVANORTH36) near North Tazewell, VA recorded 1.91 inches of rainfall during at 25 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. The Cooperative Weather Observer at Burkes Garden, VA (BURV2) recorded 1.65 inches or rain during a 2-day period ending at 7 am EST on February 18th.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Burkes Garden reported multiple streams out of their banks during the morning of February 17th due to prolonged rainfall during the 24 hours prior.  Some of the streams were observed flowing across local roads and bridges a few inches deep.  No damage was reported and the streams receded back within their banks by late morning after rainfall ended.

The Clinch River at Richlands, VA (RLRV2) crested at 11.22 feet (Flood stage is 10 feet).  This was caused by between 1.75 and 2.75 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  This caused flooding of several streets in town that typically flood when the river exceeds 10 feet, including along 4th Street, Britts Park Road and Alleghany Avenue near the Richlands Police Station.  Further west, Clinch River Road and Matney Lane were also flooded and impassible.  At least three automobiles were known to be flooded deep enough where water entered the passenger compartment.

The Cowpasture River near Clifton Forge, VA crested at 10.40 feet (Flood stage is 10 feet).  This was a little over a 2-year event (50% AEP) per USGS Streamstats. The flooding was caused by between 1.5 and 2.75 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  Minor lowland flooding was the only impact observed.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground:KVAMILLB8) recorded 1.67 inches of rainfall during at 24 hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/2023. Runoff from this location eventually flows into the Cowpasture River.

This includes about 1.6 inches that fell between 7am and 9am on the 29th, with rainfall rates of up to 2 inches per hour during this time.  Runoff from this location flows into Brush Creek.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KWVPRINC14) recorded a 24-rainfall amount of 3.48 inches. This is about a 10-year (10% AEP) Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. This includes about one inch that fell between 7am and 8am on the 29th, with rainfall rates of up to 1.5 inches per hour during this time.  Runoff from this location flows into Brush Creek.

The ASOS (Automated Surface Observing Station) at the Mercer County Regional Airport (KBLF) recorded a 48-hour rainfall total of 4.45 inches.  This includes a 3-hour total of 1.86 inches that fell between around 530 AM and 830 AM EST, which is between a 5-year (20% AEP) and a 10-year (10% AEP) Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. This is the second highest two-day total of rainfall for this station since September 1959.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Bluefield, WV (BLFW2) observed a 2-day rainfall total of 4.58 inches.  Dating back to December 1998, this is the highest 2-day total in the history of this Cooperative Observer station.

The Bluestone River near Spanishburg, WV (SPNW2), rose above flood stage and crested above 16.51 feet at 3:10 am EST (0810 UTC) on the 30th, which is 1.51 feet above moderate flood stage. This is the 4th-highest documented crest in the history of this gage. Flooding from the river was observed about a foot deep across Highway 19/Beckley Road across the parking lot of the Rich Creek Baptist Church. Water rose up to the foundation of the church itself before receding.  A local resident reported water flooded Highway 7/Gardner Road near the stream gage.

Social media photos showed Highway 19/Beckley Road flooded at least a foot deep by the Bluestone River overflowing its banks.  Portions of Soaring Eagle Lane were also flooded.  Multiple modular homes along Soaring Eagle Lane were surrounded by water by the time the river crested.  Property damage estimates are from the cleanup effort as it is unknown if water actually entered any of the homes or vehicles parked at the homes.

During the event numerous trees and power lines were blown down countywide.  Several road were blocked due to the downed trees. The majority of the damage reports were from the Creston area. Damage values are estimated.

Wind gusts blew a couple of trees down and power lines. Damage values are estimated.

Wind gusts downed four trees in the New Castle area. Winds continued to gust periodically up to 40 mph through the evening hours. Damage values are estimated.
Wind gusts downed a few trees primarily across the eastern portion of the county. Damage values are estimated.

Wind gusts downed tress throughout the county and also several power lines. A tree fell on a residence in West Warm Springs causing minor damage to the structure. Downed trees also blocked a couple of roads for a period of time. Damage values are estimated.

The East River at Willowton, WV (ERVW2), crested at 9.68 feet (3,380 cfs) at 1:00 pm EST (1800 UTC) on the 29th above the flood stage of 9.0 feet.  This is the 9th-highest documented crest of this gage since 2012, and is between a 2-year and a 5-year event (50%-20% Annual Exceedence Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

Among the fallen trees, one fell and destroyed a raptor enclosure at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center which will cost $25,000 to replace. Additionally a power pole and a telephone pole were split in two. Damage values are estimated.

Wind gusts downed trees and power lines throughout the county. Some secondary roads, including Pleasant View Road, were blocked by trees for a period of time.  Periodic wind gusts to over 35 mph were reported into the early morning hours of April 2. Damage values are estimated.

Trees and power lines were downed throughout the county. In the town of Bedford, a tree fell on a house causing damaging. Damage values are estimated.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAFORES48) recorded a 13-rainfall amount of 4.32 inches. This is about a 10-year (10% AEP) Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into Ivy Creek.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAFORES63) recorded a 14-rainfall amount of 4.18 inches. This is about a 10-year (10% AEP) Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Rainfall rates increased to around 1 inch per hour at around 9 AM EDT on the 28th, just as the cold front moved across the area.  Runoff from this location flows into Ivy Creek.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVALYNCH121) recorded a 14-rainfall amount of 3.80 inches. This is about a 10-year (10% AEP) Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Rainfall rates increased to around 2 inches per hour shortly after 9 AM EDT on the 28th, just as the cold front moved across the area.  Runoff from this location flows into Ivy Creek.

Ivy Creek in the western part of the City of Lynchburg was observed overflowing its banks due to 3.5 to nearly 4.5 inches of rainfall across nearly the entire basin within a 14 hour period. The flooded creek caused only minor damage to Peaks View Park, mainly in the form of cleanup of mud and small debris.  The property damage estimate reflects the estimated cost of cleanup for the park.

Stoney Ridge Road was flooded over one foot deep by flowing water due to an unknown-named creek having risen out of its banks.  No damage to the road was reported and it was reopened after the flooding receded.

Highway 71, from near the Rock Post Office to near Rock River Road, was flooded and impassible due to the Bluestone River rising out of its banks across the road.  No damage aside from cleanup of the debris was observed, and the road was reopened after the flooding receded.

The East River flooded out of its banks across Country Girl Road.  At some point, two vehicles became stranded in the flood waters, and the vehicles required towing after the flooding receded.  It is unclear in the occupants of the vehicles required any form of rescue from emergency personnel.  The property damage is the estimated damage to both of the vehicles.

Lorton Lick Creek rose out of its banks due to heavy rainfall and flooded across multiple roads, including portions of Lorton Lick Road.  One vehicle was stranded in the flood waters and required towing after the flooding receded.  The property damage is the estimated cost of damage to the vehicle.

A social media photo showed the Midway Tunnel at least eight feet deep as an unknown-named tributary running parallel to the railroad tracks above the tunnel overflowed its banks.  No damage was reported, and the tunnel was allowed to reopen after the flooding receded.

The WVVA-TV webpage showed standing water around two feet deep within a low spot on Bland Street.  A car was stranded in the flood water, and it appears that the flood water was high enough to enter at least one business there.  Property damage includes estimates for damage to the flooded vehicle and for the business.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Burkes Garden, VA (BURV2) recorded a 48-rainfall amount of 2.84 inches. This is between a 1-year and a 2-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into Wolf Creek.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVABENTM19) recorded a 24-rainfall amount of 4.46 inches. This is between a 5-year and a 10-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into the South Fork Roanoke River.

The South Fork Roanoke River near Shawsville, VA (SHAV2), crested at 5.64 feet (3,240 cfs) at 12:25 pm EST (1725 UTC) on the 29th above the flood stage of 5.0 feet. This event is between a 2-year and a 5-year event (50%-20% Annual Exceedence Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  Mainly only minor overbank flooding of properties along the river is observed at this stage, and no damage was observed or reported.

Walker Creek at Bane, VA (BANV2), crested at 13.84 feet (13,100 cfs) at 17:15 pm EST on the 29th (0015 UTC on the 30th) above the flood stage of 11.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 3 and 4 inches of rain covering a large area of the headwaters, most of which fell between noon EDT on the 28th and noon EDT on the 29th.  This is the 15th-highest documented crest of this gage, and the highest since May 2020. This event is a 10-year event (10% Annual Exceedence Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVABLAND12) recorded a storm-total rainfall amount of 4.04 inches during about 26 hours ending at noon EST on the 29th. This is around a 10-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Runoff from this location flows into Walker Creek.

Heavy rain caused Laurel Creek to flood out of its banks and enter two homes on Laurel Fork Road.  Portions of the road were also flooded and impassible.  The property damage is the damage estimate of flooding inside the homes.  No injuries were reported.

Wolf Creek at Narrows, VA (WOLV2), crested at 11.71 feet (9,650 cfs) at 13:30 pm EST on the 29th (1830 UTC) above the flood stage of 10.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 2.5 and locally 4 inches of rain covering a large area of the headwaters, most of which fell between noon EDT on the 28th and noon EDT on the 29th.  This is the 11th-highest documented crest of this gage, and the highest since February 2020. This event is nearly a 10-year event (10% Annual Exceedence Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVANARRO21) recorded a storm-total rainfall amount of 3.32 inches during 24 hours ending at 11 am EST on the 29th. The Bluestone River at Falls Mills, VA (BRVV2), crested at 10.96 feet at 11:15 am EST on the 29th above the flood stage of 7.0 feet, and just below the major flood stage of 11.0 feet.  This is the new flood-of-record for this gage, exceeding the previous record of 8.66 feet established in January 1996 by 2.3 feet.  The flooding was the result of between 3.5 and nearly 5.5 inches of rain covering a large area of the headwaters, most of which fell between noon EDT on the 28th and noon EDT on the 29th.  This event is a 10-year event (10% Annual Exceedence Probability) per USGS StreamStats.
A debris flow occurred along Chicory Road, making the road impassible until the debris was cleared.  Property damage is the estimated cost of the cleanup detail.

Back-water flooding of the Bluestone River up Lorton Lick Creek resulted in flooding of Lorton Lick Road.  An automobile trying to drive along the flooded road became stranded in the flood water.  The occupants had to abandon the vehicle.  Property damage is the estimate to repair the vehicle.

The Mercer County Sheriff's Department received multiple reports of flash flooding in the Bluewell Community due to 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rain falling between 5 AM and 7 AM EST, on top of 1.5 to 2.25 inches that had fallen since the evening of the 28th.  Multiple water rescues occurred as several creeks rose out of their banks and either surrounded or entered homes.  This includes a home along Lorton Lick Road that was flooded by Lorton Lick Creek, requiring the rescue of six occupants.  Another home was flooded along Ellen Avenue, requiring the rescue of another six people.  Several homes were flooded along Pinnacle Lake Road as Lick Branch rapidly overflowed its banks.  In addition, flood waters caused a portion of Warden Avenue to collapse, making the road impassible.

The Mercer County Sheriff's Office received numerous reports of flash flooding across the City of Bluefield WV due to 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rain falling between 5 AM and 7 AM EDT, on top of 1.5 to 2.25 inches that had fallen since the evening of the 28th.  The most concentrated number of reports occurred near the intersection of Bland Street and College Avenue, where 2 inches of rainfall occurred in one hour.  Both Bland Street and College Avenue were flooded by over a foot of rushing water in places.  At least one vehicle was stranded in the flood waters, with three occupants requiring help by a swift water rescue team.  Several basements in the area were also flooded by several feet of water, including in homes on Bland Street, Union Street, Jefferson Street and College Avenue.  Portions of Lynn Street and Walters Avenue were flooded and impassible until the water receded.  One swift water rescue was required for the occupant of a vehicle that became stranded by flooding along Grassy Branch Road as Grassy Branch rose out of its banks over a foot deep across the road.  Another swift water rescue occurred when a vehicle traveling on Airport Road became stranded in flood waters when a tributary of Brush Creek rose out of its banks over a foot deep.

A debris flow was observed along Mt. Horeb Road due to several hours of moderate to heavy rainfall.  The road was blocked by the debris and was reopened after the debris was cleared.  The property damage is the estimate for removing the debris.
Runoff from heavy rain caused a portion of Ada Number 29 Road to collapse, making the road impassible.

The North Fork of Brush Creek flooded out of its banks and was flowing across Ceres Road over a foot deep.  Two automobiles became stranded while attempting to pass through the flood waters and were required to be towed after flooding receded.

The East River rapidly flooded out of its banks, and began to enter homes along Ingleside Road.  A swift water rescue team was required to evacuate the residents of one of these homes by boat.  No injuries were reported.  Property damage is the estimated cost of damage to the home caused by the flooding.
Heavy runoff from rainfall flowing down a hillside caused the back wall of a building to collapse.  No injuries were reported.
School Board road was closed due to standing water across the road.  This is a road that is prone to flooding due to poor drainage during periods of heavy rain.

The Town of Narrows Police Department reported that the New River at Narrows had risen high enough to surround modular homes and vehicles parked closed to the river at the RV park off of Highway 460.  It was not clear if water entered any of the homes or rose high enough to cause any damage.
Burks Fork was flooded out of its banks and observed flowing over Weddle Road, making the road impassible.  The road was reopened after the flooding receded, and no damage was reported to the road.

Heather Street and Angel Lane were both flooded due to combination of flooding of the Bluestone River and Brush Creek.  Multiple homes along Angel Lane had at least 1 to 2 feet of water flood inside of them, forcing the resident to evacuate.  Property damage is the estimated flood damage to the homes.  No injuries were reported.

Several portions of Falls Mills Road were flooded and impassible due to the Bluestone River rising out of its banks onto the roadway.  No damage was reported to the road, and the road was reopened after the flooding receded.  The flooded road caused local residents to be stranded on their properties.  At least on home along the road was evacuated by a swift water rescue team as a precaution due to a resident being concerned that flooding would enter their home.

Heavy rain caused Beaverpond Creek to flood out of its banks at multiple locations.  Water was observed flowing up to the top of the bridge at Stockton Street, with water entering multiple homes several inches deep on Skyline Drive.  Further downstream, multiple images on social media indicate Beaverpond Creek flooding out of its banks and into businesses along both S. College Avenue and Walnut Street.

Discharge measurements are not performed at this location and no rating table is available.

Extensive flooding was observed along the Ararat River in the town of Mt. Airy, NC on the morning of the 28th due to 6 to locally 10 inches or rainfall across the headwaters in Patrick County during the predawn hours of the day.  Among the observed impacts of this river flooding, the bridge along White Sulphur Springs Road over the Ararat River was impassible for several hours.  Further downstream, water from the river spread out to cover Riverside Drive and E. Oak Street, with nearly all of Riverside Park completely flooded.  A gas station at the corner of E. Pine Street and Riverside Drive was surrounded by flood waters, though water did not enter the building.  On the south end of town, Hamburg Street was flooded up to a foot deep over the road.  Property damage is the estimated cleanup cost of the flooding, as well as any minor damage the flooding caused.

The first sign of wind damage from this storm were multiple trees blown down just east of the Jumping Branch areas along Highway 3. Additionally, along Highway 3 just southwest of Hinton, numerous hardwood trees were snapped or uprooted by the force of the wind, estimated to be up to 100 mph. One home sustained damage to both the roof and the siding in this area. Additional damage was observed along Highway 20 just to the north, where dozens of trees were blown down by estimated 105 mph wind gusts. The storm continued east, snapping or uprooting numerous trees and downing power poles from the community of Bellpoint eastbound along Highway 3 following the Greenbrier River with 100 to 105 mph wind gusts, including multiple trees blown down near the intersection of Highway 3 and Highway 12. Shortly afterward, the storm began to weaken, though still produced significant damage to dozens of trees along Judson Road near the community of Talcott with estimated 70 to 75 mph wind gusts.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for the northern half of Bath County in October after another month of precipitation that was less than 25 percent of normal. The Cooperative Weather Observer at Hot Springs (HSPV2) measured 0.70 inch of precipitation for the month, about 22 percent of the normal amount of 3.14 inches. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 2nd and 10th percentiles by the middle of the month, and deteriorating. Streamflows for the Bullpasture River and Back Creek were observed below the 10th percentiles by the end of the month per the USGS WaterWatch website. There were no reported impacts to agriculture and livestock given the late time of the year.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for the western half of Amherst County in October after another month of precipitation that was less than 30 percent of normal. The Cooperative Weather Observer at the Pedlar Reservoir Dam (PDLV2) measured 1.03 inches of rainfall for the month, about 29 percent of the normal amount of 3.50 inches. Farther east, the CoCoRaHS observer at Amherst 1.7 SW (VA-AH-4) observed a rainfall total of 1.05 inches for the month. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil between the 5th and the 20th percentiles by the middle of the month. Streamflows for several rivers including the Pedlar River and the James River were below the 10th percentiles by the end of the month per the USGS WaterWatch website. There were no reported impacts to agriculture and livestock given the late time of the year.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for most of Rockbridge County in October after another month of precipitation that was significantly below normal. The Cooperative Weather Observer at the Buena Vista (BUVV2) measured 1.01 inches of rainfall for the month, about 31 percent of the normal amount of 3.28 inches. Nearby, the Cooperative Weather Observer at the Lexington (LXGV2) measured 1.49 inches of rainfall for the month, about half of the normal amount of 3.06 inches. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil between the 2nd and the 5th percentiles by the middle of the month. Streamflows for several rivers including the Maury River and the Calfpasture River were below the 10th percentiles by the end of the month per the USGS WaterWatch website. There were multiple reports from within the county of ranchers that had to supplement hay to their livestock because of the lack of available pasture grass.

The Dan River at Danville, VA (DVLV2) crested at a stage of 22.93 feet (32,200 cfs) at 3:15 am EST on 1/11/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 21.0 feet. This is the 14th highest crest at this gage location since October 1995, and is a 10-year ARI (10% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  No damage was reported.

The Dan River at South Boston, VA (SBNV2) crested at a stage of 26.89 feet (33,200 cfs) at 7:15 am EST on 1/12/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 22.0 feet. This is the 31st highest crest at this gage, and is the highest crest since 11/15/2020.  This event is between a 2-year and a 5-year ARI (50%-20% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  Imagery from an unmanned aircraft system taken around 9:00 am, during the time of the crest, indicated that Highway 501 (Main St.) was flooded from just south of the Main Street bridge over the Dan River to within 300 feet of Highway 58/360.

The Dan River at Paces, VA (PCEV2) crested at a stage of 24.78 feet (34,100 cfs) at 7:45 pm EST on 1/11/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 22.0 feet. This is the 27th highest crest at this gage, and the highest crest since 11/14/2020. This event is a 10-year ARI (10% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.

The Dan River at Pine Hall, NC (PNHN7) crested at a stage of 24.60 feet (18,600 cfs) at 3:30 am EST on 1/10/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 23.0 feet. This is the 6th highest crest at this gage and the highest crest since 11/13/2020.  This event is around a  5-year ARI (20% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.

The Slate River near Arvonia, VA (ARVV2) crested at a stage of 13.97 feet (6,770 cfs) at 12:15 am EST on 1/10/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 12.0 feet. This is the 21st highest crest at this gage, and the highest crest since 11/13/2020. This event is between a 2-year and a 5-year ARI (50%-20% AEP) per USGS StreamStats. Flooding of low-lying fields typically occurs at this stage, however this is not impactful during the cool season, with no fields in active growth.  No damage was reported during this event.

Three trees were blown down within the county. Of these three trees, one was reported to have specifically came down near the intersection of Foggy Mountain Road and the Blue Ridge Parkway. Damage values are estimated.
Winds periodically exceeded 58 mph from the early morning hours through midday, especially near the communities of Aho and Meat Camp.
High winds blew two trees down near Hillsville. Damage values are estimated.

In and around the City of Roanoke, high winds brought a tree down on Bent Mountain Road, blocking both lanes, wires down on Ivywood Drive, and wires down over the roadway at the intersection of Bowman Street and Williamson Road. Damage values are estimated.

Lightning struck a home on Surfside Drive near Smith Mountain Lake. The bolt struck the roof and set fire to the attic. The Moneta Fire Department was able to extinguish the blaze, confining its spread to only a portion of the attic.

The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 7.11 feet at 1:00 pm EST on December 26th due to prolonged moderate to heavy rainfall. This is the 20th-highest crest in the history of this gage, and is the highest crest since June 2019. This crest (3,290 cfs) ranks less than a 2-year event per USGS StreamStats.  No damage was reported with this event.

Severe Drought conditions already in place for all of Alleghany County at the beginning of the month, persisted until December 12th, when two low pressure systems passing across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the week of December 3rd to the 10th brought rainfall amounts ranging from 2.00 to 2.25 inches to the county. This precipitation resulted in a significant increase in soil moisture, surface stream flows, and ground water levels sufficient to allow drought conditions to be improved to Moderate Drought per the U.S. Drought Monitor.  The precipitation moistened leaf litter and other fuels that support wildland fire activity, and a noted decrease in wildfires after these precipitation events was noted by the North Carolina Department of Forestry.  Additional rainfall in excess of four inches in spots resulted in removal of drought for nearly all of the county, with improvement to Abnormally Dry conditions through the remainder of the month.  There was no reported impacts to agriculture in December, with some farmers reporting that the lack of soggy ground make work in the fields easier to accomplish.

These systems brought rainfall amounts ranging from 2 to 2.5 inches, resulting in an increase in soil moisture, surface stream flows, and ground water levels sufficient to allow drought conditions for most of the county to be improved to Moderate Drought per the U.S. Drought Monitor. No additional changes occurred during the remainder of the month. The precipitation moistened leaf litter and other fuels that support wildland fire activity. There was no reported impacts to agriculture in December, with some farmers reporting that the lack of soggy ground make work in the fields easier to accomplish.

The Yadkin River at Elkin, NC (ELKN7) crested at 21.09 feet (23,400 cfs) above the moderate flood stage of 21 feet at 9 pm EST on the 9th (10/0200 UTC). The flooding was the result of between three and four inches of rain covering a large area of the headwaters, most of which fell between 2 am and 4 pm EST on the 9th. This crest is tied for the 10th-highest documented crest of this gage, and the highest since November 12, 2020. This event is between a 10-year event and a 25-year event (10%-25% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats. Backwater flooding was observed along Big Elkin Creek, flooding Memorial Park Drive, as well as the athletic fields of Elkin Municipal Park.  Portions of Crater Park were also flooded as the river came out of its banks.  Property damage is the estimated clean up and debris removal from the flooding.

The Yadkin River at Wilkesboro, NC (WKSN7), crested at 14.12 feet (11,500 cfs) at 5 pm EST on the 9th (09/2200 UTC) above the minor flood stage of 14.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between three and four inches of rain covering a large area of the headwaters, most of which fell between 2 am and 4 pm EST on the 9th. This is the 22nd-highest documented crest of this gage, and the highest since October 29, 2020. This event is less than a 2-year event (50% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats. Portions of Wilkesboro Avenue in front of Midtown Plaza were flooded, as well as some of the businesses along the south side of that portion of Wilkesboro Avenue.  Police blocked Wilkesboro Avenue from where it intersects with Wilkesboro Boulevard near the Yadkin River bridge to the intersection with Ninth Street.

The Watauga River near Sugar Grove, NC (SGWN7), crested at 10.81 feet (6,570 cfs) at 4 pm EST on the 9th above the flood stage of 6.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 3.5 and locally 4.5 inches of rain falling across the headwaters, most of which fell between 2 am and 3 pm EST on the 9th. This is the highest since 13.01 feet occurred in November 2022. This event is a little over a 2-year event (50% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  Portions of Watauga River road become flooded at this stage, but no damage was reported.

The Smith River at Eden, NC (EDSN7) crested at a stage of 12.72 feet (15,300 cfs) at 2 am EST on 1/10/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 12.0 feet. This is the 18th highest crest at this gage and the highest crest since 11/12/2020. This event is around a 2-year ARI (50% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  No damage was reported in this event.

The Mayo River near Price, NC (PRIN7) crested at a stage of 9.95 feet (10,300 cfs) at 21:00 EST on 1/9/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 8.0 feet. The Dan River at Wentworth, NC (WENN7) crested somewhere near a stage of 24.84 feet (28,800 cfs) at around 11:15 am EST on 1/10/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 19.0 feet. The gage experienced a equipment failure during the flooding event, so the stage heights were estimated by the USGS based on a crest gage. This is likely the highest crest since 11/13/2020, and would be close to a 10-year ARI (10% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  At this stage, both Dan River Road and River Road nearby the gage would become partially flooded and impassible.

The Ararat River at Ararat, NC (ARRN7) crested at a stage of 15.00 feet (12,200 cfs) at 7 pm EST on 1/9/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 13.0 feet. Portions of Radar Road just upstream from the gage were affected by flooding, but no damage was reported after the water receded.

The Ararat River at Mt. Airy, NC (ARLN7) crested at a stage of 20.92 feet, rising above the minor flood stage of 20.5 feet. No damage was reported during this event.

The Big Otter River near Evington, VA (EVGV2) crested at a stage of 19.47 feet (11,200 cfs) at 12:00 am EST on 1/10/24, above the minor flood stage of 19.0 feet. This is the 25th highest crest at this gage, and the highest crest since 11/12/2020. This event is between a 2-year and a 5-year ARI (50%-20% AEP) per USGS StreamStats. Minor lowland flooding is typically observed at this stage, however no damage was reported during this event.

Up to 1.75 inches of rainfall occurring over a roughly 10-hour period caused Strawberry Creek to overflow its banks and flow across Country Road.  No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the flooding receded.

After around 1.75 inches of rain had fallen over a roughly 10 hour period, a line of heavy rainfall, producing rates of 1.5 inches per hour, passed across Pittsylvania County, bringing a half inch to three quarters of rain over a short period of time. This resulted in numerous instances of flash flooding throughout the county.  Runoff from this rain caused Green Rock Branch to overflow its banks at least six inches deep across Concord Road.  Motleys Mill Road washed out near the intersection with Halifax Road, causing an estimated 50 thousand dollars worth of damage.  Halifax Road was also observed flooded.  Sycamore Creek was observed overflowing its banks several inches deep across Country Club Road.  Extensive damage occurred near the intersection of Walkers Well Road and Toshes Road, with three layers of the road surface washed away, causing an estimated 25 thousand dollars of damage.  Long Branch Creek was observed overflowing its banks several inches deep across Player Road, leaving a large amount of debris on the roadway.  Fall Creek rose several inches out of its banks, flooding the southbound lane of N. Main Street near Fall Creek Drive.  Cascade Creek was observed out of its banks several inches deep over Cobbs Knob Road.  Pudding Creek was observed overflowing its banks across Johnson Road, and across the Jones Mill Road bridge.  White Ridge Road was submerged several inches deep as Barker Creek overflowed its banks.  Cedar Creek was observed overflowing its banks at least several inches deep Graves Bridge Road.  Little Bearskin Creek was reported out of its banks several inches deep over Hollywood Road.  Anderson Mill Road was completely washed out and impassible near the intersection with Old Red Eye Road, causing an estimated 50 thousand dollars worth of damage.  Both Countryside Drive and Hillside Drive was observed with several inches of water flowing across the roadway surface.  Shawnee Road was observed flooded several inches deep between Sandy Bottom Road and Camp Shawnee Road.  Green Rock Branch was observed flowing well outside of its banks.  Both Berry Hill Road and Stateline Bridge Road were observed flooded several inches deep by flowing water.  Fall Creek Road was observed flooded by nearby Cane Creek overflowing its banks.  The 1000 block of Terry Road was reported flooded.  The 2000 block of Irish Road was reported flooded and impassible.  Strawberry Road was flooded and closed as the Banister River rose out of its banks.
A home owner on Cherry Lane reported that runoff from prolonged rainfall caused minor basement flooding.
Wolf Creek was reported out of its banks, flooding both Morehead Road and Trivett Farm Lane.  Both roads were impassible until flood waters receded.  No damage was reported.
Poor drainage caused a parking lot to flood, requiring several cars to be moved to avoid being flooded.  No damage was reported.
Poor drainage resulted in flooding near the intersection of Bobwhite Road and Partridge Creek Road.  No damage was reported and the roads were open to traffic after the flooding receded.
Shooting Creek was observed out of its banks due to heavy runoff from prolonged rainfall, washing out Shooting Creek Road, making the road impassible.

After around 1.75 inches of rain had fallen over a roughly 10 hour period, a line of heavy rainfall, producing rates of 1.5 inches per hour, passed across Campbell County, bringing a half inch to three quarters of rain over a short period of time. Red House Road was observed completely flooded several inches deep as Jacobs Creek overflowed its banks.  Sunnymeade Road was completely flooded several inches deep near the intersection with Candlers Mountain Road.
A clogged drain caused runoff from prolonged rainfall to flow inside a building.
A creek (name unknown) overflowed its banks and partially washed out a bridge on Rockwood Park Drive.

Runoff due to poor drainage from prolonged rainfall resulted in flooding near the 5600 block of Highway 220 near Dyer Street.  No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the flooding receded.

A vehicle stalled and became stranded in the Midway Tunnel after runoff from nearly two inches of rain falling over a 10 to 11 hour period accumulated several feet deep inside the tunnel.  This is a tunnel that floods periodically during times of heavy rainfall due to poor drainage.

Runoff from prolonged rainfall and poor drainage caused several inches of standing water to pool at the intersection of U.S. Highway 19 and Highway 52.  No damage was reported and the intersection was open to traffic after the water receded.

The Harts Run Tunnel under the railroad tracks on Harts Run Road was flooded and impassable for a few hours due to runoff from prolonged rainfall collecting in the tunnel.  No damage was reported and the tunnel was open to traffic after the flooding receded.
The Route 63/Monroe Draft tunnel under the railroad was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rain.  The tunnel was open to traffic after the water receded.  No damage was reported.

Tuckahoe Road at the railroad tunnel was flooded and impassible due to runoff from prolonged rainfall caused Dry Creek to flood out of its banks into the tunnel.  No damage was reported, and the tunnel was open to traffic after the water receded.

A portion of Anthony Creek Trail at Blue Bend Loop Trail was flooded due to nearby Anthony Creek rising out of its banks.  No damage was reported, and the road was open to traffic after the water receded.
Runoff from the passage of a band of moderate to locally heavy rainfall resulted in water entering the basement of a home.

Runoff from the passage of a band of heavy rainfall resulted in Chalk Level Road becoming flooded by several inches of water.  No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the water receded.

This is the second crest above flood stage during the month. This event is less than a 2-year ARI (>50% AEP) per USGS StreamStats. At this stage, water covered portions of Highway 501 (Main Street).

The Dan River at Wentworth, NC (WENN7) crested somewhere near a stage of 20.51 feet (18,600 cfs) at 5:00 pm EST on 1/10/24, rising above the minor flood stage of 19.0 feet. This is the second crest above flood stage at this gage during January 2024, and was around a 2-year ARI (50% AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  No damage was reported.

The Watauga River near Sugar Grove, NC (SGWN7), crested at 7.50 feet (3,620 cfs) at 8:30 pm EST on the 11th. Flood stage is 6.0 feet. This event is well-under a 2-year event (50% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  No damage was reported during this event.

Runoff from the rainfall caused flooding across multiple roads along Highway 67 between the communities of East Bend and Jonesville.  In the area surrounding the community of East Bend, Chestnut Street was flooded and impassible due to heavy runoff.  Logan Creek was observed flooding out of its banks across Mill Hill Road, causing serious damage to the road that required repairs.  Genie Road was also flooded from Logan Creek.  Further west, Highway 601 was flooded and impassible near the community of Booneville.

A YouTube video captured by storm chasers depicts multiple roads flooded by at least six inches of flowing water in the town of West Jefferson, including N. Jefferson Avenue, and W. Main Street. The Cooperative Weather Observer at Jefferson 2 E, NC (JFFN7) measured a 1-day total of 3.90 inches of rainfall, the result of thunderstorms training across the area. Radar indicates that much of the rain fell within about a 1-hour period, though multiple rounds of rain passed across the station.  This is the 3rd highest 1-day total occurring during the month of May for this station, but still does not rank in the top 30 1-day totals for JFFN7.

Trout Run Road was flooded and impassible due to Trout Run overflowing its banks several inches deep across the road.  A slow-moving thunderstorm produced between 2.5 and 3.5 inches of rainfall within most of the Trout Run watershed during a 60 to 75 minute period, or in excess of a 100-year Average Recurrence Interval for a 1-hour duration per MRMS FLASH.  The 1-hour QPE to FFG ratio was close to a 3, or nearly 3 times the 1-hour rainfall needed to produce flash flooding.  CREST Unit Streamflow indicated flows in the upper part of the basin reaching around 700 cfs/mi^2, a strong indicator of flash flooding.

The railroad tunnel on Route 63 was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rainfall flooding the creek that shares the tunnel with the road.  One water rescue was required for a vehicle stranded in the tunnel.
The Harts Run Tunnel under the railroad on Route 60 was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rainfall flooding Harts Run that shares the tunnel with the road.
The railroad tunnel on Tuckahoe Road was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rainfall flooding Dry Creek that shares the tunnel with the road.

Localized flooding occurred in the 700 block of Lee Highway given a poor drainage issue, possibly a partially blocked culvert.  The road was passable to traffic after the high water receded.  No damage was reported.

Portions of Summit Drive and Berry Hill Road were flooded and impassible due to Poplar Creek overflowing its banks across the roadways.  No damage was reported, and the roads were reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVASOUTH79) recorded a 8-hour rainfall amount of 3.96 inches. This rainfall amount has a 10-year to 25-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates at the six hour duration. Rainfall rates were measured to be as high as 1.5 inches per hour at times.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at South Boston (SOBV2) recorded a daily rainfall total of 3.89 inches, most of which fell during an 8-hour period on the afternoon and evening of the 14th.  This is the 2nd-highest daily rainfall total for the month of May at this station, and 12-highest daily total for any month, with records dating back to August 1971.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for far eastern Rockbridge County in late June after the previous 30 days of precipitation were between 1 and 2 inches, or between 20 and 30 percent of normal.  NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 5th and 20th percentiles by the end of the month, and deteriorating. Streamflows across the county, including in the Calfpasture, Maury and South Rivers, were observed below the 10th percentiles by the end of the month per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production was quickly becoming impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county.  Hay production was also becoming heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for much of Amherst County on June 25th after the previous 30 days of precipitation were observed to be between 1 and 1.5 inches, or between 20 and 30 percent of normal. The Cooperative Weather Observer at the Pedlar Reservoir Dam (PDLV2) measured 0.97 inches of rainfall in the 30 days leading up to the 25th, at which time water in the Pedlar Reservoir had fallen to 10 inches below the top of the dam's spillway.  NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 10th and 20th percentiles by the 25th, and deteriorating, while streamflows across the county were observed below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production was quickly becoming impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also becoming heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for the eastern half of Bedford County on June 25th after the previous 30 days of precipitation were observed to be between 0.75 and 1.50 inches with locally higher amounts, or between 20 and 40 percent of normal. The CoCoRaHS observer at Bedford 2.5 ENE (VA-BD-38) on the western fringe of the area identified as under severe drought observed a rainfall total of 1.80 inches for the 30-day period. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 5th and 20th percentiles by the 25th, and deteriorating, while streamflows across the eastern half of the county, including in Goose Creek near Huddleston, were observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production was quickly becoming impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also becoming heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for the western half of Campbell County and the City of Lynchburg on June 25th. The previous 30 days of precipitation were variable due to hit-and-miss thunderstorm activity, with totals ranging from 0.05 at the Lynchburg Regional Airport around 2 inches elsewhere near Lynchburg and across Campbell County.  These totals range anywhere from less than 5 percent to as high as 45 percent of normal. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 10th and 20th percentiles by the 25th, and deteriorating, while streamflows across the western half of the county, including in the Big Otter River near Evington, were observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production was quickly becoming impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also becoming heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Hail up to the size of baseballs dented vehicle roofs and hoods, and smashed windshields. The hail accumulated to a depth of one inch. The town of Beech Mountain experienced an estimated $10,000 worth of hail damage just to city vehicles and property.

Severe Drought conditions were declared for Bath County during the early half of July after another month of precipitation that was less than 30 to 70 percent of normal. The Cooperative Weather Observer at Hot Springs (HSPV2) measured 2.92 inches of rainfall for the preious 30-day period ending July 9th, about 68 percent of the normal amount of 4.31 inches for June. However, much of this rainfall occurred mainly during 2 thunderstorms events, much of the rainfall of which ran off as opposed to being absorbed by the soil. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 2nd and 10th percentiles by the middle of July, and was deteriorating. Streamflows for the Bullpasture River and Back Creek were observed below the 10th percentiles by mid-July per the USGS WaterWatch website.

Severe Drought conditions spread west during the early half of July, eventually including all of Rockbridge County by July 16th. On July 16th, the previous 30 days of precipitation were observed to be between 1.00 and 1.50 inches with locally higher amounts, or between 20 and 35 percent of normal for that period. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil had fallen to the 2nd percentile. Streamflows, including for the Maury River and Kerrs Creek, were observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. Crop production continued to be heavily impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Severe Drought conditions spread to include all of Amherst County on July 2nd after the previous 30 days of precipitation were observed to be between 0.50 and 1.50 inches with locally higher amounts, or between 20 and 30 percent of normal. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 10th and 20th percentiles by the 2nd, and was continuing to deteriorate, while streamflows across the eastern half of the county, including in the Pedlar River near Buena Vista, were observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production continued to be heavily impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also heavily impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth.

Severe Drought conditions spread to include all of Bedford County on July 2nd after the previous 30 days of precipitation were observed to be between 0.50 and 1.50 inches with locally higher amounts, or generally less than 25 percent of normal. The CoCoRaHS observer at Bedford 2.5 ENE (VA-BD-38) observed a rainfall total of 1.29 inches for the 30-day period, while the CoCoRaHS observer at Montvale 0.4 N observed a 30-day total of 0.88 inches. NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated that average soil moisture in the top 100 cm of soil was between the 5th and 20th percentiles by July 2nd, and deteriorating, while streamflows across the eastern half of the county, including in Goose Creek near Huddleston, were observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website. Crop production continued to be impacted by the dry conditions, with stunted growth of most corn across the county. Hay production was also increasingly impacted, with grasses in many pastures becoming dormant due the combination of dryness and abnormally high warmth. Improvements in drought conditions to D1: Moderate Drought were noted for most of the county by the end of July as a stalled front provided the focus for daily showers and thunderstorms.
