Chestnut Creek at Galax (CCKV2) crested at 11.46 feet (6,230 cfs) at 1915 UTC/3:15 EDT on Sept. 27th due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Storm Helene.  This is the third highest crest in the history of this gage, and the highest crest since November 2003. This crest rates between a 10-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI)(0.1 Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP)) and a 25-year ARI (0.04 AEP) per USGS StreamStats.  The flooding was the result of between 8 and 11 inches of rain that fell across the Chestnut Creek basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 500-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  Extensive flooding occurred in the northern end of the City of Galax, where homes and businesses along Meadow Street and Givens Street were flooded with up to 2 feet of water on the right bank-side of the river.  On the left bank-side, flooding from the creek entered a large industrial building between Highway 58 and Webster Street.  Drone imagery indicated that the Grayson Street bridge over the creek was inundated by several inches of water. Further upstream, Chestnut Creek flooded across Coal Creek Road from near the intersection with Pipers Gap Road to the 300 block of Coal Creek Road.  This stranded multiple residents that have to cross the creek to leave their properties.

The Little River at Peach Bottom (LPBV2) crested at 22.45 feet at 1815 UTC/2:15 EDT on Sept. 27th due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Storm Helene. This stage-only gage was installed by the Virginia Dept. of Emergency Management during spring of 2024, so had no previously-documented flood crests to compare this event with. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 16 inches of rain that fell across the Little River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Downstream of the gage, much of Little River Road on the left bank was inundated up to four feet deep from flooding of the river. Multiple properties on the right bank had water inundation, but unclear as to how much. Several trees were bent over or snapped due to the force of the water. At the gage on Old Baywood Road, a large pile of debris was lodged against the bridge over the river. Part of the road at the intersection of Little River Road and Old Baywood Road was sunken and nearly washed out, but remained passable to traffic. The width of flowing water during the peak of the flood event was estimated to be over 400 feet wide across Baywood Road based on high water marks. Further upstream, at least three camper homes were flooded along River Bottom Lane near the intersection with Cold Springs Lane. The flooding washed out a roughly 200-foot length of River Place, stranding several residents that used the drive to enter or leave their homes. No homes on River Place experienced flooding, however anything between the road and the river was flooded during the event.

The New River near Galax (GAXV2) crested at 21.26 feet (108,000 cfs) at 10:15 PM EDT on Sept. 27th (28/0215 UTC) due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene. This is the second highest crest in the history of this gage, only behind the flooding event of August 1940. This crest rates between a 100-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI)(1% Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP)) and a 200-year ARI (0.5% AEP) per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 20 inches of rain that fell across the upper New River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Extensive flooding occurred along several roads along the banks of the river, including Grinders Mill Road, Riverview Lane, Riverside Drive, Pleasant Grove Road, Little River Road, Old River Lane, Riverwood Lane, Pattons Mill Lane, Greenville Road, and Gold Hill Road. In some cases, the roads were simply flooded, cutting off access to residents living along the roads. Some of the homes had water enter the properties, destroying and/or carrying away personal equipment and buildings.

The South Fork Holston River at Riverside near Chilhowie (SHLV2) crested at 10.87 feet at 20:00 UTC/4:15 PM EDT on Sept. 27th due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene.  This is a new Flood-of-Record for this gage, with records dating back to October 1920.  The discharge of 11,300 cfs for 10.87 feet was estimated through extrapolation as this stage is above the rating curve.  This discharge would be greater than a 500-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or a 0.2% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 16 inches of rain that fell in multiple rounds across the basin between the 25th and 27th, with 3-day totals across most of the upper basin exceeding an 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

The New River near Ivanhoe (IVNV2) crested at 33.08 feet (119,940 cfs) at 8:45 PM EDT on Sept. 27th (28/0045 UTC) due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene. This is the third highest crest in the history of this gage, behind the flooding events of August 1940 (1st at 38.10 ft) and July 1916 (2nd at 34.80 ft). This crest rates around a 200-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or a 0.5% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 20 inches of rain that fell across the upper New River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. Extensive flooding occurred along Sandy River Drive, where water rose up to the bases of several homes, with water intrusion into a few.  Numerous sheds and outbuildings closer to the river were severely damaged or swept away by the flooding.  Multiple camper homes just upstream were inundated. Flooding rose up to the base of the bridge crossing the New River on Store Hill Road downstream of the gage. Multiple homes and outbuildings were flooded along Powerline Road and Mill Bank Lane.  A portion of Rose Road was flooded and impassible.

The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) crested at 21.91 feet (166,945 cfs) at 11:15 PM EDT on Sept. 27th (28/0315 UTC) due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene.  It was observed that the gage flatlined at this stage for about 3 hours, so it's possible that the crest was closer to or rose above 22 feet.  This is the second highest crest in the history of this gage, behind the flooding event of August 1940 (23.42 ft).  This crest rates just above a 200-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or a 0.5% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 20 inches of rain that fell across the upper New River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  Extensive flooding occurred along Clarks Ferry Road and Julia Simpkins Road in Allisonia, Shulls Lane and Ledge Rock Road in the Draper area, Parrott River Road in Parrott and Hazel Hollow Road in Fairlawn, where numerous homes were inundated to various extents.  Along Julia Simpkins Road, the Allisonia Pentecostal Holiness Church was partially submerged by the New River for the first documented time since it was built in 1912.  Numerous trailers that were parked at campsites along the river were carried away by the flood waters.  Claytor lake was noted filled with about 240 tons of debris washed in from the river, which covers an estimated 20 acres of the lake's surface.  Some debris originated from as far upstream as Jefferson, NC.  Roughly 65 homes in Pulaski County were majorly damaged, while 39 homes were minorly damaged.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 31.03 feet (170,159 cfs) at 4:00 AM EDT on Sept. 28th (28/0800 UTC) due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene. This is the 4th highest crest in the history of this gage, behind the flooding events of August 1940 (1st at 38.10 ft) and July 1916 (2nd at 34.80 ft). This crest rates nearly a 100-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or a 0.5% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 20 inches of rain that fell across the upper New River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

Flood waters along the New River were observed rising an average of 2 feet per hour during the flooding associated with Hurricane Helene.  At the height of the damage inflicted by Helene, Claytor Lake had a debris field that was 4+ miles long, covered 250+ acres, and weighed an estimated 240 tons.  The debris was washed in from Major Flooding along the New River upstream of the reservoir. Debris included uprooted or snapped trees, boats and docks, and portions of buildings.  About 25% of collected material is manmade.  The debris also included hazardous materials such as fuel tanks and chemical waste containers. It was estimated that it would take several months to clean the majority of the debris from the lake, with the effort conducted by dozens of organizations, some using heavy construction vehicles such as excavators loaded onto barges.  Ten swift water rescues occurred within the county, with drones considered an asset in confirming which subjects were in need of being rescued.  A total of 10 road closures were reported in Pulaski County. There were 819 structures were within the floodplain, 12 of which were destroyed, 65 were majorly damaged, 39 were minorly damaged, totaling about $5 million worth of property damage.  Total debris removal as of January 2025 was at least 600 tons, and still climbing.  Overall damage assessment for Pulaski County is estimated to be approaching $7 million.

Considerable to catastrophic flash flooding occurred across Grayson County.  This included at least 200 bridges or culverts that were completely washed out, making the roads impassible. Five large pipes were washed out in  the county: three on Route 783 (Helton Creek Lane) and two on Route 749 (Cabin Creek).
Water was observed flowing across the east-bound side of U.S. Highway 360. The water was deep enough to cover the tires of several vehicles and, in a few cases, overtop the front of some vehicles.

A slow-moving storm near Gladys and produced over four inches of rain in less than 90 minutes. Rainfall rates during the storm at times exceeded four inches per hour. Crest Unit Streamflow maxed out at over 700 cfs/mi^2, an indication of a high potential for significant flooding. The one-hour Average Recurrence Interval for this event was about a 100-year event for MRMS FLASH data.  Suck Creek overflowed its banks and flowed several inches deep across Mollies Creek Road.  No damage was reported to the road, and it was reopened to traffic after the water receded.

Severe Drought conditions in place at the beginning of the month improved on August 6th due to the passage of a low pressure system crossing the lower Mid-Atlantic on August 2nd and 3rd. This system brought scattered rainfall, with amounts ranging from 0.5 to nearly 1.25 inches (with locally higher amounts), resulting in an increase in soil moisture, surface stream flows, and ground water levels sufficient to allow drought conditions for the county to be improved to Moderate Drought per the U.S. Drought Monitor.  Additional improvement in drought conditions across the county was noted during the same week as Tropical Storm Debby brought an additional 2 to locally 4 inches of rain to the county on August 8th.  The rain was beneficial to stream water levels and soil moisture, however many types of crops did not benefit from the moisture given the later time of the growing season that it arrived.  Some farmers reported additional losses to crops from the rainfall given that the increased moisture caused some crops to become infected with disease.

The remnants of Hurricane Debby brought rainfall totals to Buckingham County of 4 to locally 6 inches.  This rainfall resulted in significant short-term improvement to both soil moisture and streamflow levels, raising each from anywhere between the 20th-30th percentile before the storm to normal levels after the storm passed.  As such, the entire county noted a one-category improvement in drought conditions as a result of the rainfall from Debby, with the northwest quarter of the county improving from Severe Drought to Moderate Drought, while the remainder of the county improved to Abnormally Dry conditions.  However, it was reported toward the end of August that many types of crops did not benefit from the moisture given the later time of the growing season that it arrived. Some farmers also reported additional losses to crops from the rainfall given that the increased moisture caused some crops to become infected with disease, and made it more difficult for heavy equipment to enter the fields given the soft soil conditions.

Dryness expanded across much of Greenbrier County during the second half of August given spotty rainfall totals ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 inches falling from August 13th through the end of the month.  Much of this was the result of brief but heavy rain during passing thunderstorm activity that was often localized.  This prevented soil moisture and streamflows from benefiting for more than a few days after the rain event, with dryness then quickly returning.  By the end of the month, soil moisture across eastern Greenbrier County ranged from the 10th to the 30th percentiles, while streamflows were falling increasingly below normal.  Pastureland grasses were reported to be insufficient to keep cattle fed, causing farmers to supplement hay much earlier than they normally would.  Some farmers were also reportedly making plans to sell livestock as they did not have the resources to keep them through the winter.

An EF 1 tornado with max winds of 90 to 95 mph initially touched down near the intersection of Dodson Road and Slatesville Road near Keeling, Virginia. The Dan River at Pine Hall, NC (PNHN7) crested at 23.44 feet (16,200 cfs) at 8:00 AM EDT on Sept. 18th (18/1200 UTC) due to runoff from heavy rain falling the evening prior. This is the highest crest on the river since January 2024, when the river crested at 24.60 feet. This crest rates between a 2-year and a 5-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or between a 50% and a 20% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 5 and locally 8 inches of rain that fell across portions of Stokes County upstream from the gage on the 17th.  The river caused portions of Joe Ayers Road along the right bank just upstream of the gage to be flooded 1-2 feet deep near Pine Hall Road, making the road impassible. Nearby River View Golf Course was observed completely flooded when the river rose out of its banks.  Several farm fields along River Road were flooded as well.  Damage estimates are related to cleanup from the flooding.

Madison River Park was observed flooded several feet deep as the Dan River at Madison rose out of its banks. It is unclear if releases from releases from Belews Lake several miles upstream from the park played a role in the flooding as there is no stream gage along the Dan River between Pine Hall and Wentworth.  Damage estimates are related to cleanup of the park after the flooding receded.

The Dan River at Wentworth, NC (WENN7) crested at 19.96 feet (19,400 cfs) at 7:15 AM EDT on Sept. 18th (18/1115 UTC) due to runoff from heavy rain falling the evening prior. This is the highest crest on the river since January 2024. This crest rates between a 2-year and a 5-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or between a 50% and a 20% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 5 and locally 8 inches of rain that fell across portions of Stokes and Rockingham Counties upstream from the gage on the 17th.

The Roanoke City Emergency Manager reported that flooding was observed at the intersection of 10th Street and Campbell Street Southwest near downtown Roanoke, an area that frequently floods during periods of heavy rain. Multiple vehicles were stranded in standing water that rose to nearly 3 feet deep as a result of poor drainage. Six individuals had to be assisted from their vehicles in the flood waters by emergency personnel. The damage estimate is the estimated damage to the vehicles due to water intrusion.
Runoff from heavy rainfall caused Jacobs Creek to be observed flowing nearly a foot deep across Red House Road. No damage was reported to the road, and it was open to traffic after the water receded.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAMARTI28) recorded a 45-minute rainfall amount, ending at 6 pm EDT on the 24th, of 2.23 inches. Extrapolating between a 30-minute event and a 60-minute event, this 1-hour total is about a 50-year Average Recurrence Interval event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

An short-duration but high-intensity thunderstorm passed across the City of Martinsville, bringing 2 to 2.5 inches of rain in less than an hour.  The intensity of rainfall overwhelmed storm drains, causing water to back up onto several city streets.  Multiple roads became flooded and impassible by several inches of flowing water, and remained closed until the water drained away, with no damage to the roadways reported.  About 6 inches of water was observed flowing across the intersection of Memorial Boulevard and Bridge Street.  At least one road was flooded near Southside Park, with multiple vehicles becoming stranded in the floodwaters while attempting to drive through it.  The damage estimate is the damage caused to vehicles becoming stranded in the flood waters.
Water around 3 inches deep was observed flowing down Frederick Street in the City of Bluefield, WV.  No damage was reported to the roadway.
Runoff from heavy rain was observed flowing about 6 inches deep in front of the Wade Center on Highland Avenue.  No damage was reported to the roadway.
The tunnel on Old Bramwell Road under the railroad was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rain.  No damage was reported to the tunnel or roadway.

A tributary of Brush Creek overflowed its banks several inches deep across Sportsman Drive near the intersection with New Hope Road, making the road impassible until the water receded. No damage was reported to the drive.
Water at least six inches deep was observed flowing across N.C. Highway 194 South, making the road impassible until the water receded.  No damage was reported to the road during this event.

Between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rain fell from a thunderstorm, with rainfall rates estimated to be between 3 and 4 inches per hour.  Railroad Avenue was flooded and impassible due to several inches of water flowing over the roadway.  The Bedford Fire Department responded to calls for three homes and an apartment building that were partially flooded, with those residents forced to evacuate.

Runoff from heavy rainfall found its way into the basement of a home, causing the basement to be flooded by several feet of water.  The runoff was caused by 1.5 to 2 inches of rainfall in a 90 minute period occurring at rates of 3 to 4 inches per hour.

Several inches of flowing water was observed passing across intersection of Howard P. Anderson and Hodges Street.  Flooding was also observed along the 1000 block of Newbill School Road, making the road impassible until the flooding receded.  Runoff was from an estimated 2.5 inches of rain that fell during a 75 to 90 minute period, with rainfall rates of up to 4 inches per hour at times.  No damage was reported to the roadways.

Runoff from an estimated 2.5 inches of rainfall caused the 3000 block of Mount Laurel Road to be flooded and impassible until the water receded. Rainfall rates at times as the thunderstorms passed were up to 4 inches per hour.  No damage was reported to the road.

The intersection of New River Parkway and Hardin Road is flooded and impassible due to nearby Brush Creek flowing out of its banks.  The Creek rose quickly when a band of heavier rainfall brought 1.1 inches within a 30 minute period ending at 6:20 am EDT. No damage was reported to the road. There were unconfirmed reports of a vehicle that may have been stranded in flood waters. Rainfall rates of less than 0.10 inch per hour over the next few hours allowed the water to recede back in the banks of the creek.
Rock Creek was reported out of its banks and was flowing across Peach Bottom Road several inches deep.

The Smyth County Emergency Manager reported that two residents along Flat Ridge Road were rescued from their home when water from Cressy Creek rose up into their homes. Water was 6-12 deeper than normal around the home and was still rising at the time of rescue.  No injuries were reported.  It is unknown if the creek water actually entered either of the homes.

The Mercer County 911 Center reported that a home was flooded along the 7000 block of New Hope Road, with both lanes of the road also flooded. The water, likely from a tributary of Brush Creek rising out of its banks, was reported to be more than 6 inches deep across the road.  No damage was reported to the road.  The damage estimate is flood damage to the home.  A little over 5 inches of rain had fallen across the local area in the 24 hours ending 11 am EDT.

The Mercer County 911 Center reports that Sparkles Road was washed out forming a deep trench and exposing a gas line.  No injuries were reported, but an elderly resident need assistance to leave his home in the direct area due to the flooding.  The damage estimate is the estimated cost of repairing the road.

Water from the South Fork Holston River rose up to the foundations of two homes in the 400 block of Riverside Road. One home was empty while the residents of the other home were evacuated as a precaution.  The stage of the USGS gage of the South Fork Holston River at Riverside was around 5.50 feet at the time, and continued to rise as the day progressed.  No injuries were reported.

The Smyth County 911 Center reported that two bridges had collapsed in the 130 block of Mulberry Lane in the Atkins area. The bridges provided access from the road to a couple of homes. Water had also risen to the level of the steps at one of the homes.  The damage estimate is the estimated cost of repairing the bridges.  About 5.6 inches of rain had fallen in the local area during the 24 hours (ending 12 pm EDT) leading up to this event, with rainfall rates since midnight generally below 0.50 inch per hour. Local creeks and rivers were reported gradually rising across the county through the morning due to the widespread rainfall.

Intensifying rainfall rates resulted in several creeks rising several feet out of their banks within the community of Sugar Grove.  Reports were received that more than one mobile home became flooded, forcing the residents to evacuate to higher ground.  Around 5 inches of rain had fallen in the 24 hours ending 12 pm on the 26th when heavier rain entered the area from the south.

The Smyth County 911 Center reported that Staley Creek had risen significantly out of its banks, and was flooding across surrounding roads and properties.  Nearly five inches of rain had fallen during the 24 hour period ending at 12 pm EDT on the 26th, causing Staley Creek to rise to bank full conditions.  Heavier rain falling during the afternoon caused the creek to rise quickly out of its banks. Some homes along the creek were reported surrounded by the flood waters.  A van became stalled on Highway 16 near the community of Marion in the flood waters.  A Swift Water Rescue Team assisted multiple people to safety during the incident.

Heavy rainfall, combined with poor drainage, caused standing water around 2.5 feet deep to pool along Kessler Mill Road.  No damage was reported to the road, which was open to traffic after the water receded.
Runoff from rainfall caused ponding of water several inches deep on the Link Road bridge over Ivy Creek.  No damage to the bridge was reported.
Several inches of standing water due to runoff from a passing thunderstorm was observed along the 1000 block of Green Level Road. This a location that frequently floods during heavy rain.

A landslide was observed covering the entirety of Highway 220 near the community of Hot Springs. Boulders, trees, and dirt was described in the landslide. The property damage was the estimated cost of removing the debris.

A Facebook post submitted by a member of the public reported the intersection of Melvin Wrenn Road and Highway 86 was covered with around 6 inches of standing water due to runoff from heavy rain.  No damage was reported to the road.

Moore Springs Road was washed out by Cascade Creek, making the road impassible until repairs can be completed.  No injuries were reported. MRMS data indicated 6-hour rainfall amounts ending 9 pm EST were 1.5 to 1.6 times that of 6-hour flash flood guidance, while the average recurrence interval for 6-hours was a 25 year event.
Dan River Shores Road was observed flooded by the Dan River due to runoff from heavy rain.  No damage was reported.

The Wilkes County 911 Dispatch Center received several reports of water flowing several inches deep across roads and bridges throughout the western half of the county as rounds of heavy rain continue to pass across the area.  With seven to ten inches of rain occurring on the 26th, creeks are already swollen and soils are saturated. Even brief periods of heavy rain have resulted in rivers rapidly flowing out of their banks and roads becoming flooded and impassible. A swift water rescue was required for two occupants of a vehicle trapped in flood waters along Roaring River Road near Tyson Feed Mill. Cub Creek was also observed rising out of its banks Friday morning, covering nearly all of Cub Creek Park. Some of the roads that were observed flooded and impassible during the morning and afternoon of the 27th include: Shumate Mountain Road, Mertie Road, Cane Creek Church Road, Vannoy Road, Colvard Road, W. Country Club Drive, Casper Hawkins Road, Avery Anderson Road, Lee Mountain Road, Twin Locust Road, Arbor Grove Church Road, Moxley Road, Sandy Creek Road, Elk Creek Road, Dehart Church Road, Reservoir Road, Glenn Carlton Road, and Highway 268.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Alleghany County per reports from the public and from the Alleghany County 911 Dispatch Center.  Rainfall totals ranging from seven to locally ten inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks and roads that were covered by several inches of flowing water.  After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded, allowing flooding to subside briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of one to two inches per hour.  Reports include Saddle Mountain Road being washed out and destroyed near its intersection with the Blue Ridge Parkway. Along the New River, the Farmers Fish Camp Road Bridge was completely submerged by the New River, with significant damage observed on the bridge once the flooding receded.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Watauga County per reports from the public and from the Watauga County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from seven to locally 11 inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks, as well as several roads that were covered by several inches to feet of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded early on the morning of the 27th, allowing flooding to slow down briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of one to two inches per hour.  Flash flooding occurred in downtown Boone, where water flowing down the several streets rose high enough to enter nearby businesses and homes. Several streets in the Beech Mountain area were flooded and closed, with multiple streets washed out and destroyed.  Multiple vehicles became stranded in the flooded roads, with some of the occupants requiring rescue by a swift water team.  A total of 1,135 buildings were impacted by flooding and/or winds. Of those, 118 were completely destroyed, 479 had major damage and 538 had minor damages. Several of the destroyed homes were in the Meat Camp community. Also significantly damaged were several buildings on the Appalachian State University campus as Boone Creek, which runs through the campus, rose out of its banks and inundated mainly the classroom buildings, forcing the cancellation of classes through October 16th. It was also noted that a large sink hole formed near the Legends Building in downtown Boone. There were 220 water rescues conducted across the county, most coming from stranded automobiles, though sixpeople were rescued from building collapses. There were two known fatalities in Watauga County related flooding from Helene. One female died when a landslide washed away her home, and a second female drowned.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Smyth County per reports from the public and from the Smyth County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from four to locally seven inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks and rivers, as well as several roads that were covered by several inches of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded early on the morning of the 27th, allowing flooding to slow down briefly, heavy rain directly associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene entered the county between 6:30 am and 7 am EDT, falling at rates of one to two inches per hour.  ||Among the reports of flooding and damage that were received, the Smyth County Sheriffs office performed several of swift water rescues through the day as several homes were surrounded by water several feet deep and the residents had to be evacuated. The majority of the rescues took place in the communities of Marion, Atkins, and Sugar Grove, though rescues were required all across the county.  Water rescues also occurred for vehicles that were stranded along flooded roads, such as in the Town of Marion where water was up to a foot deep on several roads.  Also included are rescues for the occupants of two vehicles along the 5200 block of Lee Highway near Marion.  Another rescue was required in Marion when a pickup truck was stranded near the intersection of Stoney Battery Road and Rowland Creek Lane.  The Smyth County 911 Center also reported that a portion of Hutton Road became flooded and impassable, cutting off a residence from outside access. A bridge along St. Claire���s Creek Road was also washed out.

A thunderstorm produced around 1.5 inches of rain falling at rates exceeding four inches per hour. This rain fell across ground that was nearly saturated from rainfall during Tropical Storm Helene a few days earlier.  At 6 pm EDT, FLASH CREST Unit Streamflow was as high as 400 cfs/mi^2, while the 1-hour QPE was 135 percent of FFG values.  This rainfall flooded Broad Hollow Road, making it impassible until the flooding receded. No damage was reported to the road.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced between 2 and 2.5 inches of rainfall across central Campbell County during the evening of September 30th, with rain at times falling at a rate of four inches per hour.  The CREST Unit Flow peaked at 270 cfs/mi^2, while rainfall estimates were 70 to 80 percent of Flash Flood Guidance. Regardless, the short but intense rainfall was enough to produce runoff that flooded multiple roads, making them impassible for short periods of time: Depot Street, Crows Road, Brookneal Highway near Gladys, and Campbell Highway in Rustburg. Flooding also occurred along Village Highway, where one vehicle was washed off the road, as well as along Rocky Road. It is uncertain if there was any damage to the vehicle. No damage to the roads were reported.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced about four inches of rain within a 75-minute period, with rates approaching five inches per hour.  At 7 pm EDT, CREST Unit Flow peaked at an exceptional 2,612 cfs/mi^2, while rainfall amounts rose to 220 percent of Flash Flood Guidance. Runoff from this rainfall caused several roads in the Ajax area through Gretna area of Pittsylvania County to become flooded and impassible until the water receded, including Jasmine Road (Highway 778), Sandy Road, Grassland Drive and West Gretna Road. Millstream Drive was reported washed out by Georges Creek, making the road impassible until repairs can be completed. Whitehorn Creek reportedly overflowed its bank across Chalk Level Road, making the road impassible until the flooding receded. At least four other roads, names unknown, were flooded and impassible along the western and northwestern sides of Gretna.

Runoff from heavy rainfall over nearly saturated soil caused a portion of Roanoke Street to be flooded and impassible for a brief period of time. Rainfall rates at times were close to four inches per hour, with rainfall totals of around 1.5 inches falling in a 90 minute period. Crest Unit Streamflow peaked at 464 cfs/mi^2 at around 4:30 pm EDT.

A thunderstorm produced around 1.5 inches of rain falling at rates of around three inches per hour. This rain fell across ground that was very moist from rainfall occurring during Tropical Storm Helene a few days earlier. Runoff from the rainfall caused multiple roads located northwest of the town of Appomattox to become flooded and impassible with several inches of flowing water across them. This included Phelps Branch Road where it intersects Phelps Branch, as well as North Creek Road at North Creek. No damage to the roads were reported, which were open to traffic after the water receded.

Runoff from between 1.5 and 2 inches of rain falling over moist soil caused the intersection of North James Madison Highway and Thomas Road to be flooded and impassible for a brief period of time. Further north, Randolph Creek Road was reported covered with flowing water, with one car trapped in the flood waters. The occupant was able to escape the vehicle on their own. Another vehicle became trapped in floodwaters along Clay Bank Road, with the occupant needing to be rescued by boat. The intersection of Ridge Road and Penlan Road was observed flooded. Near the community of Dillwyn, several inches of water was observed flowing across Rosney Road, as well as High Rocks Road where rainfall rates of up to four inches per hour were observed.  Cattail Creek rose out of its banks, and was observed flowing across Plank Road near the intersection with Back Mountain Road. Allens Lake Road was washed out and destroyed when a tributary of Tower Branch overflowed its banks across the roadway. A swift water rescue was required for a vehicle that became stranded where Hunts Creek flooded across Slate Hill Road.

Heavy rain occurring during the early morning hours of the 27th resulted in renewed flooding around the community of Independence, with at least 2 roads destroyed in the local area.  This includes Highway 21 near Independence, which serves about 1,800 vehicles per day and was destroyed when the ground beneath the road slid down the hillside.

Heavy rain, falling at rates of about one inch per hour, resulted in renewed flash flooding across portions of Smyth. A portion of Highway 16 was partially washed out and significantly damaged sometime during the early morning hours of the 27th, exposing multiple utility lines beneath the road surface.

Runoff from heavy rainfall has resulted in flooding of several roads throughout Wythe County during the morning of the 26th.  The following roads were reported flooded and impassible: Old Stage Road near Low Water Bridge, Fox Den Road, Locust Hill Road, Ramsey Mountain Road, the Millers Creek area, Ridge Avenue, Crouse Hollow Road, Saint Peters Road, and multiple roads that run along the New River.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Ashe County per reports from the public and from the Ashe County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from 7 to locally 11 inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks, as well as several roads that were covered by several inches to feet of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded early on the morning of the 27th, allowing flooding to slow down briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Flash flooding occurred in several communities, including in the Town of Lansing, where some buildings were flooded nearly 10 feet deep when Big Horse Creek rose out of its banks within a few hours time. Near Lansing, a landslide was observed along the 2500 block of Tucker Road, while a swift water rescue occurred just off of Highway 194 as a vehicle became stranded in flood waters. Along Cranberry Creek in the northeast corner of the county, a bridge was washed out. At least one fatality was reported when the occupant of a vehicle was swept away after becoming stranded in flood waters.  Property damage and cleanup estimates are running close to 116 million dollars.

A tributary of Moravian Creek was out of its banks and was observed flowing several inches deep across School Street. No damage was reported to the roadway, which was open to traffic after the water receded.

Snowfall totals ranged from around three to six inches across the county with the higher elevations receiving the most.  Beach Mountain and Sugar Grove each reported 6.0 inches of snow. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

Snowfall totals ranged from around two to five inches across the county with the higher elevations receiving the most. Reports from near Ashland, Creston, and Flatwood each indicated at least 4.5 inches of snow. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

Snowfall totals ranged from around four to seven inches across the county. The highest snowfall report was 7.4 inches from a cooperative observer near Burkes Garden. Key Impacts: transportation delays.
Snowfall totals ranged from around six to seven inches across this area. Anjean reported 6.0 inches of snow, and Quinwood reported 7.0 inches of snow. Key Impacts: transportation delays.
The KROA ASOS at the Roanoke airport recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.
High winds blew down four trees across the county with one of them falling on to a power line near Axton.
High winds blew down three trees on Alum Ridge Road.
Strong winds blew down one tree that fell on to a residence on School Street in Altavista and caused notable damage.

High winds blew down at least a dozen trees across the county with one of them falling on to a power line. Several roads were blocked from these downed trees, including the intersection of U.S. Highway 52 North and South Key Street in Pilot Mountain.

Strong winds blew down at least two trees in eastern Greenbrier County, including one near Maxwelton that blocked a lane on Fairview Road. Another tree was blown down near Ronceverte that blocked both lanes along Davis Stuart Road.
Up to about an inch of snow fell that caused slick roads, which contributed to a vehicle accident on North Carolina Highway 18 North. Key Impacts: vehicle accident.

The remnants of Hurricane Debby brought rainfall totals to Amherst County of 2 to locally 4 inches, in addition to the 1 to 2 inches that fell earlier in August prior to Debby's arrival. This rainfall resulted in significant short-term improvement to both soil moisture and streamflow levels, raising each from anywhere between the 10th-30th percentile before the storm to normal levels after the storm passed. As such, the southern quarter of Rockbridge County experienced an improvement in drought conditions from Severe Drought to Moderate Drought on August 6th, with the northern three quarters of the county improving to Moderate Drought on August 13th.  However, it was reported toward the end of August that many types of crops did not benefit from the moisture given the later time of the growing season that it arrived. Some farmers also reported additional losses to crops from the rainfall given that the increased moisture caused some crops to become infected with disease, and made it more difficult for heavy equipment to enter the fields given the soft soil conditions.

A tributary of the Watauga River was observed out of its banks and flowing across Vineyard Lane between the Watauga River and Highway 105.  No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the water receded.

A temporary bridge was washed out and destroyed as Winkler Creek rose out of its banks at Rainbow Mountain Road.  Additionally, unimproved parcels of property in the vicinity also experienced flooding.

The Watauga River near Foscoe, NC (FOSN7) crested at 9.10 feet at 10:35 AM EST on December 29th due to runoff from runoff of 1.75 to locally 2 inches during the early morning hours of the day.  This gage was recently restored to service in the wake of Hurricane Helene, with the flood stage based on stream conditions in place before major flooding took place on the Watuaga River during Helene.  No impacts were reported directly with this event, and flood stage may need to be adjusted based on observed flooding during future events.

The Watauga River near Sugar Grove, NC (SGWN7), crested at 8.02 feet (3,537 cfs) at 1:15 pm EST on the 29th above the flood stage of 6.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 1.75 and locally 2 inches of rain falling across the headwaters, most of which fell between 6 am and 10 am EST on the 29th. This is the highest crest since Hurricane Helene in late September 2024. No impacts were reported directly with this event, with concern that the major flooding associated with Helene may have changed stream conditions within the river.

The stream gage at Anthony Creek near Anthony (ANYW2) crested at 14.24 feet (5,580 cfs) at 1:50 am EST on 2/1/25 due to 2 to 2.25 inches of rain falling across the basin within a roughly 24 hour period. There was very little snowpack in the basin prior to the event, therefore very little melt water contribution.  This is roughly a 2-year event (50% AEP) per USGS Streamstats for this location and the highest crest on record since 2/17/23.

The Meadow River at Hines, WV (HNEW2) crested at 15.53 feet (Flood stage is 14 feet).  This was caused by between 2.25 and 2.5 inches of rain over a 24 hour period.  Snowpack was confined to western Greenbrier County, with core sample of 1.7 SWE at Quinwood prior to the rainfall, so some meltwater contributed to the flooding.  Water was observed over one lane of Highway 60 in the Hines and Rupert areas.  Water was also observed over Tommy Hall Road just upstream from Rupert.

The New River at Glen Lyn (GLLV2) crested at 24.24 feet (180,000 cfs) at 1:00 PM EDT on Sept. 28th (28/1700 UTC) due to heavy rain associated with Tropical Cyclone Helene. It was observed that the gage flatlined at this stage for about 3 hours, so it's possible that the crest was closer to or rose above 22 feet. This is the second highest crest in the history of this gage, behind the flooding event of August 1940 (27.50 ft). This crest rates just below a 100-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), or a 1% Annual Exceedance Probability per USGS StreamStats. The flooding was the result of between 10 and locally 20 inches of rain that fell across the upper New River basin between the 25th and 27th, with totals ranging anywhere from between a 200-year and more than a 1,000-year ARI per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  Near the town of Pembroke, substantial flooding of homes and property was observed along Caboose Lane, Overview Drive, and Royal Drive.  At the Riverview Campground in the Town of Narrows, 70 to 80 campers were inundated, with several of those declared uninhabitable after the flooding receded.  Only a handful of campers in the park were high enough to remain above the flooding.  The water treatment plant in Narrows was surrounded by water as well.  Backwater flooding from the New River occurred along Wolf Creek, with water entering Anna's Restaurant, as well as multiple businesses across from the Narrows Farmers Market.  Near the community of Rich Creek, several campers at Gentry's Landing Campsite were inundated, with only a few campers on the highest parts of the property unaffected by flooding.  Overall, the county assisted 48 families with relocation in the wake of the storm.  At least 200 tons of debris had to be removed from along the banks of the New River.

Wind gusts peaked at 71 mph at 3:54 AM EST at a location 0.2 miles southeast of Piney Creek with additional gusts over 58 mph. At a location one mile northeast of Piney Creek, winds gusted to 64 mph at 5:54 AM EST. The high winds also resulted in power outages which reached an estimated peak of 330 customers at 7:00 AM EST. Complete restoration did not occur until approximately 9:00 AM EST.

High wind gusts peaked at 68 mph at Mt. Jefferson, 76 mph at the Ashe County Airport, and 79 mph at a location two miles east-northeast of Baldwin. Power was lost to an estimated peak of 2206 customers at 8:00 AM EST. Complete restoration was not complete until around 9:00 PM EST.

High winds gusted to 61 mph at the Watauga Medical Center in Boone at 5:55 AM EST and to 72 mph at a location in Aho at 6:15 AM EST. Other gusts to or greater than 58 mph occurred at Aho between 6:00 AM EST and 7:00 AM EST. These strong winds prompted multiple power outages which peaked at approximately  1649 customers at 6:00 AM EST. Power was not completely restored for all customers until around 7:00 PM EST.

There was an instantaneous gust of 58 mph at a location two miles southeast of Willis. Power outages in Floyd County peaked at around 43 customers around 7:00 AM EST with complete restoration not complete until around 7:00 PM EST.

High winds gusted to 66 mph at a location 4.1 miles west of Rugby. While this is the only known wind gust equal to or greater than 58 mph, winds were gusty enough across parts of the county to generate power outages. These outages peaked at around 2366 customers around 10:00 AM EST with complete restoration not occurring until around 10:00 PM EST.

A cold front crossed the region during the mid-morning hours of December 11, 2024. Behind this front, winds increased significantly from the west-northwest. At Aho in Watauga County, a home weather station recorded a wind gusts of 62 mph. Additionally, wind gusts of 58 mph or greater were common at this location for approximately 90 minutes.

The combination of estimated winds gusts to 40 mph and wet soils allowed for trees to be blown down near Ararat, Woodville, Flat Rock, State Road, Dobson, Low Gap, Mount Airy, Bottom, Pine Ridge, and Pilot Mountain. In total, thirteen  trees were reported blown down. Damage values are estimated.
Strong winds combined with wet soils allowed trees to be blown down near Figsboro, Oak Level and Ridgeway. In total, three trees were reported down. Damage values are estimated.
Winds around 58 mph, combined with wet soils, brought down around dozen trees and a few power lines around the Cana area. Damage values are estimated.
The combination of strong winds and wet soils allowed trees to blown down in the Swansonville and Callands areas. In total, three trees were reported blown down. Damage values are estimated.

The Bluestone River at Falls Mills, VA (BRVV2), crested at the Moderate Flood Stage (9.0 feet) of 9.96 feet (1,337 cfs) at 22:30 EST on the 15th above the Minor Flood Stage of 7.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 2.75 and 3 inches of rain falling in a roughly 9-hour period from around 9 am to 6 pm on the 15th.  This event is a 10-year and a 25-year event (10%-4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.
Thunderstorm winds blew a few trees down along East Brocktown Road. Damage values are estimated.
Thunderstorm winds downed a couple of trees and which blocked Cane Creek Road in the McGrady area. Damage values are estimated.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down at the intersection of Rena Road and Cheek Road. Damage values are estimated.

The Clinch River at Richlands, VA (RLRV2), crested at the Major Flood Stage (16.0 feet) of 16.09 feet at 11:30 pm EST on the 15th above the Minor Flood Stage of 10.0 feet. This is tied for the 4th-highest crest of all-time (Records dating back at least to 1901), and about the highest crest at this gage since 1978. The flooding was the result of between 2.75 to 3.25 inches of rain falling across the entire headwaters during a 9 hour period due to training heavy showers/storms. This event is about a 25-year event (4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  Significant flooding was observed across town, with water entering many businesses and residences.  As the river rose, multiple properties became inundated along Edgewater Drive near the gage.  Water entered homes along E 1st and 2nd Streets on the east side of town.  Water also surrounded homes on Orange and Jewell Streets, though it is unclear if water did enter any of the homes.  Significant inundation occurred along Alleghany and Road and 4th Street, with multiple businesses along Front Street taking in at least 1 foot of water. Flooding of the river was also observed at the Richlands Tabernacle Church near the intersection of 4th Street and Rockbridge Street. Multiple motor homes around Page and Allen Streets were surrounded by at least 1.5 feet of water, though it did not appear that water entered any of the residences.  In the Raven area, water surrounded several homes on Kirby Road, Atmore Street and Bottom Road, though there were no reports of the water actually entering the homes.  If true, this would be about as high as water could rise without doing so.  Water crested on Kirby Road next to the Doran Grocery Store before receding again.  The elementary school at the end of Bottom Road was surrounded by water.  Water advanced across York and Daw Roads off of Bottom Road as well.  The National Guard was brought in during the flooding to help people evacuate, with at least 51 people assisted from their homes by swift water rescue teams.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down on Park Drive near its intersection with Carter Street. Damage values are estimated.

Strong winds, combined with wet soils, downed two trees, one near the Route 220/Bus 58 interchange southwest of Martinsville, and one just north of Martinsville, east of Collinsville. Damage values are estimated.

Strong winds, combined with wet soils, downed a tree in the 5900 block of Whitmell School Road near Mt. Cross. A power line was brought down in Pittsylvania County at the intersection of Scott Street and Gap Road near Chatham. Damage values are estimated.

Camp Creek at Highway 19 near Camp Creek, WV (CCKW2), crested at 10.62 feet at 8:25 pm EST on the 15th above the flood stage of 7.0 feet. This is the new flood-of-record for this gage, with records dating back to 2014. The flooding was the result of between 3 and 3.25 inches of rain falling across the Camp Creek basin in about 10 hours ending at 7:30 pm on the 15th.  The administrator for Camp Creek State Park, upstream of the gage, reported that a couple buildings in the Mash Fork Campground had water intrusion into them.  Possible that the private campground along Camp Creek Road near Highway 19/Beckley Road were surrounded and perhaps flooded.
An abundant amount of nickel size hail fell.
Hail ranged from dime to quarter size.
Hail of dime to penny size fell.
Strong winds, associated with a passing cold front, blew off the roof of a car wash located in the 800 block of North Main Street in Marion. Damage values are estimated.

The Patrick County Schools Superintendent reported that Maple Swamp Road was flooded by Maple Swamp Creek, and partially impassible.  No damage was reported to the road, which was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.

The Patrick County Schools Superintendent reported that a portion of Quebec Spring Road was flooded and impassible.  No damage to the road was reported, and the road was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.

Sewell Creek abv Little Sewell Creek at Rainelle, WV (RANW2), crested at the minor flood stage of 14.30 feet at 3:30 am EST on the 16th above the flood stage of 14.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 2 and 2.50 inches of rain falling across the Camp Creek basin in about 11 hours ending at around 9:00 pm on the 15th. There were no reports of flooding received from the Town of Rainelle, though similar flooding events of the past have resulted in flood waters entering people's properties.

The Meadow River at Hines, WV (HNEW2) crested at the Moderate Flood Stage of 16.09 feet (Flood stage is 14 feet). This was caused by between 2 and 2.5 inches of rain over an 11 hour period due to training showers along a stalled front. Some snowmelt was involved from 8 to 12 inches that had fallen 2-3 days prior.  Ground was partially frozen and soils were wet.  Streamflows were already running high from flooding events earlier in the month.  Water was observed covering Highway 60 in the Hines and Rupert areas. Water was also observed over Tommy Hall Road just upstream from Rupert.

Anthony Creek near Anthony, WV (ANYW2) crested at 15.00 feet (Flood stage is 14 feet) at 1:35 am EST on the 16th. This was caused by between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rain falling over a 10 hour period ending at around 8:30 pm on the 15th. Snowmelt was a factor given the 8 to locally 12 inches of snow that fell across the basin 2-3 days prior. Soils were partially frozen and saturated from recent heavy precipitation, and stream levels were already running high given flooding of Anthony Creek earlier in the month.

Winds gusted 67 mph at a location two miles east-northeast of Baldwin. This event continued into January 1, 2025. At 1:30 am on January 1, 2025 a gust of 59 mph was recorded at the Ashe County Airport.
Winds increased significantly in speed behind an exiting cold front on New Year's Eve. At Burkes Garden, a 58 MPH wind gust was measured.
The Bluestone River at Pipestem, WV (PIPW2) crested at 12.52 feet (10,023 cfs) at 10:30 am EST on 2/1/25 due to 2 to 2.25 inches of rain falling across the basin within a roughly 24 hour period.

The Bluestone River at Pipestem, WV (PIPW2) crested at 17.00 feet (21,391 cfs) at 9:15 pm EST on 2/15/25 due to 2.75 to 3.5 inches of rain falling across the basin within a roughly 10 hour period caused by training heavy showers. This was a 100-year flood (1% annual exceedance probability) per USGS StreamStats, was the second-highest crest recorded for this gage, and the highest crest since March 2010.

The Bluestone River near Spanishburg, WV (SPNW2), crested at 15.10 feet above the Moderate Flood Stage of 15 feet at 5:40 am EST on the 1st. This is the 6th-highest documented crest dating back to 2010. Flooding from the river was observed approaching Highway 19/Beckley Road across the parking lot of the Rich Creek Baptist Church.  Other portions of Highway 19 were flooded, including near the intersection with Old Spanishburg Road upstream from the gage.

The Bluestone River near Spanishburg, WV (SPNW2), crested at 20.00 feet above the Major Flood Stage (18 feet) at 1:35 am EST on the 16th. This is the highest documented crest dating back to 2010. Flooding from the river inundated Highway 19/Beckley Road in several places.  The Spanishburg Elementary School had flood waters enter the building.  The camper park on Soaring Eagle Lane near where the river crosses under Beckley Road was completely surrounded by floodwaters from the river. Water rescues were reported in the Lake Bottom and Matoaka areas.

The East River at Willowton, WV (ERVW2), crested at 12.88 feet (5,839 cfs) at 6:45 pm EST on the 15th above the flood stage of 9.0 feet.  This is the highest documented crest of this gage since 2012, and is between a 10-year and a 25-year flood (10%-4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  Multiple properties along Kellysville Road upstream of the gage were flooded, with 2 mobile homes destroyed by the force of the water.  Multiple pets required rescue from backyards near the banks of the river.

Indian Creek near Red Sulphur Springs, WV (INCW2) crested at 14.33 feet (6,788 cfs) at 12:15 am EST on the 16th above the Moderate Flood Stage of 14 feet (Minor Flood Stage is 10 feet). This was caused by between 2.5 and 3 inches of rain falling over a 10 hour period ending at around 8:30 pm on the 15th. Snowmelt was a factor given the 4 to locally 8 inches of snow that fell across the basin 2-3 days prior. Soils were partially frozen and saturated from recent heavy precipitation, and stream levels were already running high given flooding of Anthony Creek earlier in the month.  This is the highest documented crest of this gage since 2012 and the first documented that exceeded Moderate Flood Stage. This event is about a 5-year flood (20% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

Wolf Creek near Narrow, VA (WOLV2) crested at 12.85 feet (12,547 cfs) at 1:15 am EST on the 16th above the Moderate Flood Stage of 12 feet (Minor Flood Stage is 10 feet). This was caused by between 2.5 and 2.75 inches of rain falling over a 9 hour period ending at around 7:00 pm on the 15th. Modest snowmelt was a factor given the 2 to locally 4 inches of snow and ice that fell across the basin 2-3 days prior. Soils were partially frozen and saturated from recent heavy precipitation, and stream levels were already running high given rounds of heavy precipitation earlier in the month. This is the highest crest of this gage since March 2010, and the 5th highest documented crest since 1909. This event is about a 25-year flood (4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  One of the biggest noted impacts was the significant number of basements of homes that were flooded and needed to be pumped dry in the Narrows area. One water rescue was reported along the 4300 block of Wolf Creek Road as water from Wolf Creek surrounded the home.

Walker Creek at Bane, VA (BANV2) crested at 15.31 feet (16,065 cfs) at 3:30 am EST on the 16th above the Moderate Flood Stage of 14 feet (Minor Flood Stage is 11 feet). This was caused by between 2.25 and 2.5 inches of rain falling over a 9 hour period ending at around 7:00 pm on the 15th. Modest snowmelt was a factor given the 2 to locally 4 inches of snow and ice that fell across the basin 2-3 days prior. Soils were partially frozen and saturated from recent heavy precipitation, and stream levels were already running high given rounds of heavy precipitation earlier in the month. This is the highest crest of this gage since April 2020, and is nearly a 25-year flood (4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

The combination of strong winds and wet soils allowed for trees to be brought down within the county.  Trees were reported down near Ararat, Pilot Mountain, Mt. Airy and in Dobson. Damage values are estimated.

Tom's creek was observed rising rapidly out of its banks at multiple locations.  Water was observed flowing across Coal Bank Hollow Road near Highway 460, and flooded the nearby Montgomery County Waste Site, causing damage to one of the service buildings located there.  Further downstream, water was also observed flowing across Tom's Creek Road several inches deep.
A wind gust of 59 MPH was measured at the Ashe County Airport, and is one report from a high wind event that began on December 31st, 2024.
Wind gusts of 58 MPH, 60 MPH, and 62 MPH were measured at the Watauga County Medical Center in Boone, at Blowing Rock, and at Aho, respectively.

Between two and three inches of snow fell across Alleghany County between 3 PM and 11 PM EST. There were at least 20 different vehicle incidents, including vehicles sliding off into ditches or into guardrails, due to slick roads across the county. Two vehicles were overturned on North Carolina State Highway 18. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Around three inches of snow fell across Smyth County. Roads became slick and hazardous, and there were several vehicle accidents reported during the evening of January 3. Key Impacts: hazardous driving conditions, traffic accidents.

Between one and four inches of snow were reported around Grayson County, with the highest amounts confined to the high elevation areas including Mount Rogers and Whitetop. Several accidents were reported due to snow covered roads. Up to 50 customers were reported without power during the evening of January 3. Key Impacts: traffic accidents, power outages.

Some areas in Wythe County received one to four inches of snow, with the higher amounts confined to the higher terrain in the western part of the county. There were numerous vehicles accidents reported due to icy roads, including a rescue squad vehicle that slid off the road because of the ice. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Between 0.5 to 1.5 inches of snow fell in Pulaski County. Roads became snow covered and hazardous across much of the county, and resulted in several accidents. During the evening of January 3rd, nearly 1,200 customers were reported without power. Key Impacts: traffic accidents, power outages.
Around a half an inch of ice was reported in Floyd County, and Shawsville Pike Road was closed. Key Impacts: road closures.
In Beech Mountain, four inches of snow was reported. Snow covered roads led to numerous vehicle accidents. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.
In Quinwood, five inches of snow was reported during the evening of January 3rd. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Around four inches of snow was reported in western Greenbrier County on January 6th, along with around a quarter of an inch of ice from freezing rain. Over 900 customers had lost power by 9 AM on January 6th. Several trees were downed, and some of which brought down power lines. Key Impacts: power outages, road closures, traffic accidents.

Around four inches of snow was reported in eastern Greenbrier County, and around a quarter of an inch of ice from freezing rain was also reported. Around 900 customers were without power by the morning of January 6th. Several trees were downed from ice accumulation, some brought down power lines and closed roads. Key Impacts: power outages, road closures, traffic accidents.

Around three inches of snow fell across Alleghany County, with the highest amounts over the southern part of the county. A tenth of an inch of ice was also reported near Roaring Gap. Just over 80 customers were reported without power by the afternoon of January 6th. Key Impacts: traffic accidents, power outages.

Around three inches of snow was reported in Lawsonville  and just over a tenth of an inch of ice was reported in Danbury. Roads became snow covered and slick, and several minor vehicle accidents were reported across the county. Over 200 people lost power by the morning of January 6th. Key Impacts: traffic accidents, power outages.

Around four inches of snow was reported in Tazewell County, with around three quarters of an inch of ice also reported. By the mid morning of January 6th around 2,600 customers were reported to have lost power. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

Around five inches of snow was reported in Smyth County, and around a tenth of an inch of ice. By mid morning on Monday January 6th, over 100 customers were reported without power. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

Reed Creek at Grahams Forge, VA (GRHV2), crested at 7.80 feet (9,528 cfs) at 7:15 am EST on the 16th above the Minor Flood stage of 6.5 feet. The flooding was the result of between 1.75 and 2.25 inches of rain falling across the Reed Creek basin in about 9 hours ending at 7:00 pm on the 15th.  This is the 5th highest documented crest for this gage with records dating back to 1909, and is the highest crest of this gage since 2002. This event is between a 10-year and a 25-year flood (10%-4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.

Peak Creek at Pulaski, VA (PCRV2), crested at 9.74 feet at 19:00 EST on the 15th above the Minor Flood Stage of 8.0 feet. The flooding was the result of between 2.25 and 2.5 inches of rain falling in a roughly 9-hour period from around 9 am to 6 pm on the 15th.  The creek was reported flowing out of its banks and across portions of Dora Highway.  The creek was also observed rising out of its banks in the center of town, flowing across Main Street and Walnut Street.  No damage was reported though cleanup costs are estimated and included in the property damage.

North Fork Holston River at Saltville, VA (SALV2) crested at 12.86 feet (13,283 cfs) at 2:30 am EST on the 16th above the Moderate Flood Stage of 12 feet (Minor Flood Stage is 10 feet). This was caused by between 2.25 and 3 inches of rain falling over a 9 hour period ending at around 7:00 pm on the 15th. Soils were partially frozen and saturated from recent heavy precipitation, and stream levels were already running high given rounds of heavy precipitation earlier in the month. This is the highest crest of this gage since April 1977, and the 7th-highest documented crest since 1907. This event is between a 10-year and a 25-year flood (10%-4% Annual Exceedance Probability) per USGS StreamStats.  Around 10 homes were evacuated near the river in the town of Saltville as a precaution, though there were no reports that the river water entered any homes.

Around 3.5 inches of snow fell across Mercer County from January 5th through the 6th, and around 0.60 inches of ice accumulated. By the evening of January 6th, over 13,000 customers were impacted by power outages. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

In Monroe County, four inches of snow fell by the morning of January 6th, and around one-quarter of an inch of ice had accumulated. Over 1,200 customers lost power by the morning of January 6th. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Around four inches of snow fell across Summers County from January 5th through 6th, and one-half inch of ice accumulated. By the morning of January 6th, just over 2,000 customers were reported without power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.
Up to an inch of snow fell across the county from January 5th through January 6th. Between 0.10 and 0.15 inches of ice accumulated as well. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Over two inches of snow fell across Grayson County from January 5th through January 6th, and around one-half inch of ice accumulated. Around 760 customers were reported without power by the morning of January 6th. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Around three inches of snow fell in Bland County by the night of January 5th, and a quarter of an inch of ice accumulated. Over 850 customers had lost power by the late morning of January 6th Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Up to three inches of snow fell in Giles County, and around one-quarter of an inch of ice accumulated from January 5th through January 6th. Around 125 customers were reported without power by the afternoon of January 6. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between three and four inches of snow fell across Wythe County by the afternoon of January 6th, as well as a quarter of an inch of ice. Over 550 customers had lost power by the late morning of January 6th. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Around three inches of snow fell in Pulaski County by the night of January 5th, and around one-half inch of ice accumulation was also reported. By the morning of January 6th, over 830 customers had lost power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between one and two inches of snow fell across Montgomery County, with the highest report of two inches in the Merrimac area. Between one quarter and three quarters of an inch of ice also accumulated from freezing rain, with the highest report of 0.75 inches in Elliston. Nearly 4,000 customers were reported to have lost power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between 2.5 and four inches of snow fell across Carroll County, with the highest amount of four inches reported north of Galax and in Laurel Fork. Up to 0.40 inches of ice accumulation from freezing rain was also reported. Over 2,200 customers were reported without power by the early afternoon of January 6. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between 1.5 and three inches of snow fell in Floyd County, with the highest amount of three inches reported near Copper Valley. Between one-quarter and one-half inch of ice accumulated from freezing rain, and just over 4,000 customers had lost power by the morning of January 7th. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between 1.5 and four inches of snow fell across Craig County, with the highest amount of four inches reported in New Castle. Up to a quarter of an inch of ice also accumulated from freezing rain. By the late morning of January 6th, just over 425 customers were without power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between four and seven inches of snow fell across Alleghany County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of 7.2 inches reported near Hollins, Virginia. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Between four and six inches of snow, with a few locally higher amounts, fell across Bath County from January 5th through January 6th. The highest amount of nine inches was reported in Hot Springs. Up to 0.16 inches of ice accumulation was also reported. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

Between one and two inches of snow fell across Roanoke County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of two inches reported in to the south southwest of Roanoke. Between 0.25 to 0.6 inches of ice accumulation was reported, with the highest report of 0.6 inches in Glenvar. Almost 4,500 customers had lost power by the morning of January 6th. Around thee to four inches of snow fell across Botetourt County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amounts of four inches reported near Buchanan and Oriskany. Between 0.10 and 0.16 inches of ice accumulated in Fincastle and Oriskany as well. Around 440 customers had lost power by noon on January 6. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Around two to over four inches of snow fell in Rockbridge County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest report of 4.3 inches in Vesuvius. Up to one-quarter of an inch of ice accumulation was also reported near Vesuvius. By the morning of January 6th, over 1,300 customers had lost power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between two and 3.5 inches of snow fell in Patrick County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of 3.5 inches reported in Critz. Over 0.30 inches of ice accumulation was also reported, with 0.35 inches near Buffalo Ridge. Almost 7,900 customers had lost power by the late night of January 6th. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between one and two inches of snow, with a couple locally higher amounts, fell across Franklin County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of 2.5 inches reported near Rocky Mount. Over three quarters of an inch of ice accumulation was also reported near Burnt Chimney, with other ice amounts between 0.10 and 0.30 inches around the county. Over 10,000 customers had lost power, and several hundred trees were downed across the county. Key Impacts: power outages, downed trees and traffic accidents.

Between one and 3.5 inches of snow fell across Bedford County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of 3.5 inches reported in Boonsboro. Ice accumulations ranged mainly between one-quarter and one-half of an inch, though the highest accumulated reported was 0.63 inches in Chamblissburg. Over 5,000 customers lost power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between two to 5.5 inches fell across Amherst County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest amount of 5.5 inches measured in Falconerville. Ice accumulations ranged from 0.15 to 0.5 inches, with half an inch also reported in Falconerville. Almost 2,000 customers had lost power. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between one to two inches of snow fell across Campbell County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest of two inches reported in Rustburg. Up to one-half inch of ice accumulation was reported near Rustburg. Nearly 7,000 customers had lost power during the event. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Between one to three inches of snow fell in Appomattox County from January 5th through January 6th, with the highest report of three inches reported near Tower Hill. Ice accumulations ranged from 0.10 inch to 0.42 inches, measured near Evergreen. Almost 2,200 customers had lost power by the morning of January 6. Key Impacts: power outages and traffic accidents.

Nearby, Wesendonck Road was observed flooded and impassible at several locations due to multiple creeks overflowing their banks. This includes Nobusiness Creek.

A 74 mph gust was measured in Aho, and a 59 mph gust was measured at the Watauga Medical Center in Boone. Around 140 customers in Watauga County had lost power by the early morning of January 29th.
A 60 mph gust was measured near Rugby, and a 59 mph gust was measured in Menlo. Over 260 customers in Grayson County had lost power by the afternoon of January 29th.
A 59 mph wind gust was measured at the Roanoke Airport. Over 1,000 customers in Roanoke County and City had lost power by the morning of January 29th.

Little Sewell Creek flooded out of its banks and onto the James River and Kanawha Turnpike near Oak Street.  No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the flooding receded.
Kitchen Creek was observed flowing out of its banks and across Blue Sulphur Springs Road.  No damage was reported to the roadway, which was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.
Grassy Meadow Road was observed flooded and impassible for a brief period of time.  No damage was reported to the road, which was reopened to traffic after the water receded.
Crane Creek was observed out of its banks and was flooding across a few roads in the community of Montcalm, including Jim's Branch Road and Crane Creek Road.
Dry Creek flooded out of its banks and across Tuckahoe Road. No damage was reported and the road was open to traffic after the flooding receded.

The Bluestone River near Spanishburg, WV (SPNW2), rose above the minor flood stage of 12.0 feet to 13.81 feet by 11:59 pm on the 31st. The river was still rising heading into the early hours of February 1st, and would eventually crest at 15.10 feet at 5:40 am EST.  Flooding from the river inundated Highway 19/Beckley Road at multiple locations.  Water may have surrounded homes on Soaring Eagle Lane and Little Sparrow Drive.

The Clinch River at Richlands (RLRV2) rose to an estimated 11.2 to 11.5 feet on the evening of the 31st, though an exact crest is uncertain given the gage went out of service during the flooding event.  Water was observed covering the ball fields at Critterville Park. Homes off of Alleghany Avenue and 4th Street, as well as along 1st Street, were observed surrounded by water.  Some evacuations were conducted as a precaution, however there were no reports of flood waters from the Clinch River entering homes or causing vehicles to become stranded.
