Slick roads to due 1.5 to 4.5 inches of snowfall across the county led to at least 60 vehicle accidents, including a head on collision involving two semi-tractor trailer trucks. There were also a number a pedestrian mishaps with many falls on ice. Damage values are estimated.
A trailer home was blown off its foundation by strong winds.  The wind gust was measured from the nearby Bluefield, West Virginia airport.
A few trees were blown down in the town of Marion.
Hail varying from the size of quarters to half dollar coins fell for several minutes and covered the ground.
Hail up to the size of golf balls fell at Pine Ridge.
At least three trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds around the community of Boomer.
Multiple large trees were blown down along the intersection of Route 89 and Horseshoe Road near Francisco.
Power lines were blown down by thunderstorm winds along Pine Ridge Road.
Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds around the community of Germanton.
Several trees and power lines were blown down around the community of Walnut Cove.
Multiple large oak trees uprooted or snapped in half, and shingles blown off a house.

A tornado touched down southeast of Greensboro in Guilford County shortly after 4:00 PM EST.  This tornado later entered Rockingham County about one mile southeast of Haw River near Chrismon Road at 4:25 PM EST.  The tornado damaged numerous buildings, outbuildings, and barns.  At least twenty homes and farms suffered damage, while one house and two mobile homes were  completely destroyed.  The Oak Haven Event Center in downtown Ruffin also sustained damage.  Countless trees were snapped or uprooted.  Estimated maximum wind speeds were 110 MPH.  Seven people were injured, including a father and a seven-year-old son who were critically injured in their moving car when it struck a double-wide mobile home that was lifted on to the 1300 block of Grooms Road.  The tornado finally lifted at 4:46 PM EST about four miles north-northeast of Ruffin between Dibrell Road and Bradley Road.

A tornado touched down in Caswell County west of Pelham near Dusty Lane at 4:51 PM EST.  It snapped numerous trees and damaged several outbuildings.  By 4:53 PM EST, the tornado exited Caswell County and continued northward into Pittsylvania County of Virginia.  It would later cross through the independent city of Danville and back into Pittsylvania County before lifting about two miles southwest of Dry Fork by 5:10 PM EST.

This is the first segment in Virginia of a tornado that originated west of Pelham near Dusty Lane in Caswell County of North Carolina at 4:51 PM EST.  It crossed into Pittsylvania County at 4:53 PM EST.  The tornado snapped numerous trees and damaged a few outbuildings.  The tornado crossed into the independent city of Danville at 4:55 PM EST.  It would later continue northward back into Pittsylvania County.

This is the second segment in Virginia of a tornado that originated west of Pelham near Dusty Lane in Caswell County of North Carolina at 4:51 PM EST.  The tornado exited Pittsylvania County and entered into the independent city of Danville at 4:55 PM EST.  The tornado damaged or destroyed numerous trees, and several outbuildings were completely destroyed.  Minor roof damage occurred to numerous homes as the tornado crossed over the Westover area within the city limits of Danville.  Private property damage was assessed at about $2.2 million, while utilities and public works cleanup added another $400,000.  By 4:58 PM EST, the tornado exited the city and continued northward back into Pittsylvania County.

This is the third and final segment in Virginia of a tornado that originated west of Pelham near Dusty Lane in Caswell County of North Carolina at 4:51 PM EST.  After crossing Pittsylvania County and the independent city of Danville, the tornado continued northward and entered Pittsylvania County again at 4:58 PM EST.   Numerous trees were damaged or destroyed, several outbuildings were destroyed, and minor roof damage occurred on numerous houses.  The greatest damage was found on a farm at R and L Smith Road.  Estimated maximum winds were 110 MPH.  By 5:10 PM EST, the tornado finally lifted about two miles southwest of Dry Fork.
Hail up to the size of tennis balls fell about one mile north of Fancy Gap along the Fancy Gap Highway.
One large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Carsonville Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew over several trees and billboards.
At least three trees were snapped or topped by thunderstorm winds.
Several large tree limbs were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds on Tinkerville Road.
Two trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds on Brattons Run.

A tornado briefly touched down just south of Hawkins Lane and headed northward at 4:03 PM EST.  It crossed Hawkins Lane and Wild Cat Hollow Road before lifting at 4:04 PM EST.  The tornado caused considerable damage to trees, homes, and outbuildings.  Six homes had roof shingles and vinyl siding ripped off by the tornado.  Several outbuildings and garages were destroyed.  The tornado also flipped one truck upside down on to another damaged vehicle, and it also lofted small debris over 100 yards.  The estimated maximum winds were 105 MPH.
At least four large trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds around Rocky Mount.
A power line was blown down just north of Axton.
Large tree limbs were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
One tree was blown down on to power lines near Woodlawn Heights Road.
Multiple trees were blown down near Halifax Road.
Debris from a cattle barn was blown on to Meadors Spur Road.

At 5:10 PM EST, a tornado briefly touched down on the 1800 block of Mead Valley Road about four miles northwest of Moneta.  This tornado caused significant damage to the roof of one home, and it also caused damage to an adjacent barn and outbuilding.  About fifty mature trees were either snapped or uprooted.  Estimated maximum winds were 105 MPH.  By 5:11 PM EST, the tornado lifted near the 10000 block of Dickerson Mill Road.
Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds in the town of Halifax.
One tree was blown down along Whipping Creek Road, and another tree was blown down along the Brookneal Highway.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree along the Patrick Henry Highway.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated up to 65 MPH snapped and uprooted trees from Gladstone at 6:25 PM EST to Wingina at 6:35 PM EST.

A tornado touched down about five miles east-southeast of Rustburg near Carwile Road at 5:56 PM EST.  Several trees were uprooted or snapped during the first moments, but the tornado intensified along New Chapel Road.  A roof was blown off a garage, and a manufactured home was moved off its foundation.  In addition, a metal roof from a large shed was also peeled off by the tornado.  The estimated maximum winds reached 90 MPH.  By 5:59 PM EST, the tornado lifted just south of the intersection of New Chapel Road and Bethany Road.

At 6:38 PM EST, a weak tornado touched down on the north side of Piney Mountain and just west of Indian Creek Road in a forested area about three miles west-northwest of Lowesville.  It tracked toward the northwest and lifted at 6:41 PM EST about four miles west-northwest of Lowesville.  The tornado only uprooted trees during its time on the ground.

This is the first segment of a tornado that touched down just south of Waterlink Road near Timberlake in Campbell County at 6:00 PM EST.  The tornado uprooted trees, damaged multiple roofs from homes, damaged several businesses, and flipped several cars.  A total of 28 buildings suffered damage, and five of those buildings were completely destroyed.  The tornado crossed Timberlake Road and exited Campbell County at 6:03 PM EST.  It would continue into the western portion of the independent city of Lynchburg and further northward into Amherst County.

This is the second segment of a tornado that touched down just south of Waterlink Road near Timberlake in Campbell County at 6:00 PM EST.  The tornado crossed Timberlake Road and entered the independent city of Lynchburg at 6:03 PM EST.  The tornado uprooted trees and caused notable damage to 332 private buildings, and 34 of those buildings were condemned due to the damage.  It also damaged numerous power lines and transformers.  Two people were injured.  At 6:07 PM EST, the tornado left the independent city of Lynchburg, crossed the James River, and continued northward into Amherst County.

This is the third and final segment of a tornado that touched down just south of Waterlink Road near Timberlake in Campbell County at 6:00 PM EST. The tornado crossed through the independent city of Lynchburg and eventually tracked over the James River into Amherst County at 6:08 PM EST.  This was only the third EF3 tornado to occur in the NWS Blacksburg forecast since 1950, and was the longest track tornado within the state of Virginia for the NWS Blacksburg forecast area. The tornado reached its peak intensity with estimated maximum winds of 150 MPH as it crossed Route 130 and entered the town of Elon.  A total of 166 homes suffered damage, and 22 of those homes were considered a total loss.  A motor home was carried about thirty feet and tipped over.  The hardest hit locations were along Nottaway Drive and Deerfield Drive.  Seven people were injured and taken to the hospital from Elon.  As the tornado continued north-northeastward out of Elon, it snapped or uprooted hundreds of trees and caused more minor roof damage to homes.  At 6:25 PM EST, the tornado finally lifted as it began to head up Shady Mountain Ridge, which is about five and a half miles west-northwest of Amherst.

Flooding was reported in several locations in Monroe County. The gauge on Indian Creek near Red Sulphur Springs (INCW2) crested at 12.65 feet, above the Minor flood stage of 8 feet and County Road 23 was flooded. Emergency Management also reported flooding from Indian Creek along parts of Route 122 closing the road.
Dunlap Creek near Covington (DLPV2) crested above Minor flood stage at 9.48 feet; Minor flood stage is 9 feet.
Flooding was reported along portions of Second Creek.
Brush Creek was reported out of its banks with water over Brush Creek Road in spots.

A report from local TV showed flood damage in the Peterstown area with several homes receiving water damage and at least 2 vehicles totaled and a tractor. A shed was also damaged by flood waters. Damages are estimated.

Indian Creek was reported to be out of its banks and flowing across Route 219 at a depth of at least two feet in the Salt Sulphur Springs area. At least four homes in the same area received flood damage, including a bed and breakfast. The Union Rescue Squad office was also flooded. Several other creeks were reported to be flooded closing more roads.  Route 122 was reported with water over the road in the Raines Corner area. The Indian Creek gauge near Red Sulphur Springs (INCW2) located downstream of the heaviest rain area, crested at 11.62 feet, above the Minor flood stage of 8 feet.
Route 3 was closed due to flooding from Beech Run near Hinton.

Up to two feet of rapidly of flowing water was over the intersection of Hazelwood Terrace and Beagle Club Road along with a small debris flow and small tree pushed into the roadway. Spotter reported 4.32 inches of rain in less than 4 hours at the time of the report. Turner Branch Road in the Blue Ridge area was washed out and closed and a motorist was rescued from the flood waters.

At least six roads were flooded and closed due to flash flooding in Roanoke City. Among the roads closed was Edgewood St. along Mudlick Creek, north of Brandon Road. The Peters Creek Road off-ramp from Route 581 was also closed. An automated rain gauge in the Garden City area of Roanoke had about 3.5 inches of rain in 6 hours.
The public reported 1 to 2 feet of water flowing across Route 116 under the Blue Ridge Parkway.
WSET reported Mudlick Creek out of its banks and flowing across Halevan Road making it impassable.
Water 1 to 2 feet in depth reported flowing across Goose Creek Valley Road.
Roanoke Airport (ROA) set a daily rainfall record for May 17 with 2.71 inches. The old record was 1.43 inches in 1922. Official records at Roanoke date back to 1912.
Water was reported covering portions of Route 501 between Rustburg and Gladys.
Water was reported to be running over Valley View Road from an unnamed creek and into the basement of a nearby home.
The CoCoRaHS observer at Cave Spring 2.4 SSW had a 24-hour total of 4.53 inches. This is just below the 0.1 annual chance rainfall or nearly a 10-year recurrence interval.
Flooding closed the intersection of Copper Cove and Valleyview Roads.
Part of Epworth Road near Cana was washed away by the heavy rainfall.

Numerous roads across southwest Stokes County, mainly in the King area were closed or washed out due to flooding. This included Route 52, Brown Road, Briarcreek Road, Chestnut Grove Road, Goff Road and Priddy Road. Damage to a pipe under Briarcreek Road required a replacement. At least two bridges were overtopped but bridge damage was minimal.

The Boone 1 SE COOP (BOON7) observer recorded 3.40 inches for the 24-hours ending at 700 AM EST on the 19th. This is the 2nd highest daily May rainfall since records began at this station in 1980 and the 4th highest May rainfall all-time at Boone (since 1929) if the previous COOP station is considered.

Several roads were flooded in the Mount Airy area including Aims Avenue, Bluemont Road, Hogan Creek Road, Snowhill Drive, Old Toast Road and Quaker Road. Trees were reported down mainly due to the saturated soils. One home had water inside the house from the flooding.

The COOP observer at Mt. Airy 2W (MTAN7) recorded 3.50 inches for the 24 hour period ending 700 AM EST on the 19th. This is the highest daily May rainfall at this long-term station, with data back to 1893. The previous May record was 3.02 inches set May 15, 2012.

The observer at Foscoe 1.2 WSW (NC-WT-11) reported rainfall of 7.71 inches for the 24-hour period ending 600 AM EST. Most of the rain fell from 135 PM on the 18th. Flooding reported around the area. This is roughly a  0.04 annual chance rain event for a 24-hour period or a 25-year recurrence interval in this area per NOAA Atlas 14, although the duration of the rainfall was well below the full 24 hours.

The observer at Seven Devils 1.4 ENE (NC-WT-46) reported 6.46 inches for the 24-hour period ending 600 AM EST. This is roughly a  0.1 annual chance rain event for a 24-hour period or a 10-year recurrence interval in this area per NOAA Atlas 14.

Widespread flooding was reported across southern Watauga County. The Boone Fire Department said a woman driving on a flooded section of Bamboo Road got her SUV swept up by the flood waters. Rescue crews quickly got her to safety with no serious injuries. One foot of water was estimated to be flowing down Seven Devils Road onto Route 105 near Foscoe.  Linville Creek was reported to have flooded over the bridge at Linville Creek Road. The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 16.15 feet, the highest stage since September, 2004. Several debris flows were reported across the area, blocking roads. Overall damage to road infrastructure was around $1 million.

The COOP observer at King (KIGN7) recorded 2.70 inches for the 24 hour period ending 700 AM EST on the 19th. This is the highest daily May rainfall at this station, with data back to 1999. The previous May record was 2.17 inches set May 9, 2012.

The Danville Airport ASOS measured 3.96 inches of rain for the 24-hour period ending at midnight on May 18. This was a daily rainfall record for May 18 and the 2nd highest daily May rainfall at this station. Records at Danville date back to 1916.

The COOP observer at Martinsville (MARV2) recorded 3.85 inches for the 24 hour period ending 700 AM EST on the 19th. This is the highest daily May rainfall at this long-term station, with data back to 1931. The previous record was 3.17 inches set in 2017.

The COOP observer at South Boston (SOBV2) recorded 3.47 inches of rain for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM May 19. This was the 3rd highest daily May rainfall at this location. Records date from 1980 at this site.

The COOP observer at Elkin (EKNN7) recorded 3.00 inches for the 24 hour period ending 700 AM EST on the 19th. This is the 4th highest daily May rainfall at this station, with continuous data back to 1934.

The CoCoRaHS observer at Vinton 2.6 E had 6.86 inches of rain for the 24-hours ending at 700 AM EST. This amount exceeds the 50-year recurrence interval (0.02 annual exceedance probability) for this location and duration.

Numerous roads were flooded across the City of Martinsville and several homes were flooded. The roof of a department store partially collapsed due to the weight of water. A local state of emergency was declared by the City Council in the aftermath due to the massive cleanup required. Local sources stated that 4 to 5 inches of rain fell in approximately one hour.

Several roads in Danville City were closed due to flooding including all lanes of Riverside Drive and Arnett Boulevard. Several mudslides covered roads as well.  Parker Road near a trailer park was flooded and several mobile home isolated by flood waters.

There were numerous reports of flooded roadways from Pittsylvania County, mainly east of Danville where the heaviest rain occurred. Radar estimated up to 3 inches fell near the Halifax border. Flowing water was reported across Falls Creek Road in Ringgold and the intersection of Highway 29 and Fall Creek Road near Blair was also flooded. Water was also reported over the intersection of Reeves Mill Road and East Hightower near Kentuck.

Several roads were flooded in Halifax County where a swath of 2 to 3.5 inches of rain fell in several hours. Flowing water was reported across Howard Anderson Road in the 6000 block. and also over the intersection of Philpott Road and Sandy Beach Road.

The Smith River at Eden (EDSN7) crested at 12.55 feet late on the 18th in response to the heavy rains upstream. Minor flood stage is 11 feet. Flooding was confined to lowland areas. This was the highest reading at this gauge since January 25, 2010.
Linville Creek was flooding the bridge at Linville Creek Road.

Second Creek was reported in flood closing Second Creek Road.
Water was reported flowing over Spruce Street.

Severe flooding with numerous reports affected parts of Henry County, especially south and west of Martinsville. A car was pulled out of flood waters on Highway 220 south of Martinsville.

Several roads were flooded in the town of Tazewell with water running across them. A number of homes had flooded basements and at least six evacuations or water rescues were conducted at or near Maplewood Lane, Walnut Street, Texas Street, Mitchell Street, and Third Street. Most of the flood reports were from 930 to 1030 AM EST. In addition, the North Fork of the Clinch River was reported out of its banks and flooding Professional Drive.

A CoCoRaHS observer at Roanoke 5.8 SW (VA-RN-13) recorded 7.71 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM on the 28th but most of that rain fell in about a 4-hour period according to the observer. This is over a 1000-year rainfall event (.0001 annual exceedance probability) for that duration according to NOAA Atlas 14.

A CoCoRaHS observer Roanoke 4.3 SW (VA-RN-5) recorded 5.51 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM on the 28th but according to the observer most of that rain fell in about a 3-hour period between 200 and 500 PM local time (1-4 PM EST) according to the observer.
A spotter with an automated rain gauge recorded 2.21 inches in 30 minutes. This is right at the 200-year rainfall event (.005 annual exceedance probability).
Electric Road was reported closed in the 2500 block due to high water.

Multiple reports of flash flooding in Roanoke County.  Most of the reports were between 230 and 500 PM EST.  Several roads were closed or damaged and at least 20 homes partially flooded. Garst Mill Park was flooded to a depth of several feet. The main cause of flooding was from Mudlick Creek which rose approximately 10 feet in elevation to an estimated flow of 2400 cubic feet per second per a post-flood survey.  The survey indicated that the flood was approximately a 10-year recurrence interval (0.1 annual exceedance probability).

Extensive flooding occurred from Mudlick Creek along Grandin and Garst Mill Roads with water getting into many homes. Post-flood survey indicated a recurrence interval of about 10 years (0.1 annual exceedance probability) on Mudlick Creek as the stream rose roughly 10 feet above baseflow.

The Princeton COOP measured 5.78 inches for the 24 hours ending at 7 AM on July 30th which was an all-time daily rainfall record at this station. The old record was 5.00 inches on January 22, 1906.  Precipitation records exist from 1900-1914 and 1940 to the present at the site. Per NOAA Atlas 14 this was approximately a 500-year (.002 annual exceedance probability) recurrence interval for a 24-hour period, although most of the rain fell over a much shorter duration, roughly 3 to 5 hours.
