Runoff from heavy rainfall caused water to enter at least one home and wash away the all the gravel at a construction site.

The COOP site at Chatham (CHMV2) measured 5.10 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 23rd. This was the 6th highest daily rainfall recorded at this station since records began in 1922 and 4th highest in September.

Flash flooding occurred in downtown Galax, with Main Street closed and several businesses badly flooded. Water was rapidly flowing through Blevins  Building Supply store and was described as a 'river' running through it. Damage to the store and inventory was estimated to exceed $1 million. Eight cars were reported stalled out in the flood waters and a Carroll County squad car was totaled as a result. Evacuations were required from a nursing home facility and several other businesses suffered damage.

The COOP station at the Galax Water Plant (GAAV2) measured 5.50 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 9th, although most of the rain fell in just a few hours. This was the highest measured daily rainfall at this station since records began at this site in 2000, and the 6th highest daily since data collection began at any COOP station in Galax in 1955. The 5.50 inches in 24-hour value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (5.33-6.50 inches) for a 50-year average recurrence interval (.02 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

The COOP site at Rocky  Mount (RYMV2) measured 4.56 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 23rd. This was the 9th highest daily rainfall recorded at this station since records began in 1894 and 3rd highest in September.

Multiple roads were reported throughout Rockingham County due to heavy rainfall of 2 to 3 inches in several hours. This followed heavy rains the day before as well. At least two roads were severely damaged as culverts were washed out and sinkholes formed. The most damage occurred on Webb Road where pipes under the road collapsed and the road was swept away. A tobacco farm nearby suffered flood damages with approximately $100,000 in losses. A private road was damaged cutting off access for nine persons living along Sunrise Acres Road.
Up to two feet of water was reported flowing over Lake Lemar Road due to overflow from Lake Lemar.

Reidsville 2 NW COOP station (RDVN7) measured 2.67 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM EDT on the 3rd. This was the highest ever for this date and the 8th highest August daily rainfall amount, with data back to 1962.
Eden COOP station (EDEN7) measured 2.30 inches for the 24-hour period ending at  700 AM EDT on the 3rd. This was the highest ever for the date with continuous station data back to 1950.
A TV viewer reported flooding at Bridge Street and Memorial Boulevard.
Martinsville FP COOP (MARV2) measured 1.93 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 8 AM EDT on the 3rd. This was the highest ever for this date, with nearly complete data back to 1931.

A CoCoRaHS station at Lynchburg 1.3 SSW (VA-BD-19) measured 6.05 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 330 AM EST on the 3rd. According to local mesonet stations and NWS radar most of the rain fell in intense storms during about a 3-hour period between 500 and 800 PM  late afternoon and evening on August 2nd. For a 24-hour period this is roughly a 25-year rain event (.04 annual exceedance probability) but much more extreme (near 1000-year event) for the approximately 3-hour duration of the rain.

A CoCoRaHS station at Lynchburg 2.5 NNW (VA-LYC-1) measured 6.00 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 800 AM EST on the 3rd. According to local mesonet stations and NWS radar most of the rain fell during intense storms over about a 3-hour period between 500 and 800 PM on August 2nd. For a 24-hour period this is roughly a 25-year rain event (.04 annual exceedance probability) but much more extreme (near 1000-year event) for the approximately 3-hour duration of the rain.

Extreme rainfall of 4 to 6 inches in several hours produced widespread flash flooding in the City of Lynchburg. The first reports began around 515 PM local time (415 PM EST) and continued for several hours with numerous roads closed by water running over them, vehicles flooded, water rescues and several properties flooded or threatened.  Several apartment complexes and nearby cars were flooded. The runoff into College Lake caused water to overflow the dam (which is also Lakeside Road) to a depth of at least 12 to 18 inches and into Blackwater Creek. The overtopping is considered a partial failure of the dam but a  complete failure of the structure was possible. This resulted in a Flash Flood Warning for a dam failure and subsequent evacuation of about 120 homes in the downstream watershed of Blackwater Creek. According to local City officials flood damage exceeded $18 million in roads, property and water control structure damages, the biggest to College Lake Dam.
Big Elkin Creek flooded large portions of Elkin Municipal Park to a depth of 4 to 5 feet and water up to 2 feet deep was observed running across Memorial Park Drive.
Thunderstorm winds brought down trees along Congo Road and Buck Road. One of the trees came down on a power line causing a fire.
Heavy rains combined with thunderstorm winds brought down trees and power lines in Woolwine.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree onto Phil Road.
Thunderstorm winds brought down several trees two miles north of Penhook Palmers Marina.
Thunderstorm winds knocked a tree over onto Penns Store Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a tree at the intersection of Mount Olivet Road and U.S. Business 58.
Thunderstorm winds caused substantial damage along Dearing Ford Road in Lynch Station. Numerous trees were brought down and the steeple was blown off of the Bethany Ebenezer United Methodist Church.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree three miles southwest of Hurt.
Thunderstorm winds brought down a tree three miles north of Blairs.
Thunderstorm winds brought down a couple of trees from Stony Mill Road to Silver Creek Road.
Thunderstorm winds damaged or destroyed several tents at the Beaver Dam Farm Sunflower Festival.
Lightning struck a tree and caused damage to the siding on a house.

Gusty winds brought down one tree on Route 421 near the Tennessee state line and another near the intersection of Bamboo and Deerfield Roads. Both instances caused temporary road closures. Other trees were blown down around Boone.
CoCoRaHS observer measured 5.10 inches for 24-hours ending at 7 AM EDT. This is roughly a 10-year event (0.1 annual exceedance probability).
Route 880N at Stateline Bridge Road was closed due to flooding.
Road closed due to flash flooding from Bearskin Creek near the intersection of Irish and Bearskin Roads.
The COOP observer at Chatham measured 2.50 inches for 24-hours ending at 7 AM EST on the 20th. This was the highest ever for this date. Continuous records at this site date back to 1922.
Jack Pointer Road was closed due to flash flooding along Kilgore Creek, with water reported over the bridge.
The COOP observer at Bluestone Dam recorded 1.90 inches for the 24 hours ending at 7 AM on the 31st of August, the highest ever for the date and 6th highest in the month of August.
County dispatch reported flooded roads in Princeton including portions of Stafford Drive and Kirk Road.
Several roads were flooded in the Athens area.

Flooding closed several streets in Radford with water over 2 feet deep reported on 2nd Street. In addition, up to 15 building on the Radford University campus had some water damage, with 12 of those described as significant damage. Two roads in Radford were also damaged, Wadsworth and Fairfax Streets.
Several roads were closed including North Fork Road and several around the Virginia Tech campus.

A few trees were blown down due to strong winds. One fell on Route 18 near the intersection with the Blue Ridge Parkway. A second fell onto Napco Road in Sparta. A third was also reported down over Shawtown Road in Glade Valley.

Beginning as early as Friday the 14th, Emergency Services had already reported eight separate instances of trees or power lines brought down by strong winds. Winds would continue through Sunday when a rain soaked ground in Surry County would help to bring down many more trees.

Strong winds combined with saturated ground toppled numerous trees across the county. Wilkes County Communications fielded about 60 call regarding fallen trees beginning around noon on Sunday. By Sunday night, 1,300 customers within the county were without power.
Strong winds combined with saturated ground caused at least three trees to be blown down, mainly near Route 421 to the west of Yadkinville.
Strong winds and saturated ground combined to knock over at least 40-50 trees beginning on Friday through Sunday night.

Several reports of flash flooding from the Timberlake area of Campbell County. Sunburst Road was flooded and impassable with more than a foot of water over it. Three feet of was over Timberlake and Woodhaven Road with a vehicle trapped. Buffalo Creek was well outof its banks and flooding Route 460. A swift was rescue was reported in this area. In addition, water was observed flowing over the spillway of Timberlake Dam. In the aftermath up to eight roads in the county were reported with some type of structural damage. Two homes were also reported to have been damaged.
There were several reports of roads washed out or overtopped in the Forest area  including Spring Lake Road, Bethel Church Road, Terry Place and Goose Hollow Road.
The CoCoRaHS observer at Hyco (NC-CS-1) measured 3.00 inches in 24-hours ending at 730 AM local time.

The COOP observer ay South Boston (SBNV2) measured 5.20 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12, 2018. This was the 5th highest 24-hour rainfall on record for this station and easily the highest in October. Complete records date back to 1980 at this station.

The COOP observer at Keysville 2 S (KYSV2) measured 9.02 inches for the 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time, October 12, 2018. This was the highest 24-hour rainfall amount at this station with partial data back to 1979. The old record was 5.50 inches in July, 2005. In addition, the 9.02 inches is the 3rd highest 24-hour amount for any COOP station in the climate record for the NWS Blacksburg. According to the observer, most of this rain fell in about a 3.5 hour period on the afternoon of the 11th. For the 24-hour duration 9.02 inches falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (8.19-10.2 inches) for a 200-year (.002 annual chance event). For a duration of even 6 hours (being very conservative) the rainfall frequency was in excess of the 1,000 year event (.001 annual chance).
The CoCoRaHS site at Saxe 4.3 SE (VA-CH-1) measured 6.15 inches in 24-hours ending 700 AM local time, October 12, 2018.
The CoCoRaHS site at Brookneal 2.9 E (VA-CM-10) measured 4.90 inches for 24-hour period ending at 700 AM local time, October 12, 2018.

Strong winds combined with saturated ground knocked over multiple trees, most noticeably in the areas of Cana and Lambsburg Mountain. A tree also fell on a car on Paul's Creek Road, but the driver was not injured.
Strong winds and saturated ground caused multiple trees to fall. One tree that fell over Northside Drive in Martinsville caused a three vehicle accident that shut down the road for two hours.
Strong winds combined with saturated ground caused an estimated ten trees to fall, mainly on the night of Sunday the 16th.
Strong winds combined with saturated ground caused multiple trees to come down across the county, but mainly noted in the Baywood area.
Strong winds caused multiple power lines to come down on Norfolk Street and the Southern Main Rail Line.

Strong winds combined with saturated ground knocked over a couple of trees. One tree fell at the intersection of South Constitution Route and Self Road, and the other fell at intersection of Sharon Church and Betties Branch Roads. Both trees caused some impact to travel.

Strong winds combined with saturated ground caused many trees to fall down, taking out power lines and creating road closures. By 3 PM Monday, 320 customers within the county were still without power.
In Laurel Springs, trees were blown down near route 18.
Thunderstorm winds below down a power line on Barney Venable Road.

The COOP site at Boone 1 SE (BOON7) measured 5.24 inches in 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 11th. This was the 2nd highest 24-hour rainfall total in October (after the 5.95 inches October 24, 2017) and 8th highest for any day since records began in 1980.

The COOP site at Sparta 3.5 SSW (SPRN7) measured 4.45 inches in 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time. This was the 5th highest 24-hour rainfall total for any October day, with data from 1942-2009 and starting again in 2018.

The COOP site at North Wilkesboro (WKSN7) measured 5.17 inches in 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 11th. This was the 2nd highest 24-hour rainfall during the month of October and 6th highest for any day, with records dating back to 1921. This value also falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (4.88-5.82 inches) for a 10-year recurrence interval event (.10 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.
The Little Falling River overflowed Morris Church Road (Route 646) southwest of Red House. The road was closed by State Police.
A spotter reported running water up to hubcaps on several vehicles on Magnolia Aveune near 22nd and 23rd Streets.
Rocks Church Road (SR 620) was closed by flooding near Suanee Creek Road.

The COOP station at Appomattox, VA (APXV2) measured 2.92 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time on September 2nd. This was the highest ever for the date (the old record was 1.30 inches in 1957) and the 11th highest ever in the month of September. Nearly continuous data back to 1938 exists at this location.
U.S. Route 58 and Fieldview Road in western Carroll County was flooded and closed with water over the road. Flash flooding was also reported in several creeks in the Faddis Hill area.

The COOP station at Lewisburg 3 N (LWBW2) had 2.00 inches in the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM local time on September 8th which is the highest ever on this date. The old record was 1.90 inches in 1969. Nearly continuous climate records at this station date back to 1900.
Evans Road near Ennice was reported under water and Glade Valley Road was reported to have been underwater where it crosses Brush Creek.

The COOP observer at Elkin (EKNN7) measured 5.00 inches for the 24-hours ending 700 AM local time on September 17th. This was the 2nd highest daily rainfall for any day in September and the 6th highest for any date. Continuous records extend back to 1933 at this station.

Glade Valley 3.0 ENE CoCoRaHS (NC-AG-3) measured 8.09 inches for the 24 hours ending 0900 local time on the 17th. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (7.28-8.91 inches) for a 100-year average recurrence interval (.01 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2. The observer had a 2-day storm total of 9.13 inches.

The COOP observer at Sparta (SPRN7) measured 7.64 inches for the 24-hours ending 700 AM local time on September 17th. This was the highest daily rainfall for any date on record at this station. The old record was 7.10 inches August 31, 1964. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (7.02-8.57 inches) for a 50-year average recurrence interval (.02 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2. Continuous precipitation data began in 1942 and ended in mid-2010 but resumed in mid-2018 at this station.

The COOP observer at Boone 1 SE (BOON7) measured 5.00 inches for the 24-hours ending 700 AM local time on September 17th. This was the 2nd highest daily rainfall for any September day at this station. The existing record is 7.64 inches September 8, 2004. Continuous precipitation data began in 1980 at this location.

Boone 4.5 SE CoCoRaHS (NC-WT-24) station measured 6.70 inches for the 24 hours ending 0700 local time on the 17th. This value falls into the confidence interval (5.82-6.97 inches) for a 10-year average recurrence interval (.10 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

Willis 2.7 SE CoCoRaHS (VA-FL-6) measured 7.78 inches for the 24 hours ending 0700 local time on the 17th. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (7.63-9.31 inches) for a 25-year average recurrence interval (.04 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

Copper Hill 6.2 S CoCoRaHS (VA-FL-2) measured 7.10 inches for the 24 hours ending 0600 local time on the 17th. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (6.66-8.07 inches) for a 50-year average recurrence interval (.02 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

Meadows of Dan 2.3 E CoCoRaHS (VA-PR-5) measured 7.60 inches for the 24 hours ending 0800 local time on the 17th. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (7.01-8.37 inches) for a 25-year average recurrence interval (.04 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

The COOP observer at Yadkinville 6 E (YKNN7) measured 4.11 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12. This was the 2nd highest 24-hour rainfall in the month of October at this station, behind October 11, 1990 at 4.50 inches and the 11th highest all-time daily rainfall. Nearly complete records date back to 1940 at this station. Most of the rain actually fell in a much shorter time period, between 3 and 6 hours.

The COOP observer at Eden (EDEN7) measured 6.08 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12. This was the 2nd highest 24-hour all-time rainfall at this station, behind the 7.92 inches on August 31, 1996. Nearly complete records date back to 1950 at this station. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (5.73-6.68 inches) for a 25-year average recurrence interval (.04 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2. Most of the rain actually fell in a much shorter time period, between 3 and 6 hours.

Patrick County was declared a Major Disaster under the Presidential Declaration. Calls to 911 dispatch about flooding began shortly 1250 AM EST with water reported near some homes Riverside Drive along Poorhouse Creek in Stuart. At the same time water was also over the road on portions of  Jeb Stuart Highway (Route 58) just north of Stuart. Several other roads were later reported closed with up to 1.5 feet of water flowing across Jacks Creek Road. The river gage on the Smith River near Woolwine (SMWV2) gage showed a rise in less than six hours to a crest of 12.35 feet, Minor flood stage is 9 feet and Moderate flood stage 11 feet. This was the 2nd highest reading at this gage since data started there in 1995 and was roughly a 5-10 year annual recurrence interval (0.20 to 0.10 annual exceedance probability).

Numerous roads were closed across Floyd County with the first report along Thunderstruck Road. Other reports of roads flooded and closed included Woods Gap Road, Franklin Pike, Poor Farm Road, Shooting Creek Road, Twin Falls Road, Spring Dale Road, and Spangler Mill Road. The road at Spangler Mill was reported damaged. County officials urged people in about 300 households in floodplains to evacuate. National Guard units rescued one person from a vehicle stranded in a flooded roadway around 500 AM local time.

Halifax County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Rainfall of 4 to 8 inches in several hours triggered widespread flash flooding across the county with numerous roads closed and extensive damage. County officials described it as 'the worst, most devastating storm we've ever seen in the county'. The 911 dispatch center had more than 300 calls for assistance between 5:00 and 7:00 PM on the 11th and more than 700 by 7:00 AM the next day Among the reports received was Lawless Creek as much as 300 feet out of its banks and flooding a church. News photos showed a portion of Pumping Hill Road near Nathalie completely destroyed. Several water rescues were made, including one on Terry���s Bridge Road near Scottsburg on Friday morning the 12th. A debris flow closed a portion of Route 58 in southwest Halifax.

Charlotte County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. There was widespread flash flooding across the county with numerous roads closed and damaged. Two people lost their lives after being swept off a bridge into floodwaters. The fatalities occurred after a car stranded on a Mt. Harmony Road bridge around 728 PM local Thursday. The Charlotte County Sheriff's office stated that the vehicle originally had three occupants who were said to be clinging to the bridge railings. A 17-year-old male was able to be rescued, while the two other adults, one male the other female were swept away in the flood waters.

Significant flash flooding occurred across Yadkin County with at least a half-dozen roads closed as of early Monday morning, the 17th.  These included Dinkins Bottom Road, Butner Mill Road, South Jonesville Boulevard, Richmond Hill Road at the Rockford bridge, Aquila Creek Road and Old 421 East in the Forbush area remained closed to traffic due to flooding on the roads.

Numerous roads were closed across the county with the first reports received around 830 PM local time. Many roads were still closed the next morning according to newspaper accounts. Jacobs Creek near Madison and Troublesome Creek near Reidsville were both reported out of their banks and flooding nearby areas.

The river gage on the Mayo River near Price, NC (PRIN7) in northwest Rockingham County rose above the flood stage of 8 feet and crested in the Moderate flood category at 11.20 feet (13,600 cfs) mid-morning of the 17th. This was the 6th highest stage on record at this gage with over 65 years of data. According to USGS analysis, the flood frequency for the event was between a 5- and 10-year (0.2 to 0.1 annual chance of occurrence). Parts of Mayo Beach Road near the river were flooded.

The river gage on the Dan River near Wentworth, NC (WENN7) rose above the flood stage of 19 feet and crested just below the Moderate flood category (25 feet) at 24.88 feet (28,900 cfs) mid-morning of the 17th. This was the 8th highest stage on record at this gage since records began in 1940 and the highest since 2003. According to USGS analysis, the frequency for the event was approximately a 10-year flood (0.1 annual chance of occurrence). Several roads were flooded and closed near the confluence of the Mayo and Dan rivers in the Madison area per local news reports.

Town Fork Creek was reported out of its banks and flooding portions of Walnut Cove. Flat Shoals Creek was also flooding parts of Sunset Park. The Dan River was out its banks and flooded Dan River Shores Road.

Several low water bridges along the Roaring River and East Prong of the Roaring River were flooded and closed. Several culverts were blocked and caused flooding in North Wilkesboro. A small pond overtopped in Moravian Falls and caused flooding on Falls Road.|In the Broadway community a man clearing debris from the mouth of a culvert was sucked into the culvert up to his waste by the strong current of the rain-swollen stream. Reports said the man freed himself by the time Broadway firefighters arrived. The man received scratches but declined treatment at the scene.

There were numerous reports of flash flooding in Danville. A home was collapsed on Mt. Carmel Baptist Street with the residents being rescued by boat. Another person was rescued from rising waters along Riverside Drive even as others passed through the floodwaters. Up to 69 vehicles were damaged or destroyed at Woodall Chevrolet in Danville along with some building damage as water from local runoff and possibly from an unnamed stream just to the west of the dealers rose.  A nearby NAPA auto parts store was also flooded.  Four vehicles were fully or partially submerged along Timberlake Drive and Northmont Boulevard with no injuries or rescues.

A personal weather station in the Woodbury Hills area of Danville measured 2.64 inches of rain in one-hour between about 1000 and 1100 PM local time and 4.17 inches in 3.5 hours. Flash flooding was widespread in the city.
Water was reported flowing over Highway 122. A private bridge over the East Fork Beaverdam Creek was badly damaged from the flooded creek, shown in a video on local media.

The CoCoRaHS observer at Cave Spring 2.4 SSW (VA-RN-1) measured 5.55 inches of rain in the 24-hours ending at 0700 local time on the 23rd. Most of this fell in thunderstorms over several hours during the late evening hours of the 22nd. Flash flooding was reported in the County.

There were several reports of flash flooding in Roanoke County including water flowing across Cotton Hill Road and Penn Forest Boulevard. Back Creek Road was flooded and closed. In addition, Mud Lick Creek overflowed in the Garst Mill area.

Several roads were reported to have been flooded in northern Franklin County. Little Ellie Creek flooded Sample Road near Peters Pike Road. Foul Ground Creek flooded Brooks Mill Road and a vehicle was swept away in the water but no injuries were reported. Doe Run flooded Ashpone Tavern Road.
Riverbend Road in Altavista and Johnson Creek Road were flooded and closed.
Doe Run flooded Ashpone Tavern Road near Doe Run Road.

The CoCoRaHS observer at Boones Mill 5.5 E (VA-FR-15) measured 5.24 inches of rain in the 24-hours ending at 0700 local time on the 23rd. Most of this fell in thunderstorms over several hours during the late evening hours of the 22nd. Flash flooding was reported in various locations across the county.

There were several reports of flash flooding in the county including water over Highway 58 near Cloverdale Lumber. County Road 729 southeast of Keeling was washed out and a vehicle stuck in the water and another vehicle was stuck in high water along Little Sandy Creek. On Twitter the public tweeted that a bridge on Birch Creek Road off Route 360 was flooded. News reports said 13 roads were closed in the county, some sustaining heavy damage.

Significant flooding took place in the Peterstown area as  home along WV Highway 12 northwest of town was flooded and had to be evacuated as water rose in the home. A car in Peterstown was submerged and the passengers rescued. Extensive flooding also occurred in the Linside area with several cars flooded and abandoned along Route 219 and a water rescue of several passengers from one car. A home was badly damaged in Linside as a basement wall collapsed.

There were several reports of flash flooding across Greenbrier County. The tunnel on Route 63 at Howards Creek was flooded as the creek was out of its banks. A car was reported stuck in flood waters in the tunnel. Route 92 was flooded in various locations and there were several mud and rockslides along the road.

State Route 755, Persimmons Road was closed by flooding. The nearby South Fork Roanoke River gage at Shawsville  (SHA 2) crested at just over Minor flood stage of 5 feet, altough it is not clear if this flooding was related.
Calvary Road (Route 119) near Alton was flooded by swift-moving water and closed.
Extensive flooding occurred in the Rich Creek with the downtown area flooded. Some mudslides were reported along Route 460 between Narrows and Rich Creek. State Line Road was flooded and closed.

The COOP site at Bedford (BEDV2) measured 3.95 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 23rd. This was the 4th highest daily rainfall recorded at this station in the month of September with  rainfall records from 1893-1902, 1931-2005 and 2017-present.

Charlotte County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. A report was received of 10 to 12 inches of water flowing over Route 631 from Tanyard Branch. Bluestone Creek also spilled out of its banks and flooded a portion of Route 92. Sunnyside Road was also closed due to flooding from a nearby stream. Runoff per the CREST Hydrologic model was highest in far eastern parts of the county.

The COOP site at Keysville 2 S (KYSV2) measured 3.91 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 18th. This was the 3rd highest daily rainfall recorded in September at this station since records began in 1979 (with a break from 2012-2014) and 9th highest in any month.
Lightning struck a student at Central Middle School while washing their hands in an art classroom. Reports indicate the student was released from the hospital that evening.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 16.30 feet, just over Moderate flood stage of 16 feet very early on the 18th. The peak discharge of 59,800 cfs was very close to a 5-year event (.20 annual chance flood).

The New River at Galax (GAXV2) crested at 10.04 feet (Minor flood stage is 9 ft.), which was the 11th highest stage on record (records back to 1930) and highest stage since November 19, 2003 (11.0 ft.), excluding the ice jam flood of January 2010. According to USGS  this was slightly in excess of a 5-year flood (.20 annual chance) at this is gage.
The river gage at Danville (DVLV2) the crested at 22.96 (32,300 cfs) well above the Moderate flood stage of 20.5 feet and very close to a 10-year event (0.10 Annual chance flood) per USGS data.

A landslide caused by the heavy rains from Florence knocked down a power pole and brought the lines down on a business in Warrensville, causing a large fire. Photos showed the two-story structure enveloped in flames.
A road was closed along Beaverpond creek at Route 102.
A mudslide was reported in the Falls Mills area.

Flash flooding was observed in parts of Roanoke City. Ore Branch flooded near the Ramada Inn on Franklin Road with some hotel customers moved to different locations. Water was also reported flowing over Franklin Road, Brambleton Road and in the Raleigh Court area. A home basement was flooded along Northwest Hershberger Road.

Emergency calls were first received just after midnight related to flash flooding mainly along and near Electric Road. Water was reported flowing over Electric Road and the road was closed, but Roanoke County police rescued five stranded drivers in the general area.  Brambleton Road in the County was also flooded.

The South Fork of the New River near Jefferson (JFRN7) crested at 9.43 feet (Minor flood stage is 8 ft.) in the early morning of the 17th. Several roads are affected at this stage. This was the highest stage since January 31, 2013 at this gage. The discharge of 9460 cfs was approximately a 5 to 10-year event (0.2 to 0.1 annual chance) per USGS. Several roads close to the New River were flooded and damaged according to NC DOT officials.

A 53-year old woman was reported to have drowned in the Roanoke River during flooding from Florence although details were lacking in terms of location and timing. The Roanoke River at Roanoke (RONV2) crested at 11.41 feet (10,200 cfs) around mid-day on the 17th. Minor flood stage is 10 feet. Several low water bridges and the Roanoke Greenway were flooded and closed. This was the highest stage since September 30, 2015 and was roughly a 2- to 5-year flood event (0.5 - 0.2 annual chance flood).

Roanoke County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures.  Route 744E from Bottom Creek Road to Bent Mountain Road was closed due to a  washout. Radar estimated 4 to 6 inches of rain over the southwest part of the county in the 24- hours ending 1200z (700 AM local time) and several IFLOWS rain gages had 4+ inches including 4.40 inches at Witt's Orchard (WITV2) and 4.21 inches at Poor Mtn. (POOV2). The areal extent of flooding was adjusted per runoff from the CREST hydrologic model.

Halifax County was part of Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant flood damage to roads and other structures.  There were several flash flood reports across the county with roads closed across Halifax County including Highway 119 near the VA-NC state line, Railroad Avenue in South Boston and Summit Drive in South Boston.

The Dan River at Paces (PCEV2) flooded into the Moderate category (24 ft.) cresting at 25.74 feet (32900 cfs) early on the 19th. At least one road was flooded and closed, Route 658 (Melon Road). The flooding was just below a 10-year event (0.10 annual chance flood) per USGS data.

The Dan River at South Boston (SBNV2) flooded above the Moderate flood stage category (25 ft.), cresting at 27.06 feet (33,800 cfs) on the 20th. Several roads were closed and businesses along Route 501 in the Riverdale area were affected. Wolftrap Road was also flooded east of the airport.
Flash flooding closed Sycamore Creek Road (3200 Block) as water was flowing across the road.
Rock Island Creek exceeded its banks by almost five feet in depth. Water was also reported over several roads in the county.
Powder Mill Creek flooded a portion of School Board Road behind the Sheetz in Rocky Mount.

Pittsylvania County was part of Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant flood damage to roads and other structures. The time and spatial occurrence was based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model. This indicated that the flash flooding was worst across the eastern parts of the county.

Henry County was part of Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. There were nearly a dozen calls to the county 911 for flooding, including several road washouts and motorists trapped in a flooded vehicle. Residents of Blackberry Mobile Home Park also reported flooding. The time of occurrence is based on reports and the time of highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model.

Martinsville City was included as part of the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. The time of occurrence is based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model.

Franklin County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. The time of occurrence is based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model. Flash flooding was worst across the western parts of the county.

Craig County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with some damage to roads and other structures although the amount of rain and runoff was coniserably lower than areas to the southwest. Radar estimated 1 to 1.75 inches fell across the southwest part of the county.

Botetourt County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. The time of occurrence and spatial extent of flooding is based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model. Flash flooding was worst across the southern parts of the county.

Danville City was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with some damage to roads and other structures. The time of occurrence is based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model. Flash flooding was worst across the eastern part of the city. Danville ASOS (DAN) had 2.09 inches of rain on the 17th. the 3rd highest ever for the date with data back to 1916.

Grayson County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. The automated ran gage at Galax (GAXV2) measured 3.23 inches in the 24-hours ending 1200z (700 AM local time). The time of occurrence is based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model. Flash flooding was worst across the southeastern parts of the county.

The stream gage on Chestnut Creek at Galax (CCKV2) crested at 9.05 feet (4310 cfs) in the early morning hours of the 17th. Minor flood stage is 7 feet. Several roads were closed, including Chestnut Drive at this stage. This was the highest stage since June, 2013  (9.30 ft.) at this gage and was close to a 10-year flood event (0.10 annual chance) per USGS information.
Several low water bridges were flooded in Douthat State Park along Douthat Park Road.
A resident reported a driveway washed out in Millboro with creek nearby running very high.
The Jackson River Turnpike was flooded and the road closed by VDOT.
Minor street flooding was reported in Clifton Forge.

The COOP station at Covington FP (CFPV2) had 2.79 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM local time on the 28th. This was the highest ever on this date (old record 1.77 inches in 2004) and the 4th highest September daily rainfall at this site, with climate records dating back to 1960.
Minor street flooding was reported in Covington.
The James River went into minor flood (flood stage - 16 ft.) at the Lick Run gage (LIRV2) in northern Botetourt County cresting at 17.19 feet (29,200 cfs) early on the 28th.
Fleshman Hollow Road was closed by WV DOT due to flooding.
A TV viewer reported that Stafford Drive in Princeton was flooded.
A viewer reported Greenbrier Avenue in Rainelle was flooded.

The COOP station at Lewisburg (LWBW2) had 1.84 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM local time on the 28th. This was the 2nd highest ever on this date (record is 2.56 inches in 1967). Continuous climate records at this site date back to 1900.

The James River went into minor flood (flood stage - 17 ft.) at the Buchanan gage (BNNV2) in southern Botetourt County cresting at 17.08 feet (32,800 cfs) early on the 28th. Mainly agricultural land was flooded.
Spruce Street in Martinsville was closed due to flooding.
The County dispatch center reported Jones Ridge Road (Route 616) closed due to flooding.

A spotter reported water of 2 to 3 foot depth over Garvey Bridge Road near Rivercamp USA campground in Piney Creek. Flooding may have been from the South Fork of the New River which was above flood stage at the Jefferson gage upstream.

Flooding was observed along portions of the Dan River in Stokes County including at  Moratock Park in Danbury. The Dan River downstream at the Pine Hall gage (PNHN7) crested at 24.91 feet  (15,700 cfs), the highest stage since January, 2010 (25.77 ft.) and the 2nd highest in the short period of record (since 2008) at this gage. Small stream flooding was also reported including Flat Shoal Creek near Sunset Park campground.

The COOP site at Stuart (STUV2) measured 4.49 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 17th. This was the 4th highest daily rainfall in September with nearly complete climate date back to 1923. The record is 6.03 inches set September 28, 2004.

The COOP station at Copper Hill (COHV2) measured 4.61 inches for the 24 hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 17th. This was the 6th highest recorded in the month of September with nearly complete rainfall records extending back to 1940.

The COOP observer at Transou (LSPN7) measured 5.69 inches for the 24-hours ending 700 AM local time on September 17th. This was the 4th highest daily rainfall for any day in September and the 11th highest for any date. Continuous rainfall records extend back to 1946 at this station.

The North Mayo River near Spencer (NMRV2) crested above the Minor flood stage of 8 feet, reaching 9.31 feet (5590 cfs) near midday on the 17th. It was the highest stage since January 25, 2010 (10.95 ft.) and according to USGS studies it was approximately a 5-year event (.20 annual chance flood).
Gambetta Road at the New River Trail was flooded by Chestnut Creek. The stream gage on Chestnut Creek upstream crested about two feet over flood stage.

Pulaski County was included in the Presidential Major Disaster declaration with significant damage to roads and other structures. The time and spatial occurrence was based on the highest runoff from the CREST hydrologic model.

The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) rose very rapidly and crested in the Moderate flood category at 11.52 feet (60900 cfs) mid-afternoon of the 17th. It was the highest stage since the January 31, 2013 flood (12.91 ft.) and was approximately a 5-year flood event (.20 annual chance event) per USGS studies. Several roads close to the river were flooded and closed including Clarks Ferry Road and Julia Simpkins Road.

The New River at Ivanhoe (IVNV2) rose very rapidly and crested at 18.02 feet (44400 cfs) late morning of the 17th. It was the highest stage since the January 31, 2013 flood (19.66 ft.) and the 8th highest since gage records began in 1931.  It was approximately a 10-year flood event (.10 annual chance event) per USGS studies. Shady River Drive in Ivanhoe near the gage was flooded.

The COOP station at Appomattox (APXV2) measured 2.92 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time on September 2nd. It was the highest rainfall for this date with records dating back to 1937.

The Roanoke River IFLOWS gage at Salem Pump Station (SPSV2) rose above the minor flood stage of 7 feet on the morning of the 17th and crested at 10.1 feet. The Mill Lane bridge was closed and flooding occurred along portions of Riverside Drive.

The Roanoke River IFLOWS gage at Salem Pump Station (SPSV2) rose above the minor flood stage of 7 feet on the morning of the 23rd and crested at 9.5 feet toward midday. The Mill Lane bridge was closed and flooding occurred along portions of Riverside Drive.

The CoCoRaHS observer at Cave Spring 2.4 SSW (VA-RN-1) measured 5.40 inches of rain in the 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 12th. Most of the rain fell in thunderstorms over several hours from mid-morning to early afternoon on the 11th. Widespread flash flooding was reported in the County.

The CoCoRaHS observer at Roanoke 5.8 SW (VA-RN-13) measured 5.41 inches of rain in the 24-hours ending at 0700 local time on the 12th. Most of this fell in thunderstorms over several hours  from mid-morning to early afternoon on the 11th. Widespread flash flooding was reported in the County.
The CoCoRaHS observer at Meadows of Dan 2.3 E (VA-PR-5) measured 5.29 inches of rain in the 24-hours ending at 0700 local time on the 12th. Flash flooding was reported in the County.

The COOP observer at Chatham (CHMV2) measured 4.52 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12, 2018. This was easily a date record but also the 10th highest 24-hour rainfall on record for this station and second highest in October (after 6.00 inches on October 3, 1927). Nearly complete rainfall records date back to 1922 at this station.

Several roads were flooded in the county including Bamboo Road near the Boone Airport, a road near the South Fork of the New River and several low water bridges along the Watauga River. The Watauga River gage at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 8.41 feet, over the Minor flood stage of 6 feet.

A trailing band of heavy rain moved across the piedmont during the early to mid-morning hours of the 17th and produced a broad swath of 2 to 4 inches of rain in several hours across central Caswell County. A CoCoRaHS site 2.4 SW of Yanceyville (NC-CS-5) had a storm total of 4.97 inches ending at 700 AM local time on the 18th, much of which fell in during this several-hour period. Dispatch and emergency management reported numerous road closures across the county including portions of Walters Mill Road, Route 62, Route 119, Route 158 East, Jack Pointer Road, Race Track Road and Doll Branch Road. The spatial extent and duration of flooding was partially delineated by unit streamflow from the CREST hydrologic model.

The COOP site at Galax Water Plant (GAAV2) measured 4.50 inches in 24-hours ending at 700 AM local time on the 11th. This was the highest 24-hour rainfall during the month of October and 4th highest for any day, with complete records dating back to 2000 and a brief period from 1907-1910. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (4.00-4.81 inches) for a 10-year recurrence interval event (.10 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

The automated rain gage located at the USGS Galax River gage site (GAXV2) measured 5.03 inches in 24-hours ending 700 AM local time on the 11th. This value falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (4.74-5.73 inches) for a 25-year recurrence interval event (.04 annual exceedance probability) per NOAA Atlas 2.

Brush Creek was reported out of its banks and observed flowing  over Scenic Valley Road which was also shown in a social media post. Other social media posts also showed flash flooding with water over six inches deep flowing across several roads including the intersection of the Blue Ridge Parkway and Highway 18 and Saddle Mountain Church Road near the Blue Ridge Parkway.

Rainfall of 3 to 6 inches in just a few hours caused widespread flash flooding in Caswell County and a local state of emergency was declared at 200 PM local time.  Significant damage occurred to roads and other structures. A high water rescue was reported along a creek flooding over Highway 700 in northern Caswell County and two other calls for water rescues were logged by the 911 dispatch center. Farmer Road near Old N.C. Highway 86 in Blanch was washed out flooding from a small creek. Many roads were reported closed by flooding especially near the Dan River. The County was later included in a request by the state of North Carolina for a Presidential Major Disaster declaration.

There were numerous reports of flash flooding in the Wilkesboro and North Wilkesboro areas as 2 to 4 inches fell in a just a few hours.  News reports called it some of the worst street flooding in 'years'. A mud slide temporarily blocked River Road near the Colonial Drive intersection and North Wilkesboro police helped a woman and a young child exit their car and get to safety when the car stalled in high waters on East Main Street. Flooded locations in Wilkesboro included College and East Main streets. Cub Creek left its banks and flooded portions of Cub Creek Park.
A local mesonet site in downtown North Wilkesboro measured 2.00 inches of rain between about 415 and 515 PM local time. Numerous flash flood reports were received in the area.

The stream gage on Chestnut Creek at Galax (CCKV2) crested at 9.77 feet (4860 cfs) in the evening hours of the 10th. Minor flood stage is 7 feet. Several roads were closed, including Chestnut Drive at this stage. This was the highest stage since Novenber, 2003 (11.91 ft.) at this gage and was between a 10- and 25-year flood event (0.10-0.04 annual chance flood) per USGS information.

All the animals were evacuated from the Galax Veterinary Clinic on Stockyard Road after a mudslide along the road above the clinic brought down a power pole and caused its lines to fall onto the clinic. The Galax Volunteer Fire Department evacuated both pets and staff from the building.
News reports showed a large mudslide along East Stuart Drive that closed the road for several hours.

Mill Creek flooded and several people were evacuated from a mobile home park off of Glade Street. Social media had several reports of flooded roads in Galax including the intersection of Swanson Street and McArthur Street and Glendale Road and Hebron Road.
Social media reported Delhart Road (Route 622) flooded in eastern Grayson County.

Wythe County 911 dispatch reported numerous road closed due to flooding|in eastern Wythe county, mainly in the Max Meadows and Fort Chiswell|areas. Locust Hill Road, Felts lane, Danner Road and Archer Road were|flooding. Ivanhoe Road was also closed.

The New River flooded with the gage at Ivanhoe (IVNV2) rising above the Moderate flood stage of 19 feet, and reaching a peak of 20.05 feet (53100 cfs) on the afternoon of the 11th. This was the highest stage in over 40 years, since November 7, 1977 when the river reached 28.88 feet. According to USGS studies flooding from Michael was between a 10- and 25-year flood event (0.10 to 0.04 annual chance flood). Several roads close to the river were flooded and closed including Ivanhoe Road in Ivanhoe.

The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) flooded,  cresting above the Major flood category (14 feet) at 15.12 feet (99000 cfs) the night of the 11th. It was the highest stage since January 15, 1995 (16.56 ft.) and was approximately a 25-year flood event (.04 annual chance event) per USGS studies. Several roads close to the river were flooded and closed including Clarks Ferry Road and Julia Simpkins Road. Fllooding from the rive was reported along portions of Claytor Lake.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 23.83 feet, over the Major flood stage of 20 feet late on the 11th. The peak discharge of 109,-000 cfs was very close to a 25-year event (.04 annual chance flood) per USGS studies. Several roads close the river were flooded.
Flash flooding was reported on social media along Old Quaker Road near Pipers Gap where Wards Mill Branch crosses the road.  A home was surrounded by rapidly moving water in the photos.

The CoCoRaHS site at Glade Valley 3.0 ENE (NC-AG-3) reported 7.49 inches for the 24 hours ending at 800 AM local time. Streets and fields were flooded and water draining off the hills. According to NOAA Atlas 2, this 24-hour amount falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (6.49-7.85 inches) for a 50-year rain event (.02 annual chance).  The observer also reported 4.21 inches in 8 hours from 800 AM to 400 PM local time.

The CoCoRaHS site at Boone 4.5 E (NC-WT-37) reported 6.73 inches for the 24 hours ending at 730 AM local time.  According to NOAA Atlas 2, this 24-hour amount falls into the 90 percent confidence interval (6.51-7.91 inches) for a 25-year rain event (.04 annual chance).

The Roanoke River at Roanoke gage (RONV2) crested at 16.64 feet on the afternoon of the 11th, above the Major flood stage of 16 feet. It was the 7th highest crest since the current datum was established in 1937 and the highest since September 28, 2004 when the river reached 17.82 feet as the remains of Hurricane Jeanne swept through the area.  In terms of flood frequency the event fell roughly between a 10- and 25-year event (0.10-0.04 annual chance flood).

The outer bands of rainfall associated with now Tropical Storm Michael began reaching Watauga County in the early morning hours of October 11th. Several roads were reported closed and extensive flooding occurred in the town of Boone. The South Fork of the New River was well out if its banks and flooding homes along it in the Holiday Hills area east of Boone. Flooding was also reported at the Watauga Village Shopping Center during the afternoon.

The Roanoke River at Lafayatte (LAAV2) crested at 12.44 feet (16100 cfs) on the evening of the 11th. Moderate flood stage is 11 feet. It was the 6th highest reading at this location since USGS records began in 1944 and the highest since September 28, 2004 (12.45 feet) with the remains of Hurricane Jeanne. In terms of flood frequency it fell between a 10- and 25-year event (0.10-0.04 annual chance flood).

The South Fork of the Roanoke River near Shawsville (SHAV2) crested at 9.18 feet (7880 cfs) on the afternoon of the 11th. Major flood stage is 9 feet. It was the 4th highest reading at this location since USGS records began in 1961. In terms of flood frequency it fell near 10-year event (0.10 annual chance flood). Several roads were closed near the river and homes threatened.

The New River at Glen Lyn (GLLV2) crested at 19.47 feet (121000 cfs) on the morning of the 12th. Major flood stage is 18 feet. It was the 3rd highest reading at this location since USGS records began in 1940 and the highest since January 16, 1995 (19.83 feet). In terms of flood frequency it fell near a 25-year event (0.04 annual chance flood). There were considerable impacts along the New River including several mobile home parks flooded.

The Dan River at Danville (DVLV2) crested at 30.01 feet (50300 cfs) on the evening of the 11th. Major flood stage is 25.5 feet. It was the highest reading at the current gage location since USGS records began in 1996 beating the previous record of 28.65 feet set on September 6, 1996 with the remains of Hurricane Fran. In terms of flood frequency (using regional regression equations) it fell between a 25-and 50-year event (0.04-0.02 annual chance flood). Significant flooding took place in Danville.

The Dan River at Paces (PCEV2) crested at 31.36 feet (55400 cfs) early morning on the 13th. Major flood stage is 27 feet. It was the 4th highest since records began in 1951 and highest since September 7, 1996 (31.43 feet) during the remains of Hurricane Fran. In terms of flood frequency it fell just above a 25-year event (0.04 annual chance flood). Significant flooding took place with several roads closed, although no structures. A water rescue was reported when a motorist went into the flood waters near Paces. Another water rescue also was successful Friday morning for a motorist trapped in a car in the 4000 block of River Road, possibly from the Dan River.

The Dan River at South Boston (SBNV2) crested at 31.36 feet (50900 cfs) on the afternoon of the 13th. Major flood stage is 29 feet. It was the 6th highest reading at this gage since records began in 1924 and the highest since September 8, 1996 (33.32 feet) during the remains of Hurricane Fran. In terms of flood frequency it fell near a 10-year event (0.10 annual chance flood). Significant flooding took place in the South Boston area.

The Yadkin River at Wilkesboro (WKSN7) crested at 14.05 feet (11400 cfs) just above minor flood stage of 14 feet for the first time since August 1994 and the 6th highest since the completion of W. Kerr Scott Reservoir just upstream in 1962. A portion of Wilkesboro Avenue in North Wilkesboro was flooded by the Yadkin River for the first time in over 15 years according to news reports.

The Yadkin River at Elkin gage crested at 21.02 feet (23,200 cfs) on the afternoon of the 11th, just over the Moderate flood stage of 21 feet. It was the 7th highest level since the completion of W. Kerr Scott Reservoir in 1962 and the highest since August 17th, 1994. News reports showed the river well out of its banks and affecting a home along Old U.S. Highway 421.

The Sandy River near Danville (SDRV2) crested at 11.46 feet (14,000 cfs) on the afternoon of the 11th. Moderate flood stage is 10 feet. It was the highest reading at this location since USGS records began in 1943, although nowhere close to the discharge in the record August 1940 flood (23,000 cfs).  In terms of flood frequency it fell near 25-year event (0.04 annual chance flood) according to USGS reports.
Rainfall of 7.75 inches was measured at the Pittsylvania County 911 Center between 1240 PM and 540 PM local time.

Water was reported over Route 100 due to flooding from Walker Creek. The gage at Bane (BANV2) briefly touched minor flood stage of 11 feet (7,800 cfs) very early on the 11th in response to the PRE (Predecessor Rainfall Event) and then had a more significant second rise from the rains directly associated with Michael, reaching a crest of 13.46 (12,000 cfs) feet early on the 12th. Moderate flood stage is 14 feet.

Galax City was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. There were numerous flash flood reports across the City of Galax starting as early as 1100 AM local time and continuing for several hours. Numerous roads were closed and damaged and several evacuations took place.
Seven roads were reported closed across Floyd County due to high water with the first reports at of 1013 AM local time.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 9.0 inches at Neola to 18.0 inches at Alderson.  Several minor traffic accidents occurred due to the snow.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 9.0 inches about three miles east of McRoss to 18.5 inches about two miles east of Lawn.  Several minor traffic accidents occurred due to the snow.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.0 inches at Bramwell to 18.0 inches at Oakvale.  Bluefield received 15.0 inches of snow, which is the second highest storm total in the month of December since records began in 1909.  It is also the earliest in the winter season that an amount this high has ever been recorded.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.0 inches at Lindside to 20.0 inches about two miles south-southeast of Sweet Springs.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 17.0 inches at Bluestone Lake to 20.0 inches about three miles east of Ellison.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 16.0 inches about four miles south-southwest of Sparta to 19.0 inches about two miles south-southeast of Whitehead.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 16.0 inches about two miles southwest of Ashland to 25.0 inches about three miles southeast of Fleetwood.
A snowfall accumulation of 15.4 inches was reported about four miles southeast of Yanceyville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.5 inches at Eden to 16.5 inches about two miles northwest of Reidsville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 10.2 inches at King to 16.1 inches about three miles east-southeast of Woodville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.0 inches about two miles west of Mount Airy to 17.5 inches about four miles north-northeast of Roaring Gap.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 15.0 inches about one mile southeast of Boone to 26.0 inches at Aho.  Six vehicle wrecks were reported with four involving unknown amounts of property damage and two with unknown numbers of injuries.  The Boone police department reported 56 stranded motorists.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 16.0 inches at West Kerr Scott Reservoir to 17.8 inches at North Wilkesboro.  The storm caused 26 vehicle accidents and stranded 41 motorists.  The weight of the snow downed 57 trees, and there were 29 electrical hazards reported mostly due to trees on power lines.  In addition, about 20 people from five families that also included small children were stranded in their homes without power for three days.  Several people from the North Carolina National Guard rescued the families and took them to a shelter.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.0 inches about six miles east of Yadkinville to 14.5 inches at Boonville.  One indirect fatality occurred when a male truck driver got stuck on Interstate 77 several miles north of the Route 421 intersection due to the heavy snow.  He tried to dig his tractor trailer out of the snow but suffered a heart attack while shoveling.  The man later died at a nearby hospital.
A snowfall accumulation of 15.0 inches was reported at Covington.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 11.0 inches about three miles east-southeast of Amherst to 15.4 inches at Pedlar Dam.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 11.0 inches about three miles west-northwest of Evergreen to 13.4 inches at Appomattox.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 4.2 inches about two miles south of Williamsville to 14.0 inches at Millboro.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 10.5 inches at Bedford to 16.3 inches about two miles west-southwest of Chamblissburg.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 14.2 inches about three miles southwest of Long Spur to 17.0 inches at Bland.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.5 inches at Laymantown to 17.5 inches about two miles east of Lithia.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 9.8 inches about seven miles southeast of Dillwyn to 11.0 inches at Buckingham.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 11.0 inches about two miles east of Forest to 15.0 inches at Rustburg.  Lynchburg received 11.7 inches of snow, which is the third highest storm total in the month of December since records began in 1893. It is also the earliest in the winter season that an amount this high has ever been recorded.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 15.0 inches at Galax to 22.0 inches about four miles north-northeast of Woodlawn.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 14.0 inches about three miles north of Wylliesburg to 15.5 inches about two miles south of Keysville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 14.0 inches at New Castle to 14.5 inches about three miles northeast of Abbott.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.5 inches at Copper Hill to 18.4 inches about five miles east-northeast of Alum Ridge.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.5 inches about two miles northeast of Burnt Chimney to 18.5 inches at Snow Creek.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.0 inches at Newport to 14.3 inches about one mile northeast of Pearisburg.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 17.0 inches about three miles south of Comers Rock to 25.8 inches about four miles south-southwest of Elk Creek.
A snowfall accumulation of 15.0 inches was reported at South Boston.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 15.0 inches at Martinsville to 16.8 inches at Bassett.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.2 inches about one mile east south-east of Christiansburg to 15.5 inches about four miles west-southwest of Pilot.  Blacksburg received 13.7 inches of snow, which is the third highest storm total in the month of December since records began in 1952.  It is also the earliest in the winter season that an amount this high has ever been recorded.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.4 inches about three miles west-northwest of Charity to 17.0 inches about three miles east-southeast of Buffalo Ridge.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 11.4 inches about three miles north-northwest of Ringgold to 17.4 inches at Chatham.  Danville received 12.5 inches of snow, which is the second highest storm total in the month of December since records began in 1916.  It is also the earliest in the winter season that an amount this high has ever been recorded.  Also, the weight of the heavy snow collapsed the canopy of the Carrington Pavilion at Danville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.3 inches at Graysontown to 15.8 inches about two miles east of Pulaski.

Snowfall accumulations ranged from 11.0 inches about two miles north-northeast of Salem to 15.2 inches at Roanoke.  The 15.2 inches of snow at Roanoke is the third highest storm total in the month of December since records began in 1912.  It is also the earliest in the winter season that an amount this high has ever been recorded.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 13.5 inches about three miles north-northeast of Rockbridge Baths to 20.0 inches about four miles west-southwest of Buena Vista.
A snowfall accumulation of 13.0 inches was reported about one mile north of Saltville.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 12.0 inches at Richlands to 15.0 inches at Burkes Garden.
Snowfall accumulations ranged from 16.0 inches about one mile north-northwest of Wytheville to 17.4 inches at Wytheville.

A Tornado touched down four miles east-southeast of Crystal Hill at 714 PM EST, traveled northeast, and lifted/dissipated four miles west-southwest of Mt. Laurel|at 717 PM EST. At the maximum of its intensity, it caused EF2 level damage.||Where the tornado touched down was wooded in the 1200 block of Hundley Road. Here, several large trees were uprooted, blown to the north. As the tornado tracked northeast at 40 to 45 mph, it blew several large bales of hay westward across Hundley Road. Farther along its path, the tornado completely lifted the roof of a porch off a single family home, blowing the debris nearly 200 feet to the north into nearby woods. Several large trees were both uprooted and snapped as well.||Farther northeast when the storm reached its peak intensity, several mature 24-36 inch diameter pine trees were snapped while two nearby single family homes sustained significant roof damage. A car on one of the properties was crushed by falling trees. Additionally, when winds were estimated to be at 125 mph a roof was completely blown off a residence. Numerous mature trees on the same property snapped or uprooted with their debris blown in multiple directions. The tornado finally blew the roof off a nearby barn several hundreds yards to the north.||Damage amounts are estimated.

Numerous roads were closed due to flooding and a number of roads were damaged. Reported flooding included Taylor Road and Binkley Road at Baltimore Road. Bloomtown Road sustained damage from the flood waters, causing a portion of the roadway to wash away.  The County was later included in a request by the state of North Carolina for a Presidential Major Disaster declaration. Significant agricultural damage was reported in Yadkin County as well and the county submitted a request for agricultural disaster relief.

Dispatch reports of roads closed by high water started as early as noon with 13 roads reported closed at one time. The CREST hydrologic model indicated the highest runoff across western sections of Surry County. Two water rescues were rerported, one of those  on Rockford Road just before reaching the Yadkin River bridge, and the other was on Longhill Road in the Pilot Mountain area. Flooding along Big Elkin creek flooded portions of the the Elkin High School athletic fields, the Elkin Park and closed Memorial Park Drive. There was damage in to walking trails in the park. In addition, flooding along the Mitchell River destroyed the historic Kapp's Mill dam in the Mountain Park area. The County was later included in a request by the state of North Carolina for a Presidential Major Disaster declaration.

The COOP observer at Elkin (EKNN7) measured 5.50 inches for the 48-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12. This was the 3rd highest 48-hour rainfall in the month of October at this station. Rainfall was 2.20 inches ending at 700 AM on the 11th and 3.30 inches ending at 700 AM on the 12th. Nearly complete records date back to 1913 at this station.

The COOP observer at Reidsville 2 NW (RDVN7) measured 4.65 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM local time, October 12. This was the highest 24-hour rainfall in the month of October at this station, ahead of October 9, 1975 at 4.10 inches and the 5th highest all-time daily rainfall. Nearly complete records date back to 1962 at this station. Most of the rain actually fell in a much shorter time period, between 3 and 6 hours.

The first calls about flooded roadways came in around 1045 AM local time with water reported over a road in Sparta.  Shortly after, a mobile home park was evacuated along Bledsoe Creek near the Sparta bypass and Highway 21. Several other roads were reported to be flooded and closed as well. Rich Hill Road near Ennice was flooded and damaged according to reports. Rainfall estimates per radar and rain gages across eastern Alleghany County ranged up to 6 inches in the 24 hours ending at 700 AM on the 12th.

Multiple roads were reported closed due to flooding across Stokes County, including the Walnut Cove and King areas. The first reports were shortly before 230 PM local time. The County was later included in a request by the state of North Carolina for a Presidential Major Disaster declaration.

Pittsylvania County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Rainfall of 4 to 8 inches in several hours triggered widespread flash flooding across the county with numerous roads closed and extensive damage.  A man lost his life when his automobile was washed off Sandy Creek Road near the 600 block during intense flooding along Sandy Creek.  Media reports indicate the incident occurred around 330 PM local time, with one witness observing that water was flowing rapidly at least two feet above the road surface.

These gusty winds, when combined with the effects of saturated ground due to heavy rain from the storm, resulted in over a dozen trees and power lines down across the county.  One of the the fallen trees landed on a home along Andersonville Road, causing structural damage.

The river gage on the Dan River near Wentworth, NC (WENN7) rose above the flood stage of 19 feet and crested just below the Moderate flood category (25 feet) at 24.27 feet (27,100 cfs) in the evening of the 11th. This was the 9th highest stage on record at this gage since records began in 1940 and just below the crest set during September 2018 with the remains of Florence 2003. According to USGS analysis, the frequency for the event was approximately a 10-year flood (0.1 annual chance of occurrence). Several roads were flooded and closed near the confluence of the Mayo and Dan rivers in the Madison area per local news reports.

Danville City was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Catastrophic flash flooding occurred across the City of Danville as extreme rains of 4 to 8 inches in several hours fell. Two people were killed in Danville after being were caught inside vehicles in the floodwaters and were pulled under rising waters as rescuers struggled to reach them. The first was 53-year old man that occurred at 500 PM local time in the 100 block of Colonial Court. The second occurred around 1020 PM on Goodyear Boulevard, as a 60-year old woman was trapped in her car in floodwaters and drowned. There were at least a dozen other high water rescues reported several of these along Riverside Drive where water was reported up to four feet deep. There was severe road and property damage across Danville with costs running into the millions of dollars. According to an early assessment from the Danville Fire Chief, five properties were completely destroyed, 19  sustained major damage, 55 received minor damage and 117 structures were affected.

Brentwood Community (KVADANVI13) mesonet site reported an hourly precipitation amount of 4.66 inches between 3:04 and 4:04 PM local time with a daily total of 7.68 inches when the power failed. Almost all the rain fell after 11:30 AM. 4.66 inches in 1 hour exceeds the 1000-year (.001 annual chance) precipitation frequency uncertainty interval listed in NOAA Atlas 14 for Danville.

Campbell County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. There were several reports of flash flooding on the afternoon of the 11th with roads closed and verified flood damages exceeded $300 thousand.

Appomattox County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Purdums Branch was several feet out of its banks and flooding apartments along Red House Road. In the town of Appomattox, a woman and boy were rescued after fast-moving water trapped the two in a creek behind their home on Church Street. A team of about 17 first responders with the Concord Appomattox Swiftwater Team responded to the rescue effort around 4:45 PM Local time. The two victims were quickly pulled from the waters without injury according to news reports.

County-wide flooding was reported by law enforcement with at least seven roads were reported closed across Floyd County. An Amateur Radio report said Hale Road in the Terry's Fork area near Check was closed due to flooding and several creeks were well out of their banks. Four vehicles were abandoned in high water on Buffalo Mountain Road, Spangler Mill Road, Daniel's Run Road and Stonewall Road.

Franklin County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Rainfall of 3 to 6 inches occurred in several hours with flash flooding across much of the county. At least eight roads were reported blocked by flowing water across the county with significant damage to infrastructure.

Roanoke County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael. Extremely high sustained rain rates (2-4 inches per hour) became concentrated across parts of the Roanoke area between 1100 AM to 200 PM local time. At 243 PM a rare Flash Flood Emergency was issued for Roanoke City, City of Salem and Roanoke County after consultation with local Emergency management amidst reports of numerous water rescues in the area. Radar and rain gages showed 3 to 6 inches of rain during this period from the southern part of Roanoke City into the adjacent portions of Roanoke County. There were numerous reports of flash flooding across mainly the South County area where the heaviest rains fell, 5 to 6 inches in some locations. Mudlick Creek flooded across Cresthill Drive to a depth of at least one foot. Several small mudslides occurred and numerous roads were closed. There was also reports of high water rescues in several areas including a motorist stranded on Ferguson Valley Road along Back Creek. The USGS gage on Back Creek near Dundee (BCKV2) crested at 23.09 feet (17,000 cfs) in the evening of the 11th at the 2nd highest stage and discharge since records began in 1971 and only slightly below the record flood in November 1985 of 25. 1 feet.

Montgomery County was included in a Presidential Major Disaster declaration due mainly to the severe flooding associated with Tropical Storm Michael.  At least four roads were reported closed across the county including in the Ellett Valley area. At least six inches of moving water was reported over Toms Creek Road near Redbud Road and Toms Creek was out of its banks and flooding Meadowbrook Road in Blacksburg. Elsewhere in Montgomery County 13-year-old became trapped in an all-terrain vehicle in a flooded creek and the New River Valley swift-water rescue team helped to rescue the teenager.

Extremely high sustained rain rates (2-4 inches per hour) became concentrated across parts of the Roanoke area between 1100 AM to 200 PM local time. At 243 PM a rare Flash Flood Emergency was issued for Roanoke City, City of Salem and Roanoke County after consultation with local Emergency management amidst reports of numerous water rescues in the area. Radar and rain gages showed 3 to 6 inches of rain during this period from the southern part of Roanoke City into the adjacent portions of Salem. At least 25 roads or intersections were closed at some point due to flooding in Salem. Mason Creek flooded several mobile home communities in Salem as shown on social media. More than 40 people were evacuated from threatened homes. Mason creek crested at the upstream IFLOWS gage (MSCV2) at 7.90 feet around noon, NWS Minor flood stage is 7 feet.   The state of Virginia declared Salem as a Small Business Administration Disaster area.

The Roanoke River through Salem flooded due to the heavy rainfall from Michael and the predecessor rainfall event. Several roads were closed and businesses affected by the flood waters. The Riverwalk Apartments along the Roanoke River in Salem were evacuated and 42 units received flood damage. The crest at the Salem Pump Station IFLOWS gage (SPSV2) was 14.6 feet very early on the 12th, just over the Moderate flood stage of 14 feet and well above Minor flood stage of 7 feet. It was the 3rd highest crest at this gage in the existing record back to 1972 and the highest since the November 1985 flood when the river reached 20.5 feet at this location.

The Roanoke River at Glenvar (GNVV2) crested at 17.10 feet (18600 cfs) on the evening of the 11th. Major flood stage is 16 feet. Several roads were closed near the river but it is unclear if homes or structures were affected. It was the 4th highest reading at this location since USGS records began in 1992 and the highest since September 28, 2004 (12.45 feet) with the remains of Hurricane Jeanne. In terms of flood frequency it near 10-year event (0.10 annual chance flood) per USGS studies.

There were several reports of flash flooding in Wythe County with a number of roads closed in Wytheville and the eastern portions of the county as early as 900 AM local time. Reed Creek reportedly flooded East Lee Highway bear Carter's Park. The New River trail was flooded near Max Meadows although probably from the flooded New River itself.

Several roads were closed in Pulaski County and the town due to flooding. Peak Creek flooded several roads including Crescent Street, Lottier Bottom Road and Main Street. The creek crested at around 8 feet on a staff gage in town calibrated to the IFLOWS gage (PCRV2) which was out of service during the event. Minor flood stage is 8 feet.

The USGS automated Data Collection Platform located at the Roanoke (Staunton) River gage near Randolph (RNDV2) measured 4.73 inches in 3 hours and 5.78 inches in 4 hours. For the 3-hour duration the 500-year recurrence confidence interval (.002 annual chance rainfall) is 4.41-5.92 inches.

Bands of heavy rainfall from Tropical Storm Michael began rotating across the county in the mid-morning and amounts from 2 to 4 inches in several hours were observed. According to later news reports several businesses on 10th Street in North Wilkesboro had water enter their buildings. Cub Creek flooded a portion of Cub Creek Park in Wilkesboro. Flooding was also reported in the Roaring River community where part of the road between NC 268 East and the bridge over the Yadkin was flooded. The Reddies River at North Wilkesboro (REDN7) contributed to the flooding and crested at its highest stage (11.35 feet) since November, 1989 when it reached 11.72 feet.  Several bridges across the upper Reddies were flooded.

Numerous roads were closed due to flooding in Carroll County. A daycare center was evacuated near a small creek flooding along Fisher Road. Brush Creek near Ivanhoe was reported out of its banks and entering several nearby homes.
Wards Mill Branch was flooded and out of its banks, flowing across Coal Creek Road.

Heavy rains of 3 to 6 inches caused numerous creeks to escape their banks forcing the closure of several primary and secondary roads. The river gage on the Smith River near Woolwine (SMWV2) showed a rise in less than six hours to a crest of 12.15 feet, Minor flood stage is 9 feet and Moderate flood stage 11 feet. This was the 4th highest reading at this gage since data started there in 1995 and was roughly a 5-year annual recurrence interval (0.10 annual exceedance probability).

Heavy rains led to some flash flooding as to 2 to 3 inches fell in a short period. Lynchburg Airport ASOS (LYH) set a daily record rainfall for October 11th of 2.58 inches, with records back to 1893. The old record was 1.76 inches in 1990. Flooding was reported along a Ivy Creek with water flowing across Ivy Drive.  City of Lynchburg officials activated the Emergency Action Plan for College Lake dam early Thursday as a result of the heavy rain but did not have to evacuate any residents or businesses downstream of  the dam along Blackwater Creek. Several other roads were reported closed in Lynchburg including Greenwood Drive where it crosses Ivy Creek.

The Danville ASOS rain gage (DAN) failed due to a power outage during the fierce storm, but the backup site measured 6.00 inches for October 11th (24-hour period ending at midnight). This is the highest daily rainfall ever recorded at Danville with data back to 1916. The previous record was 5.81 inches on August 27, 2008.
