Downpours from Michael dropped 3 to 6 inches of rain in a just a few hours Henry County causing numerous road closures starting as early at 100 PM local time. There were several water rescues from cars stranded in the water, including one on Reeves Road near Martinsville.

Rainfall of 3 to 5 inches in just a few hours caused flash flooding across parts of Buckingham County. A road was washed out near the intersection of Sycamore creek abd Wood land Church Road. Sharps Creek was flooded across Diana Road washing a vehicle into the stream and some distance downstream before a successful water rescue was carried out. The Slate River near Arvonia (ARVV2) crested at 15.1 feet, above the Minor flood stage of 12 feet.

A bridge over Catawba Creek on Hogan Hollow Road (Route 737) was reportedly underwater. The USGS gage on Catawba Creek near Catawba (CTWV2) crested at 7.92 feet (Minor flood stage is 7 feet), its highest level since September, 2004 when it reached 10.3 feet.

Sinking Creek was reported flooding a portion of New Zion Road (Route 625), closing the road. A temporary USGS gage on Sinking Creek near Newport showed a rise of over 4 feet in stream height from the onset of rain on the 21st to the pea of 8.15 feet on the evening of the 23rd.

Danville ASOS (DAN) recorded 1.88 inches of rain for the 24-hours ending at midnight which was a record for the date (Feb. 23). The previous record was 0.99 inches in 1961. Precipitation records at Danville date back to 1916.

Water was reported over Robertson Bridge near Memorial Drive by the public and relayed by local media. The Dan River at Danville crested at 23.3 feet late on the 23rd, well above the Minor flood stage of 17 feet and above the Moderate flood stage of 20.5 feet.

A car was reported to be stuck in flood waters on Lurich Road along the New River. The New River at Glen Lyn (GLLV2) crested at 15.1 feet, just above the Minor flood stage of 15 feet just before noon on the 24th. The peak discharge at this gage of 75400 cfs was close to a 5-year recurrence interval (0.20 annual chance flood) according to USGS data.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 15.79 feet early on the 24th. Minor flood stage is 14 feet. The peak discharge of 57900 cfs was slightly less than a 5-year annual recurrence interval event (0.20 annual chance flood) per USGS studies. Several roads close the river were flooded.
County dispatch reported that Old Ebenezer Road west of Marion was flooded and closed.
Thomas Bridge Road near Adwolf was flooded and closed.
Coles Creek Road was closed from flooding.
Carwile Spring Road was closed due to flooding, possibly from Wards Fork Creek.
Cobbs Knob Road from Cascade Road to the NC state line was closed due to flooding.
Northside Drive near the intersection with Cheney Lane was closed due to urban type flooding, no stream was involved.
Jacobs Road near the intersection with Shula Drive was closed due to urban type flooding, no stream was involved.

A portion of Riverside Road near Adwolfe was closed due to flooding, likely from the South Fork of the Holston River. The South Fork Holston River at Chilhowie gage about 3 miles downstream from Adwolfe crested at 6.60 feet around 700 PM on the 23rd, slightly below the Minor flood stage of 7 feet. The peak discharge of at this gage of 2740 cfs was very close to a 2-year recurrence interval (0.50 annual chance of exceedance) according to USGS data.
A portion of Hutton Branch Road was reportedly washed out by flood waters, most likely from Hutton Branch. The road was also reported closed by VDOT due to the flooding.

Several roads along the Bluestone River in Montcalm were flooded with high water signs placed in several locations. The Bluestone River gage at Spanishburg (SPNW2) crested at 13.10 feet, slightly above the Minor Flood Stage of 12 feet. Well downstream at Pipestem (PIPW2) the Bluestone crested at 11.84 feet early on the 24th, above the Minor flood stage of 10 feet.
A water rescue was reported of two occupants stranded in a car in rising waters on Laurel Creek Road. The victims were transported to the hospital with no further updates.

The COOP station at Princeton (PRIW2) measured 1.12 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM local time on February 23rd, which is the highest ever for the date. The old record was 0.85 inches in 1987. Nearly complete precipitation data for this station exists from 1901-1914 and from 1941 up until the present.

Several news sources reported a large landslide along Route 112 near Oakvale. Photos from the scene showed a home had been moved downhill and the road was blocked by a large mass of debris. The area had received several days of rainfall ranging from 1 to 2.5 inches which was preceded by snow and mixed precipitation.

Numerous roads were closed across the county but further details were not provided. The South Fork New River at Jefferson (JFRN7) crested at 6.89 feet, which is above the Action Stage of 5 feet, but below the Minor Flood stage of 8 feet.
The County dispatch center reported Butner Mill Road in East Bend closed by high water.
The Dan River at Wentworth (WENN7) crested above the Minor Flood stage of 19 feet reaching 22.63 feet. Several roads were flooded near the river.
The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) crested at 10.64 feet, above the Minor Flood stage of 8 feet. Several roads near the river were flooded including Julia Simpkins and Clarks Ferry Road.

The Dan River at Paces (PCEV2) crested at 26.22 feet, above the Moderate Flood stage of 24 feet and close to the Major Flood stage of 27 feet. The only reported impacts were roads closed, including Route 658. The peak discharge of 38900 cfs was roughly mid-way between a 10-year recurrence interval (0.10 annual chance of exceedance) and 25-year recurrence interval (0.04 annual chance flood) according to USGS data.

A winter storm produced freezing rain, sleet and snow in Eastern Greenbrier county. Ice from freezing rain reached a depth of 0.13 inches near Lewisburg, while 0.5 inches of sleet was reported across the county. Snow amounts ranged from 2 to 3 inches across the county.
A winter storm produced freezing rain and snow in Western Greenbrier county. Ice from freezing rain was reported to a thickness of 0.1 inches, while snow amounts ranged from 2 to 5 inches.

A winter storm produced freezing rain, sleet and snow in Summers county. Ice from freezing rain was reported in trace amounts, and sleet accumulated to a depth of 0.5 inches near Hinton, while snow amounts ranged from 1 to 3 inches around the county.
A winter storm produced freezing rain and snow in Mercer county. Ice from freezing rain reached a thickness of 0.15 inches near Athens, while snow amounts ranged from 0.1 to a maximum of 4.0 inches.

A winter storm created freezing rain, sleet and snow in Monroe county. Ice from freezing rain reached depths ranging from trace amounts to 0.5 inches, and 0.5 inches of sleet were reported near Wayside. Snow amounts ranged from 2 inches to 4 inches.

The Roanoke (Staunton) River flooded with the Randolph gage cresting at 26.12 feet, above the Minor flood stage of 24 feet. Flood stage categories were raised at this gage in August 2018. Black Walnut Road road in Halifax County was closed as a result of the flooding.

The Roanoke River at Brookneal (BROV2) crested at 25.67 feet early on the 24th above the Minor flood stage of 23 feet. This was the highest stage at Brookneal since January 26, 2010 when the river reached 28.2 feet. Flooding was mainly in lowland fields and woods. According to USGS data however the peak discharge of  31500 cfs was only about a 2-year recurrence interval event (0.50 annual chance flood).

The Dan River at South Boston (SBNV2) crested at 27.3 feet on the evening of the 25th, above the Moderate Flood stage of 25 feet.  Several roads were closed and businesses in the Riverdale area threatened. Several roads were closed, although several. The peak discharge of 34700 cfs was only about a 2.33 year event (0.43 annual chance flood) according to USGS data.

A large boulder and debris blocked the right lane of traffic on Interstate 81 near Chilhowie. Rainfall of 1.5 to 2 inches over a 48-hour period ending at 8 AM on the 21st was observed across much of Smyth County. The COOP station at Saltville 1N measured 1.48 inches for that period.

The official climate site at Bluefield (BLF) measured 1.11 inches February 20th (24 hours ending at midnight on the 21st), which was a record for the date. The old record was 0.89 inches in 1922. Climate records for Bluefield date back to 1909.

Emergency officials reported the evacuation of 11 families from the low-lying areas near Ada. The East River at Willowton gage (ERVW2) crested twice in two days above the Action Stage of 8 feet, reaching 8.94 feet on the 21st and 8.37 feet on the 23rd. Rainfall at the gage was over 2.25 inches in that period.

A portion of Route 220 was blocked due to a landslide. Several days of moderate to heavy rainfall occurred in the area.  A nearby CoCoRaHS site at Covington 4.1 E had 2.96 inches in the 4-day period ending 7 AM local time on the 24th.

Wolf Creek near Narrows (WOLV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 10 feet, cresting at 10.34 feet on the evening of the 24th. Old Wolf Creek Road was flooded. The peak discharge of 7050 cfs was roughly between a 2- and 5-year annual recurrence interval (0.50 to 0.20 annual chance flood). This was the highest stage since April, 2015 at this gage.

An EF-1 tornado touched down about 5.5 miles southwest of Red House at 3:35 PM EST on May 11, 2019. The tornado traveled 4.1 miles and grew up to 275 yards wide along its path. Winds inside the tornado reached 90-100 MPH, which caused minor damage to three homes and severely damaged or destroyed four outbuildings. In addition, the tornado overturned one modular home and uprooted or snapped numerous trees. By 3:46 PM EST, the tornado lifted about 1.5 miles southwest of Red House.

A tornado touched down just to the north of Oak Level.  It then moved northeastward, significantly damaging three structures while heavily damaging or destroying ten outbuildings. The Jefferson 2 E COOP station (JEFN7) had 5.15 inches in the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EDT on June 9th, the highest ever for any day in June. The old record was 4.52 inches set in 2006. The Watauga River flooded along much of its course from Shulls Mill to Sugar Grove with several low water bridges flooded and other roads near the river. Several people were rescued from a car stranded in flood waters from the Watauga River in the Shulls Mill area. Several buildings in the Valle Crucis area received some flooding. The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 15.40 feet, just short of Moderate Flood Stage (16 feet) on the afternoon of the 9th, the highest level since the May 2018 flood and 2nd highest since 2004. According to USGS data it was approximately a 5-year recurrence interval (0.20 annual chance flood). The IFLOWS stream gage upstream near Foscoe (FOSN7) crested at 11.48 feet (Minor Flood Stage - 9 ft.), which was the 2nd highest in the fairly brief history at this gage (since about 2010).

The South Fork New River near Jefferson (JFRN7) crested the afternoon of June 9th at 10.44 feet (11,600 cfs), the 7th highest level on record (nearly continuous data since 1925) and highest since September 2004 (remains of Hurricane Frances). This was also very close to the 10-year recurrence interval (0.10 annual chance flood).  Several roads near the river were flooded and blocked.

Severe drought (D2) was shown across most of northeast Greenbrier County on the U.S. Drought Monitor from October 1 to October 22nd. Impacts were primarily agricultural and included pasture losses and reduced hay cuttings.  The NWS COOP site at Lewisburg 3N (LWBW2) in Greenbrier County recorded a mere 0.08 inches of rain in September. This was the driest September and 2nd driest of any month on record at this station with nearly complete data back to 1900. The previous record was 0.04 inches in October, 2000.

Severe drought (D2) was depicted across nearly all of Monroe County on the U.S. Drought Monitor from October 1st to October 22nd. An extremely dry and very warm September led to the worsening conditions in the county. The COOP site at Greenville 1 SE (GRVW2) had only 0.53 inches of rain in September. Agricultural damages were severe, with estimated losses per the USDA Farm Service Agency at $920,000 from pastures and $1.4 million from hay losses.

The NC DoT in Watauga County reported numerous roads damaged by flood waters, mainly in the Watauga River basin. Among the roads that sustained damage were Watauga River Road, Shulls Mill Road, Flannery Fork Road and Payne Branch Road. Damage was mainly due to erosion of shoulders. The Watauga River at Sugar Grove crested at 10.49 feet around 1 AM on January 12th (Minor flood stage is 6 feet). Low water bridges across the Watauga River were flooded.
The intersection of NC Highway 18 South and Green Acres Drive was totally impassable due to high water.

The COOP observer at Boone 1 SE (BOON7) reported 3.10 inches in the 24-hour period ending 700 AM on January 12th. This was a daily record for the date beating the old date record of 3.00 inches just recently set in 2018. Records at this site began in June, 1980. It was also the 3rd highest daily rainfall for any January day, behind January 31st, 2013 at 6.90 inches and January 15th, 1995 at 5.79 inches.
Flooding was reported from several areas in Ashe County including NC Highway 16 South and other parts of Jefferson, along Three Top Road in Todd and Claybank Road in West Jefferson.

The COOP observer at Jefferson 2 E (JFFN7) reported 2.42 inches in the 24-hour period ending 700 AM on January 12th. This was a daily record for the date beating the old date record of 1.98 inches set in 1994. Nearly continuous records at this site date back to 1910.

The NWS Cooperative station at Boone 1 SE (BOON7) set a date rainfall record of 1.52 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 6th, the old record was 1.37 inches in 2010. The next day the station set a February rainfall record of 4.35 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 3.91 inches on Feb. 14, 1984 (complete data since 1981). It was the 2nd highest February one-day rainfall at Boone if the previous COOP site in Boone is included (after Feb. 13, 1966 with 4.46 inches). That has nearly complete data back to 1929. The two-day rainfall total of 5.87 inches ending 700 AM on the 7th was also a February two-day record at both Boone COOP sites. That broke the old record of 4.06 inches in 1984, which itself was eclipsed the next day, Feb. 8th at 4.46 inches.

The NWS Cooperative station at Danbury (DNBN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 4.06 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.27 inches on Feb. 3, 1996 (complete data since 1947). The station also set a February two-day record with 4.89 inches ending 700 AM on the 7th, easily eclipsing the 3.21 inches on February 25-26, 1979.

The NWS Cooperative station at Eden (EDEN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.93 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.25 inches on Feb. 14, 1984 (complete data since 1950). The station also set a February two-day record with 4.69 inches ending at 700 AM on the 7th, eclipsing the 3.32 inches on February 25-26, 1979.

The NWS Cooperative station at Elkin (EKNN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.07 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.75 inches on Feb. 13, 1966 (complete data since 1934). The station also set a February two-day record with 3.77 inches, eclipsing the 3.20 inches on February 25-26, 1979.

The Dan River flooded throughout Rockingham County closing several roads. The USGS gage at Wentworth (WENN7) crested after midday on the 7th at 28.39 feet, just below the Major flood stage of 29 feet. It was the highest stage since Hurricane Agnes in June 1972 (31.60 feet) and 2nd highest on record since 1940. According to USGS studies, the peak discharge of 40,100 cubic feet per second equates to a 50-year flood event (.02 chance annual exceedance probability or AEP).

The NWS Cooperative station at Yadkinville 6 E (YKNN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.91 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.53 inches on Feb. 22, 1971 (nearly complete data since 1940). The station also set a February two-day record with 5.10 inches ending 700 AM on the 7th, easily eclipsing the 3.18 inches on February 27-28, 1987.

The NWS Cooperative station at Chatham (CHMV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.95 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.61 inches on Feb. 14, 1984 (complete data since 1923). The station also set a two-day February rainfall record with 4.80 inches for the period ending 700 AM on the 7th, breaking the previous February record of 3.15 inches set Feb. 25-26, 1979.

The NWS Cooperative station at Stuart (STUV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.40 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.82 inches on Feb. 19, 1927 (nearly complete data since 1923).

The NWS Cooperative station at Galax (GALV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 2.48 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 1.96 inches on Feb. 23, 2003 (data since 2000).

The NWS Cooperative station at Saltville 1 N (SLTV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 2.10 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 6th. The previous February record was 2.08 inches on Feb. 21, 1897 (sporadic data since 1895). This station also set a date record the following day, for the 24-hours ending 700 AM on the 7th of 2.00 inches, breaking the old record of 1.82 inches set in 2019. The two-day total of 4.10 inches was also a February record for the site, breaking the previous two-day high of 3.04 inches in 1897.

The NWS Cooperative station at Martinsville (MARV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.31 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.65 inches on Feb. 23, 1984 (nearly complete data since 1931). The station also set a two-day February rainfall record with 4.36 inches, breaking the previous record of 3.32 inches set Feb. 25-26, 1979.

The NWS Cooperative station at Reidsville 2 NW (REDN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.15 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.65 inches on Feb. 14, 1984 (complete data since 1962).

The NWS Cooperative station at Richlands (RCLV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 2.38 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 6th. The previous February record was 2.05 inches on Feb. 11, 2018 (complete data since 1990). This station also set a date record for the 24-hours ending 700 AM on the 7th of 1.05 inches, breaking the old record of 0.90 inches set in 2019. The two-day total of 3.43 inches ending on the 7th was also a February record for the site, beating the previous record of 2.99 inches set the day before, February 6, 2020 and previously in 2018 at 2.59 inches.

The greatest flood impacts occurred along the Clinch River in Tazewell County, VA where the Richlands gage (RLRV2) crested at 14.33 feet (6205 cfs) which was the 9th highest on record and the highest stage since November, 2003 (14.65 ft.). This was above the Moderate flood stage of 13 feet but below Major flood stage of 16 feet. The USGS report cited above indicates approximately a 10-year (0.1 AEP) flood frequency for this event, yet flooding along lowland areas was extensive from Cedar Bluff downstream through Richlands and into the Doran and Raven communities.  News reports mentioned water up to four feet deep in parts of Richlands. There were numerous evacuations conducted and homes and businesses flooded along with numerous roads flooded and some damaged. Preliminary damages for Tazewell County estimated at around $1.65 million by VDEM. This included $273,000 in damage to public property, $573,0000 in residential damage and $808,000 to commercial property. An additional $200,000 in road damage was reported by VDOT.

Strong winds blew down a large pine tree about one mile south-southwest of Dobson on to a mobile home.  The fallen tree destroyed the mobile home and injured a two-year-old girl as it pinned her to her bed.

The Danville Airport ASOS (DAN) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.18 inches for the 24-hour period ending at midnight on February 7th. The previous February daily record was 2.98 inches on Feb. 14, 1984. The station also set a two-day February rainfall record with 3.40 inches, breaking the previous record set just the previous day (Feb 6th, 2020) of 3.38 inches. This broke a record from Feb. 25-26, 1979 at 3.01 inches. Official records (ThreadEx) at Danville date back to April, 1916.

Several locations, from near Marion to Chilhowie to near|Saltville, experienced numerous snapped and uprooted trees, |several of which fell onto homes. In addition, a few outbuildings|and barns were destroyed in the Chilhowie area. No injuries were|reported. All damage was consistent with straight line winds |as there were no signs of rotation in the damage patterns. Maximum|wind speeds were estimated to be in the 75-80 mph range.
Trees and limbs were blown down, along with some minor structure damage to a home due to thunderstorm wind gusts.
Multiple trees were blown down along Route 42 west of the the town of Bland due to thunderstorm winds.

Numerous roads were flooded and at least six incurred significant damage as a result of the flooding. Among the reports from the 911 call center was Eurins Creek flooding Pine Hall Road and Danbury Creek flooding a portion of Goff Road.
One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along highway 311 near the Craig and Roanoke County line.
Around a dozen trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds across the county.

The Dan River at Pine Hall (NWS ID: PNHN7) crested at 27.94 feet in the early morning of February 7th. This was highest crest on record at the gage, although the continuous period of record dates back only to 2009. Still, it was was higher than the peak in either tropical storms Florence or Michael in September and October of 2018, respectively. The peak discharge of 27,900 cubic feet per second (cfs) is estimated to be above the 25-year flood event (.04 annual exceedance probability) per USGS data. A co-located automated rain gage measured nearly 4.13 inches of rain in 24-hours ending at midnight on the 7th.

The Ararat River at Ararat (ARRN7) crested at 14.98 feet in the early morning of February 7th. Minor flood stage is 13 feet and Radar Road near the gage was flooded and closed along with several other roads in Surry County, according to news reports. This stage was the 2nd highest crest since 1992 and 8th highest overall since 1947, although records are not continuous before 1965.  The peak discharge of 12,100 cubic feet per second (cfs) is estimated to be near a 10-year flood event (.10 annual exceedance probability) per USGS data.
Approximately 10 to 15 roads were closed across Rockingham County in response to the record daily February rainfall.
Numerous streets were flooded in Richlands due to urban runoff and and rapidly rising waters from the Clinch River and other streams especially Big Creek.
Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds around the City of Galax.
One tree was snapped off about 30 feet up by severe thunderstorm winds. The tree landed on power lines, subsequently downing them and partially blocking Virginia Avenue in Vinton.
A measured wind gust of 60 MPH was observed on a mesonet.
A tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds and downed a power line.
Several large limbs were broken by thunderstorm winds.
One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds on Carriage Court in Henry County.
One tree was blown down on Giles Road by thunderstorm winds.
A large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds on Preston Road in Henry County.
Several trees were reported blown down by thunderstorm winds along Virginia Highway 103 in the Dry Pond Area of Patrick County.
Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds along Abram Penn Highway near the town of Critz.
There were at least 15 trees blown down by thunderstorm winds throughout Pittsylvania County.
Power poles were broken by thunderstorm winds near the Lynchburg Regional Airport.
One tree was blown across North Fork Church Road due to thunderstorm winds.
A roof was blown off of a restaurant by thunderstorm winds.
One tree was blown down across Old Tower Hill Road by thunderstorm winds.
Virginian Road to Thomas Jefferson Highway was closed due to power lines blown down by  thunderstorm winds.

About a half dozen trees were blown down by severe thunderstorm winds across the county. A few trees were also noted to have fallen onto power lines. A barn was also damaged and blown into a mobile home.
At least 45 trees were blown down across the county by severe thunderstorm winds. Some of the downed trees caused damage to cars, homes, and power lines.
Numerous trees, power poles, and power lines were blown down by severe thunderstorm winds from Stoneville to Eden.
One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds at the intersection of Highway 62 and Baynes Road.
A few trees were reported blown down across Roanoke due to strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts.
Two trees were blown down by non-thunderstorm wind gusts, including one on New Hope Church Road.
Numerous roads were flooded and damaged across Wilkes County due to flooding. At least 19 gravel roads required stabilization or repair. Costs were estimated around $118,000.

The NWS Cooperative station at North Wilkesboro (NWBN7) set a daily record for February 7th for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST, with 2.62 inches. The previous date record was 1.86 inches in 1951 (nearly complete data since 1922). It was also the 6th highest one-day total in the month of February. The station also set a February two-day record with 4.12 inches ending at 700 AM on the 7th, eclipsing the 3.54 inches on February 14-15, 1984.
Water was reported flowing over Ruritan Road from Story Creek.

The ASOS climate station at Bluefield Airport (BLF) set a daily rainfall record of 2.09 inches for the 24-hour period ending at midnight on February 7th. The old record was 1.55 inches set in 1955. It was also the 2nd highest February one-day rain since records began in 1909, the record is 2.66 inches set February 27th , 1987. In addition, it was the 2nd wettest two-day event in in February at Bluefield with 2.69 inches, behind 1987 at 2.95 inches.

The NWS Cooperative station at Alderson (ALDW2) set a daily rainfall record of 2.09 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 6th, breaking the old record of 1.33 inches set in 1955. It was also the 2nd highest one-day rain in February, behind the existing record of 2.69 inches on Feb. 21, 1953 (nearly complete data since 1944).

The NWS Cooperative station at Princeton (PRIW2) set a daily rainfall record of 1.37 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 6th. The previous date record was 1.14 inches in 1955. The station set another date record in the ensuing 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on the 7th, with 1.53 inches, breaking the previous record of 0.76 inches in 1955. Nearly complete station data exists back to 1941, with some additional records back to 1900.

The NWS Cooperative station at Bluestone Lake (BLUW2) set a daily rainfall record of 1.47 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 6th. The previous date record was 1.42 inches in 2010. The station set another date record in the ensuing 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on the 7th, with 1.15 inches, breaking the previous record of 1.06 inches in 1955. Nearly complete station data exists back to 1944.

The NWS Cooperative station at South Boston (SOBV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 2.32 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 1.76 inches on Feb. 17, 1990 (complete data since 1981).

Peak Creek was reported to be flooding a portion of Route 640 and in several other locations around Pulaski. The IFLOWS stream gage on Peak Creek (PCRV2) crested at 7.90 feet, just below the Flood Stage of 8 feet.

The NWS Cooperative station at Pulaski 2 E (PSKV2) set a date rainfall record of 1.75 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 6th. The previous record for the date was 1.27 inches in 2010. The station set another date record in the ensuing 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on the 7th, with 1.70 inches, breaking the previous record of 1.33 inches in 2004. The 2-day total of 3.45 inches was a February record for 2-days, breaking the old record of 3.41 inches set February 27-28, 1987. Nearly complete station data exists back to 1941, with some additional records back to 1920.
US 460 was reported closed due to a washout near Pembroke.

Walker Creek near Bane (BANV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 11 feet, cresting at 12.71 feet near midnight on February 7th, and flooding portions of Rye Hollow Road and Route 42. The peak discharge of 10,600 cfs was between and 2 and 5-year flood event (0.50 and 0.20 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies.

Heavy rain associated with thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding in Smyth county. Several roads including Highway 91,42,and 16 were closed because of flooding. Sulphur Spring creek, Stanley creek, and Walker creek  |came out of their banks. Flash flooding occurred in the Marion, Sugar Grove, Chilhowie and Broadford areas.
Heavy rains created a rock slide on Highway 52 and flash flooding in the Pinnacle Rock area.

The North Fork Holston River at Saltville (SALV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 10 feet, cresting at 11.37 feet on the evening of February 6th. This was the highest stage since November, 2003 (15.46 ft.) and 13th highest on record with data back to 1921.  The peak discharge of 10,600 cfs was between a 5-year and 10-year flood event (0.20 and 0.10 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies. Several roads were closed by flooding in the Saltville area.

The Bluestone River at Falls Mills (BRVV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 7 feet, cresting at 7.93 feet early the evening of February 6th. This was the highest stage since March, 2010 (8.54 ft.) and 5th highest on record with data back to 2005 and a period from 1981-1996. The peak discharge of 1,370 cfs was only 2-year flood event (0.50 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies.

The Dan River at Danville (DVLV2) exceeded Moderate flood stage of 26 feet, cresting at 27.22 feet on the morning of February 8th. This was the 3rd highest stage at the current gaging site since the remains of Hurricane Fran in September 1996 (28.65 ft.) and Hurricane Michael in October, 2018 (30.01 ft.). Flood stage categories on the Dan River were adjusted upward by several feet in May 2019. The peak discharge from this flood of 43,000 cfs was estimated to be slightly in excess of a 10-year flood event (0.10 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies. Several roads were closed by flooding in the Danville area with cars stranded. There was also a large mudslie that closed Memorial Avenue in Danville.

The Dan River at Paces (PCEV2) exceeded Moderate flood stage of 29 feet, cresting at 29.75 feet in the late evening of February 8th. This was the 6th highest stage at this gaging site since continuous records began in 1951 and including the August 1940 flood. Flood stage categories on the Dan River were adjusted upward by several feet in May 2019. The peak discharge from this flood of 51,000 cfs was estimated to be slightly above the 25-year flood event (0.04 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies.  Route 658 was flooded and closed by the river.

The Dan River at South Boston (SBNV2) exceeded Moderate flood stage of 29 feet, cresting at 30.56 feet on the morning of February 9th. This was the 8th highest stage at this gaging site since records began in 1924, although there are breaks in the period of record. Flood stage categories on the Dan River were adjusted upward by several feet in May 2019. The peak discharge from this flood of 47,300 cfs was estimated to be near the 10-year flood event (0.04 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies. Several roads around South Boston were flooded and businesses in the Riverdale area flooded.

Wolf Creek near Narrows (WOLV2) exceeded it's Minor flood stage of 10 feet, cresting at 11.72 feet the evening of February 6th, and flooding portions several roads near Narrows. The peak discharge of 10,400 cfs was approximately a 10-year flood event (0.10 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies.

The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) flooded into the Minor flood category (8 feet) and cresting at 10.47 feet midday on February 7th.  The peak discharge of 51,600 cfs was approximately a 5-year flood event (.20 annual exceedance probability) per USGS studies. Several roads close to the river were flooded and closed including Clarks Ferry Road and Julia Simpkins Road.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 14.74 feet, over the Minor flood stage of 14 feet on the afternoon of the 7th. The peak discharge of 52,300 cfs was between a 2- and 5-year event (0.50 to 0.20 annual exceedance probability) per USGS studies. Some parking lots at Radford University were closed.
Poplar Creek, a tributary of the Dan River, was flooding Summit Drive near the intersection of Railroad Avenue.
Heavy rains over a two-day period caused flooding with up to 50 roads closed or impassable across the county, including in the communities of Rural Retreat, Sugar Grove and Saltville.

The NWS Cooperative station at Burkes Garden (BURV2) set a date rainfall record of 1.86 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 6th. The previous February 6th record was 1.608 inches in 2010 (nearly complete data since 1896). This station also set a date record the following day, for the 24-hours ending 700 AM on the 7th of 1.70 inches, breaking the old record of 1.18 inches set in 1965. The two-day total of 3.56 inches was a February record for the site, breaking the previous two-day high of 3.55 inches set in 1897.

The NWS Cooperative station at Transou (LSPN7) set a two-day February rainfall record of 4.76 inches for the 48-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous record was 4.32 inches on Feb. 20-21, 1954 (complete data since 1947).

The NWS Cooperative station at Mt. Airy 2W (MTAN7) set a two-day February rainfall record for the 48-hours ending at 700 AM on February 7th with 3.89 inches. The old February two-day record was 3.40 inches in 1966. Nearly complete data at this station extends back to 1893.

Flooding was reported countywide across Mercer County with many streams and rivers out of their banks. The Bluestone River near Spanishburg (SPNW2) rose above flood stage of 12 feet midday on February 6th after roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of rain had fallen across parts of the county. The river crested the morning of the 7th at 16.81 feet, over the Moderate flood stage of 15 feet. The river flooded portions of Route 19 and Route 10 and caused the evacuation of some mobile homes, including a rescue done by boat. Another person was rescued from their car after driving into flood waters on Route 19 from the Bluestone River. This was the 3rd highest stage at this gage since records began in 2010 and the highest since March 2015. There was a public report of water flowing over Lorton Lick Road from Lorton Lick, making the road impassable. A large mudslide was reported along Ingleside Drive just outside the Bluefield, WV city limits.

The Roanoke (Staunton) River near Randolph (RNDV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 24 feet last on the 6th and crested at 27.41 feet feet on the morning of February 7th, flooding portions several roads including Black Walnut Road.
A portion of Stoney Fork Road was flooded from Stoney Creek.
County Line Creek overflowed and flooded Race Track Road making it impassable.
At least 34 gravel roads were damaged by floodwaters and  number of paved roads as well. Damages were estimated at $139,000.
Oldtown Road was flooded and impassable.
Several roads were damaged by floodwaters in Surry County and flooding was reported along the Fisher River and Stewart's Creek.

Multiple roads were closed across Yadkin County due to flooding and several creeks were reported flowing out of their banks. Cornelius Road, Griffin Road and Swan Creek Pypass were all reported as damaged and out of operation for up to several weeks. The NC Department of Transportation reported several paved roads and 20 gravel roads needing repair with total estimated cost of around $145,000.
Numerous creeks were reported out of their banks across the county and several roads were closed due to high water.

The NWS Cooperative station at Alderson (ALDW2) set a date rainfall record of 2.20 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 6th. The previous date record was 1.33 inches in 1955. The station also set a two-day February rainfall record with 3.03 inches ending at 700 AM on the 7th. The old two-day February record was 2.73 inches Feb. 16-17, 2003. Nearly complete station data exists back to 1945 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at White Sulphur Springs (WSUW2) set a date rainfall record of 1.34 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 7th. The previous date record was 1.15 inches in 1956 and 1933. It was the 3rd wettest two-day rainfall in February with 2.18 inches ending at 700 AM on the 7th.  Nearly complete station data exists back to 1921 with broken data back to 1888 at this site.
Blue Sulphur Springs Road was flooded where it crosses over Muddy Creek.

Multiple creeks were reported out of banks across all of Greenbrier County with roads closed in White Sulphur Springs, Lewisburg and Crawley. Anthony Creek near Anthony (ANYW2) crested at 13.12 feet, just below the estimated flood stage of 14 feet late on February 6th. The Meadow River at Hines (HNEW2) crested at 15.44 feet, over the Flood Stage of 14 feet on the afternoon of the 7th.
The East River at Willowton (ERVW2) crested above the flood stage of 9 feet, reaching 10.30 feet at 1400 EST on the 6th. This is the highest stage in the short period of record at this gage.

Monroe County had flooding serious enough to warrant state of emergency declaration. Indian Creek at Red Sulphur Springs (INCW2) crested above flood stage of 8 feet at 12.01 feet on the evening of the 6th. This was the 3rd highest crest in the short period of record at this gage (since 2012). Several roads along Indian Creek were flooded.
The mayor of Alderson reported that strong winds blew a secured metal building off its foundation in town that had been anchored by fourteen stakes.

The NWS Cooperative station at Yanceyville 4 SE (YAVN7) set a daily February rainfall record of 2.38 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 1.98 inches on Feb. 16, 1998 (complete data since 1997). The station also set a February two-day record with 2.52 inches ending at 700 AM on the 7th, eclipsing the 2.48 inches on February 15-16, 1998.

The NWS Cooperative station at Brookneal (BRKV2) set a daily February rainfall record of 3.06 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous February record was 2.32 inches on Feb. 25, 1979 (nearly complete data since 1951).  The two-day total of 3.43 inches was the 2nd highest in February, just shy of of the record two-day high of 3.45 inches Feb. 25-26, 1979.

The Roanoke (Staunton) River at Brookneal (BROV2) exceeded Moderate flood stage of 27 feet, cresting at 27.41 feet early the morning of February 7th. This was the highest stage since January, 2010 (28.24 ft.). The peak discharge of 34,200 cfs was only slightly above a 2-year flood event (0.50 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies.

Several roads were closed including Fairview Church Road, flooded by the South Fork of Reed Creek and Millers Creek Road from Millers Creek.  The USGS gage on Reed Creek at Grahams Forge (GRHV2) crested just over flood stage (6.5 ft.) at 6.60 feet early on February 7th. The peak flow of 6,500 cfs was approximately a 5-year flood event (0.20 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies. Several roads in the Meadows area are flooded at this stage.

The NWS Cooperative station at Keysville 2 S (KYSV2) set a February daily rainfall record of 2.56 inches for the 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on February 7th. The previous February record was 1.53 inches February 7, 2004. The 2-day total of 2.85 inches was a February record for 2-days, breaking the old record of 1.95 inches set February 17-18, 1998. Nearly complete station data exists back to 1980.

The NWS Cooperative station at Meadows of Dan (MODV2) set a date rainfall record of 3.33 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on February 7th. The previous date record was 2.27 inches on Feb. 23, 1984 (nearly complete data since 1951). The station also set a two-day February rainfall record with 5.41 inches for the period ending 700 AM on the 7th, breaking the previous February record of 4.42 inches set Feb. 17-18, 1966.

The Yadkin River flooded in parts of Yadkin County and floodwater damaged two fields in the Yadkin County Park. Dinkins Bottom Road was closed with extensive flooding in the area. Despite flood control provided by W. Kerr Scott Dam, the Yadkin River at Elkin (ELKN7) still crested at 20.18 feet, above the flood stage of 18 feet. It was the highest stage since the remains of Hurricane Michael in October 2018 (21.02 ft.) but aside from that event, this was the highest stage on the Yadkin River since August 17, 1994 at 22.80 feet. Overall, this flood  was the 10th highest on the river since W. Kerr Scott was completed in 1962.

The Mayo River near Price (PRIN7) rose above it's flood stage of 9 feet and crested at 10.40 feet on the evening of February 6th. According to USGS data, the peak discharge of 11,000 cfs was very close to a 5-year recurrence interval (0.20 annual exceedance probability). The crest was the highest stage since the remains of Hurricane Florence in September 2018 (11.20 ft.) and was the 10th highest on record at this gage with records from 1930 to 1971 and 1994 until the present.

The Little Yadkin River at Dalton (DALN7) stream gage, with a drainage basin of 43 square miles, rose rapidly to 14.92 feet with a peak discharge of 6,350 cfs in the mid-afternoon of February 6th. Although no flood stage has been established, this was the highest stage since September 28, 2004 (15.82 ft. during the remains of Hurricane Jeanne) and the 9th highest on record at this gage with data back to 1961. According to USGS studies the recurrence interval was between a 5- and 10-year flood event or 0.20-0.10 annual exceedance probability.
Several roads were reported to have been flooded due to the heavy rainfall and runoff.

Numerous roads were flooded across Watauga County with substantial damage to several roads and stabilization stone needed for up to eighteen gravel roads. The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 8.40 feet, above the flood stage of 6 feet, early on the 7th, covering several low water bridges and affecting roads along the river.
Numerous roads were flooded and at least 15 gravel roads incurred significant damage as a result of the flooding.
Quarter-size hail fell at a gas station in the community of Raphine, near Exit 205 on Interstate 81.
Hail, ranging in size from 0.88 to 1.5 inches in diameter, was observed falling from a severe thunderstorm across several locations within the community of Lindside.
Thunderstorm winds blew down two trees, caused damage to a shed, and overturned a camper.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one large tree along the Red Sulphur Turnpike, as well as another large tree along Mercer Springs Road.
A large tree was blown down by strong thunderstorm winds on Wagon Wheel Road.
A large tree was blown down by strong thunderstorm winds at the intersection of Pagetown Road and Kerrs Chapel Road.
A large tree was blown down by strong thunderstorm winds on Solomon Lea Road.

A strong thunderstorm with damaging winds brought large limbs down and peeled back metal roofing on a building in Reidsville. Other buildings had shingles and tiles stripped off. A flag pole had a flag ripped from it.

Heavy rain associated with thunderstorms produced flash flooding in Greenbrier county. Milligan Creek flooded Route 60 west of Lewisburg. A woman was rescued from a vehicle in the Friars Hill area as water came over Highway 9 from Indian Creek. Muddy Creek flooded Blue Sulphur Springs Road and Asberry Road.
A thunderstorm produced damaging winds that blew down two trees onto Indian Hill Road.
Thunderstorm winds with gusts up to 60 mph downed trees and power lines. Trees were blown down on Ellisboro Road and the Anglin Mill area.
Several streams were out of banks and roads covered by flood waters.
A line of thunderstorms blew down several trees across Mountain Valley Road near Blowing Springs Campground.

A line of thunderstorms produced damaging winds that blew down a tree onto a home near the community of Hot Springs, and caused damage to the communications tower for the Bath County 911 Center.  This line of storms produced a 62 mph wind gust measured by the AWOS at the Ingalls Field Airport.
A line of thunderstorms produced damaging winds that blew down or snapped several large trees.
A line of thunderstorms produced an 84 mph wind gust at the Mountain Lake Biological Station.

Thunderstorms produced damaging winds that blew down a tree near Red Hill Road.  The storms also blew down multiple branches in the surrounding area and caused one other tree to be split down the middle.

A line of thunderstorms producing damaging winds brought down numerous trees from central Rockbridge County along a swath into the city of Lexington, including on High Street and Valley Pike Road. Some of the trees that were downed in Lexington landed on power lines, resulting in the loss of power for roughly 600 residents. One home had a tree fall on it, resulting in it needing to be evacuated.
Large hail left dents in vehicles on Stoney Mountain Road.
A line of thunderstorms with damaging winds blew down a tree at the intersection of Buck Hill Road and Petunia Lane in Natural Bridge.
Thunderstorms winds blew down a tree on Thomas Road.
Thunderstorms winds blew down a tree on Old Galilee Road.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted or snapped multiple large trees.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large limbs that were up to 12 inches in diameter.  Pea-size hail was also observed with this storm.
Thunderstorms winds blew down several large trees along Oak Lane in the community of Marion.
Thunderstorms winds blew down several trees across the community of Saltville.

A total of eleven roads across the county were blocked due to downed trees. The trees blew down as a result soils being saturated from recent heavy rains combined with 30 mph wind gusts. Damage values are estimated.
Wind gusts of 60 mph were recorded at both in Jefferson and near Baldwin.
Wind gusts of 63 mph were recorded at near Blowing Rock.
A thunderstorm produced damaging winds that blew down two large trees in the community of Fieldale.
Thunderstorm winds blew down six trees and at least one power line within the City of Martinsville.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto a nearby vehicle along Mitchell Farm Lane.
A thunderstorm producing damaging winds blew down an estimated half-dozen trees and one power line within the community of Bassett.  One of the trees fell onto a modular home.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree along Mill Run Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees along Route 8.
A thunderstorm producing damaging winds blew down a power line near the intersection of Broce Drive and Tom's Creek Road in the community of Blacksburg.
A thunderstorm producing damaging winds blew down several trees along Muse Field Road.

The CoCoRaHS site at Danbury 4.6 NNW (NC-SK-2) measured 5.24 inches in a 24-hour period ending at 800 AM EST. According to NOAA Atlas 14 this was approximately a 10-year rainfall event (0.10 annual chance of occurrence) at this location.

The NWS Cooperative station at Jefferson 2 E (JFFN7) set a date rainfall record for the 24-hours ending at 700 AM EST on February 7th with 3.20 inches. The previous record for the date was 1.48 inches set in 2004. It was the 3rd wettest February day on record as well. Nearly complete records date back to 1910 at this station, with sporadic data back to 1896.
Thunderstorm wind gusts to 60 mph downed trees in northeast Stokes county.
Thunderstorm wind gusts to 60 mph downed trees between Stoneville and Eden.

An EF-0 tornado touched down in Alamance county North Carolina, moving north into southern Caswell county. Winds were estimated to be between 70 and 75 mph. This tornado was on the ground sporadically for one half mile crossing Vinson Road south of Anderson before lifting. This tornado caused damage to a barn near Vinson Road and downed several trees. It downed a large tree on a home along Vinson Road, blew a detached garage off its foundation and downed several large trees before lifting about one mile south of Anderson.
A roof was blown off a residence on Baynes Road due to straight line winds. One minor injury occurred as a roof collapsed.
Thunderstorm winds downed a twelve inch diameter tree.
Several large tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.
Trees were downed by thunderstorm gusts of 60 MPH. Road were covered with pieces of trees. Power lines were also downed by winds in the Miller Creek area.
Multiple trees and power lines down across Mount Airy.
Thunderstorm winds downed trees and power lines. Power outages reached a peak of about 4,500.
A home on Alene Loop in Madison received minor structural damage when thunderstorm winds downed a large pine tree, power and cable lines on to the house.
Power lines were blown down in the town of Mount Airy.
A tree was blown down on John Davis Road.
Winds blew down power lines in the town of Elkin.
A tree was blown down in the town of Mount Airy.
Trees were blown down on the east side of Dobson.
A tree was blown down along U.S. Route 601, 1 mile southeast of Dobson.
A tree was blown down along Old Highway 601 near the White Plains community.
A large tree was blown down 2 miles southeast of Ararat.
Trees were blown down along Hall Road, two to three miles west of Danbury.
Trees were blown down onto power lines in Yadkinville.

Thunderstorm winds downed a carport on to a 1998 Dodge truck along Beasley Road in the Flat Rock community. The 30 foot by 30 foot carport with a shingled roof was anchored by a series of large wooden posts which snapped|by the wind.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree on Highway 220 southwest of Ridgeway near State Line.
Thunderstorm winds damaged a mobile home, porch, aluminum sheds and a dog kennel.
A large tree was blown down along Elon Road by thunderstorm winds.  These winds also caused screen damage to a front porch in the Tobacco Row area.
A line of thunderstorms produced damaging winds that blew down numerous trees and tree limbs.  This includes a report of a tree blown down on Lucas Street in the community of Christiansburg.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and tree limbs within the community of Chatham.  This includes a tree reportedly blown down along Route 57.  Two homes sustained damage to the roof caused by a falling tree, including one on Holt Street.  An additional six homes sustained minor roof damage.  At least five power poles were also snapped in the area by these winds, knocking out power to roughly 1,100 residents.
Thunderstorm winds caused roof damage to a building along Queens Knob Road.  These winds also blew down an apple tree.

Several roads and culverts roads were damaged in flash flooding across Ashe County. A culvert collapsed on Frank Dillard Road causing a truck to fall into a large hole. The shoulder of the road at the intersection of Cranberry Springs Road and Liberty Grove Church Road was damaged.

The NWS Cooperative station at Mt. Airy (MTAN7) set a daily April rainfall record of 4.12 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April record was 3.84 inches on Feb. 14, 1984 (complete data since 1893).

The NWS Cooperative station at Boone 1 SE (BOON7) set a daily April rainfall record of 4.71 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13, 2020. The old record was 3.94 inches on April 24, 2018 (complete data since 1981). It was also the highest April one-day rainfall at Boone if the previous COOP site in the Boone area is included, the old record was 4.68 inches April 5, 1957. The previous site has nearly complete data back to 1929.

The NWS Cooperative station at Transou (LSPN7) set a daily April rainfall record of 4.76 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous record was 4.41 inches on April 14, 1980 (complete data since 1947).

The NWS Cooperative station at Jefferson 2 E (JFFN7) set an April daily rainfall record for the 24-hours ending at 700 AM EST on April 13th with  4.65 inches. The previous record for the date was 3.78 inches set on April 24, 2017. Nearly complete records date back to 1910 at this station, with sporadic data back to 1896.

Radar Road was closed north of the intersection with Ararat Road due to flooding from the Ararat River. The river exceeded flood stage of 13 feet between around 800 AM EST and 1200 PM EST, cresting at 13.48 feet.

Significant flash flooding occurred in the Boone area with multiple housing units being evacuated. Several roads were closed including Bamboo Road, Deerfield Dr. and Meadowview Road. The worst flooding was from the East Fork of the South Fork of the New River and along Goshen Creek where several water rescues from homes were undertaken. Several mudlslides were reported across the area as well and significant road damage occurred. A person was stuck on top of their vehicle, due to the rising waters, in the area of Deerfield Road near the golf course, according to scanner dispatches in the 500 AM time frame and around 600 AM another vehicle was washed off the road in the area of the Moose Lodge.

The CoCoRaHS station at Fleetwood 3.1 SSE (NC-AS-22) measured 6.02 inches in 24 hours ending at 600 AM EST. According to NOAA Atlas 14 this falls in the 90 percent confidence interval (5.36 to 6.53 inches) for a 10-year rainfall event (0.1 annual chance of occurrence).

The CoCoRaHS station at Boone 4.5 SE (NC-WT-24) measured 7.50 inches in 24 hours ending at 600 AM EST. According to NOAA Atlas 14 this falls in the 90 percent confidence interval (7.02 to 8.49 inches) for a 25-year rainfall event (0.04 annual chance of occurrence).

The CoCoRaHS station at Blowing Rock 2.2 ENE (NC-WT-10) measured 7.38 inches in 24 hours ending at 600 AM EST. According to NOAA Atlas 14 this falls just below the 90 percent confidence interval (7.40 to 8.94) for a 25-year rainfall event (0.04 annual chance of occurrence).

The CoCoRaHS station at Boone 4.6 E (NC-WT-37) measured 6.40 inches in 24 hours ending at 600 AM EST. According to NOAA Atlas 14 this falls in the 90 percent confidence interval (5.43 to 6.53 inches) for a 10-year rainfall event (0.1 annual chance of occurrence).
The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 10.24 feet, above the flood stage of 6 feet early on April 13th, covering several low water bridges and flooding roads along the river.

The North Fork Holston River at Saltville (SALV2) exceeded Minor flood stage of 10 feet, cresting at 11.95 feet around mid-day April 13th. This was the highest stage since November, 2003 (15.46 ft.) and 11th highest on record with data back to 1921. The peak discharge of 11,500 cfs was between a 5-year and 10-year flood event (0.20 and 0.10 annual exceedance probability) according to USGS studies. Several roads were closed by flooding in the Saltville area.

The Clinch River at Richlands gage (RLRV2) crested at 12.77 feet, well over the Minor flood stage of 10 feet and just below Moderate flood stage of 13 feet. This was still somewhat below the 14.33 feet just back in February of 2020, but still the 12th highest on record at this gage, with records dating back to 1944.  Several roads were closed and damaged due to the flooding and some homes had water in them again. Information on damage to roads and infrastructure provided by Virginia DOT.

The Smith River near Woolwine gage (SMWV2) rose quickly in the early morning hours and exceeded the flood stage of 9 feet, cresting at 9.65 feet (2310 cfs) around 500 AM EST. This was the 5th highest crest on record at this gage with data back to 1995. According to USGS data this was approximately a 10-year flood event (0.10 annual chance of occurrence). There was some damage to roads in the county according to VDOT.
Several roads were reported closed in Franklin County most in the Snow Creek area, including Goose Dam Road. VDOT reported damage to several roads in the county.

Numerous roads were closed across Bedford County and there was significant damage to some roads. A man was rescued by a swift water team from the roof of a van stalled in flood waters from Sycamore Creek along Otterville Road.

Tinker Mill Road was closed due to high water and several other roads in the Buchanan area. Poor Farm Road near Fincastle was also reported to be underwater. There was some damage to roads in the county per VDOT.

The NWS Cooperative station at Big Island (BGIV2) set a daily April rainfall record of 4.30 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April record was 3.00 inches on April 25, 2018 (complete data since 1961).
The CoCoRaHS station at Woolwine 0.4 SW (VA-PR-1) measured 4.18 inches in 24 hours ending at 700 AM EST.

The NWS Cooperative station at Bedford (BDFV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 3.68 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST.  The previous date record was 2.00 inches in 1949. It was also the 3rd wettest for any April date. The record is 4.70 inches on April 22, 1992. Nearly complete data exists back to 1932 at this site, with broken data back to 1893.

The NWS Cooperative station at Saltville 1 N (SLTV2) set a daily April rainfall record of 3.50 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April record was 2.86 inches on April 17, 1998. (sporadic data at the site since 1895).

Several roads were reported to be flooded and blocked. These incuded Justus Mill Road, St. Peter Road, Cripple Creek Road and Hope Road. Millers Creek Road was damaged by flowing water from Miller Creek. Information on damage to roads and infrastructure provided by Virginia DOT.

The NWS Cooperative station at Wytheville 1S (WYTV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.49 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.00 inches in 1966 and 1959. It was also the 4th wettest for any April date. The April record is 2.70 inches on April 19, 1901. Nearly complete data exists back to 1930 at this site, with data also from 1893 to 1904.

The gage at Reed Creek at Grahams Forge  (GRHV2) exceeded flood stage of 6.5 feet, cresting at 7.40 feet (7990 cfs) in the late afternoon of the 13th. This was the 6th highest crest on record at this gage with data back to 1927 at the current datum. According to USGS data, it was just below a 10-year flood event (0.10 annual chance of occurrence).

The NWS Cooperative station at Pedlar Dam (PDLV2) set a daily April rainfall record of 4.21 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April record was 3.08 inches on April 25, 1987.  Nearly complete data exists back to 1939 at this site with sporadic data to 1927.

The NWS station at Blacksburg (RNK) set a daily rainfall record for April 13th with 2.41 inches for the 24 hours ending at midnight local time. The old record was 1.01 inches in 1959. It was also the 3rd wettest April day on record, the existing record is 3.42 inches on April 22, 1992. Precipitation data exists at Blacksburg back to 1952 at this time.

Several reports of flash flooding from Brush Creek in the Pilot area were received and there was street flooding in urban areas of Christiansburg and Blacksburg. In addition, the South Fork of the Roanoke River at Shawsville (SHAV2) rose very rapidly to a crest of 6.83 feet (flood stage is 5 feet) at 725 AM EST. According to USGS data the peak discharge of 4550 cfs was somewhere between a 2- and 5-year flood (0.5 to 0.2 annual chance of occurrence). Several roads in the county sustained damage according to VDOT.

The NWS Cooperative station at Pearisburg 4 SSE (STFV2) set a daily April rainfall record of 3.17 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April record was 2.81 inches on April 16, 2018 (nearly complete data since 1952).

The USGS gage on Walker Creek at Bane rose above Minor flood stage of 11 feet early on the 13th and crested at 15.73 feet (16,700 cfs) in the afternoon. Moderate flood stage is 14 feet. According to USGS data this would have been approximately a 25-year flood event (0.04 annual chance of occurrence). Several roads were closed but no structures were reported to have flooded. This was the 8th highest stage on record and the highest stage since 3/13/2010. VDOT reported substantial flood damage to several roads in the county as well. A power pole was snapped by flood waters along Green Valley Road due to flooding from a tributary of Walker Creek, Big Spring Branch.

Route 614 was flooded by Craig Creek with over six inches of water reported across the bridge. The IFLOWS stream gage at this location was out of service at the time, but the upstream IFLOWS gage on Craig Creek near Abbott (ABBV2) crested at 11.6 feet. This was over the flood stage of 10 feet and the 2nd highest (highest is 11.9 feet in Oct. 2018 with remains from Hurricane Michael) in a fairly short period of record (back to 2010). A water rescue was also preformed in the Abbott area, where a car drove into flood waters.

The NWS Cooperative station at New Castle (NWCV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.54 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.22 inches in 1949. It was also the 2nd wettest for any April date, with the existing April record still at 2.60 inches on April 20, 1940. Sporadic data exists back to 1907 at this site.
A car had to be towed out of floods water on Carver Road. Several other roads in the county were flooded, especially in the Bassett Forks area. VDOT reported damage to several of the flooded roads.

Several roads were close due to flooding including High Water Lane, Low Bridge Lane, and the intersection of Plank Road and Wild Fox Lane. The USGS site at Kerrs Creek near Lexington (KCKV2) crested at 9.24 feet (3700 cfs) in the morning of the 13th. This was just below a 10-year flood event (0.1 annual chance of occurrence) per USGS data.
Several roads across Floyd County were reported to be impassable due to high water including Sowers Road and at least one creek was reported out of its banks. VDOT reported damage to several roads.

The Roanoke River at Roanoke crested at 11.74 feet (10,500 cfs) on the afternoon of the 13th, above the Minor flood stage of 10 feet. Several low water bridges were flooded along with the Roanoke Greenway.
Beaver Creek was reported out of its banks and flooding some adjacent corn fields.

A road washout occurred at the intersection of Leesville Road and Johnson Mountain Road as a result of flooding from the Big Otter River. The nearby river gage on the Big Otter River near Evington (EVGV2) crested at 21.53 feet (16,600 cfs) in the afternoon of the 13th. This was the 11th highest stage on record and highest since January 2010 and was close to a 5-year flood event (0.2 annual chance of occurrence) per USGS data.
Thunderstorm winds blew down at least two trees into a home in the Millers Creek area.
Thunderstorm winds blew down at least one tree on Edwards-Lakeview Drive.
A thunderstorm with damaging winds blew several trees down in the Yadkinville area, as well as across Yadkin County.
A thunderstorm with damaging winds blew three trees down on Rockett Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down multiple trees in the Parsonville area.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree in the community of Roaring River.

Thunderstorm winds blew a tree onto a wooden outbuilding on J. A. Russell Drive.  A man was inside the building at the time the tree fell, and was later transported to the hospital with minor injuries.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down onto a home in the Stoneville area.
Thunderstorm winds blew multiple trees down along W. Gretna Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew multiple trees down on Keeling Drive, as well as multiple power poles in the nearby area.

The IFLOWS stream gage at Pulaski (PCRV2) rose from near baseflow to flood stage (8 feet) in less than 6 hours and crested at 11.4 feet around 730 AM EST on the 13th. Moderate flood stage is 11 feet. This was the highest crest in the fairly short and erratic history of this gage (back to around 2010), It exceeded the previous record of 11.2 feet set on March 13, 2010. Other small tributaries of Peak Creek flooded as well and local news reports spoke of the 'worst flooding in 40 years' with up to a dozen homes flooded into the living areas. Three water rescues were conducted as well around Pulaski.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down along intersection of Max Kendall Road and North Fork Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree down along Snow Creek Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down along Highway 220.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down along Winfrey Inez Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down near the intersection of Highway 60 and Scotts Bottom Road.

The NWS Cooperative station at Pulaski 2 E (PSKV2) set a daily record for April 13th rainfall with 2.60 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The previous April 13 record was 1.02 inches in 1949 (nearly complete data since 1940). It was also the 5th highest rainfall for any April day, the record being set just last year, 2019 at 3.28 inches on April 20th.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down near the intersection of Virginia Avenue and Oak Level Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down just south of South Boston on Highway 501.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down onto a power line along Melon Road near Stebbins Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down along Old Well Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew a tree down at 6000 Danville Pike near the community of Hillsville.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree down along Keno Road near the community of Laurel Fork, and blew down another tree down along Bellspur Road.

Thunderstorm winds blew down multiple trees across Henry County and the City of Martinsville.  This includes several trees blown down near the intersection of Prospect Hill Drive and Spruce Street.  A tree was blown down near the intersection of Terrys Mountain Road and Barrows Mill Road.  Yet another tree was blown down near the intersection of Stultz Road and Dexter Street.  One tree was blown down onto both a nearby car and a power line.
A wind gust of 69 MPH was measured by a mesonet weather sensor located at James Monroe High School.
At least two trees were blown down by strong winds across Franklin County.  One tree fell along Calloway Road.  Another tree was blown down along Sontag Road.
At least five trees and tree limbs were blown down by strong winds across portions of Henry County.

There were several reports of flash flooding around Roanoke City including a car that was submerged in flood waters covering the intersection of Walnut Avenue and 4th Street. The intersection was closed. Social media photos showed flooding on Franklin Road at Wonju Street. A mudslide at a car dealership caused two cars to slide into the resulting sinkhole with some damage to the vehicles.
A massive landslide along Highway 16 between Thompson Valley and Tannersville washed out part of the roadway and closed the southbound lane. Repairs were expected to take several weeks.

River camp next to the South Fork of the New River flooded and the bridge at Kings Creek Rd. was covered over with water.  The South Fork New River gage at Jefferson (JFRN7) upstream crested at 9.89 feet (10,400 cfs). This was above the minor flood stage of 8 feet and the 11th highest crest on record, with data as far back as 1916. Per USGS studies this was between a 5- and 10-year recurrence interval (0.2 to 0.1 annual chance flood).
Highway 8 North was closed due to flood waters.
A CWOP gage in Bland recorded 2.76 inches of rain in the 24-hour period ending 800 AM on the 13th. A nearby automated gage also reported 2.52 inches.

The New River at Galax flooded with a crest of 9.36 feet (34,900 cfs) on the afternoon of the 13th. According to USGS data it was roughly a 5-year flood event (0.2 annual chance of occurrence). Several roads were flooded and there was some damage. Information on damage to roads and infrastructure provided by Virginia DOT.

The NWS Cooperative station at Elk Creek 4 SSW (PDLV2) had 4.06 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST on April 13th. The site has only been operating since early 2017 but it was the highest 24-hour rain total for any day since that time. Per NOAA Atlas 14 this 24-hour amount was in the 90 percent confidence interval (3.55 to 4.13 inches) for a 10-year rainfall event (0.1 annual chance of occurrence).

The New River at Allisonia (ALSV2) flooded into the Minor flood category (8 feet) and cresting at 11.26 feet midday on April 13th. The peak discharge of 53,2600 cfs was approximately a 5-year flood event (.20 annual exceedance probability) per USGS studies. Several roads close to the river were flooded and closed including Clarks Ferry Road and Julia Simpkins Road.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree along Highway 58 on the east side of Danville.
Thunderstorm winds downed two large pine trees down across Route 622 in Lynch Station.
Thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph downed a tree six miles west of Alton.
A tree was downed by thunderstorm winds on Calvary Road.
Judyville Road was reported flooded.
Two trees were downed by thunderstorm wind gusts along Oakville Road near Gladstone.

The Bluestone River flooded portions of Route 19 as the gage near Spanishburg rose above the flood stage of 12 feet, with a peak of 12.78 feet early on April 14th. Widespread lowland flooding occurred as well.

The NWS Cooperative station at Lewisburg 3N (LWBW2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 1.89 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.14 inches in 1949. It was also the 7th wettest for any April date. Nearly complete data exists back to 1900 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at Bluefield (BLFW2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.07 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.35 inches in 1949. It was also the 2nd wettest for any April date, after the record is 2.15 inches on April 16, 2004. Nearly complete data exists back to 1999 at this site.
Thunderstorm winds downed trees on Webb Spring Road in Marion.
Thunderstorm wind gusts to 60 mph downed a tree across Route 94 near Wytheville.
Automated wind equipment 5 miles north of Hillsville measured a 59 mph gust.
Several roads were flooded and damaged in Carroll County.
Numerous roads were reported flooded and impassable across Campbell County by VDOT and Lynbrook Road near Clark���s Road in Campbell County was bady damaged due to flooding.

The ASOS at Lynchburg Airport (LYH) measured 3.10 inches on April 13th. This broke the date record for April 13th of 1.43 inches set just last year in 2019. It was also the 2nd wettest April day on record, after the 3.67 inches on April 26, 1978. Records date back to 1893 at Lynchburg.
The ASOS at Roanoke-Blacksburg Airport (ROA) measured 1.78 inches on April 13th. This broke the date record for April 13th of 1.05 inches set in 1949. Records exist back to 1912 at Roanoke.
Trees were downed by thunderstorm winds in the Claytor Lake area.
Thunderstorm winds downed trees on power lines near Henry.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a metal building along Route 8 south.
Numerous trees were downed by thunderstorm winds in the Meadows of Dan area.
Several large tree limbs downed by thunderstorm winds.
A couple of trees were downed by thunderstorm winds in Fairy Stone State Park.
Law Enforcement reported trees down on power lines on Route 890.

The NWS Cooperative station at Rocky Mount (RYMV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.93 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.51 inches in 2004. It was also the 5th wettest for any April day. A broken period of record dates back to 1894 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at Martinsville Filter Plant (MARV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.55 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.90 inches in 2019. It was also the 5th wettest for any April day. Nearly data exists back to 1931 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at Christiansburg (CRBV2) tied its wettest April day on record with 2.25 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The same amount was recorded on April 24, 2017.  Nearly complete data exists back to 1995 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at Woolwine 1 SE (BDFV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 4.38 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 2.00 inches set in 1979. It was also the 4th wettest for any April date. The record is 4.80 inches on April 10, 1983. Nearly complete data exists back to 1951 at this site.

The Roanoke River at Glenvar (GNVV2) crested at 13.14 feet (11700 cfs) in the early afternoon of the 13th. Flood stage is 9 feet. Several roads were closed near the river including Southwest River Road. Bohon Hollow Road bridge (Route 734) about 1 mile upstream from gage was overtopped.
Substantial road damage was reported by VDOT in the aftermath of heavy rainfall and flooding in Amherst County.
Numerous roads were flooded and some damage reported in Roanoke County.

The NWS Cooperative station at Buckingam (BUKV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.01 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.75 inches in 1901. It was also the 8th wettest for any April date with nearly complete data back to 1951 and broken data back to 1895. Significant road damage was reported by VDOT in Buckingham County.
A CoCoRaHS observer (VA-PT-9) measured 2.19 inches in the 24-hour ending at 700 AM EDT. VDOT reported damage to several roads in Pittsylvania County.
NWS radar showed 1 to 1.5 inches of rain fell in western Halifax County and some minor road damage was reported by VDOT.
Heavy rain fell over far northwest Appomattox County with radar estimates of 1.5 to 2 inches, with resulting minor damage to several roadways.
Heavy rain fell over far northwest Charlotte County with radar estimates of 1 to 1.25 inches, with resulting minor damage to several roadways.

The NWS Cooperative station at Richlands (RCLV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 2.39 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 1.27 inches in 2004. It was also the 2nd wettest for any April date, the record is 2.40 inches on April 16, 2018. Nearly complete data exists back to 1990 at this site.

The NWS Cooperative station at Huddleston 4 SW (HUDV2) had its wettest April 13th on record with 3.43 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EST. The previous date record was 2.81 inches set in 2019. It was also the 3rd wettest for any April date. The record is 4.55 inches on April 16, 1987. Nearly complete data exists back to 1951 at this site.

The CoCoRaHS station at Copper Hill 6.2 S (VA-FL-2) measured 4.85 inches in 24 hours ending at 700 AM EST on April 13th. This is between a 5- and 10-year annual recurrence interval (0.2 to 0.1 annual chance) per NOAA Atlas 14.

Reports from a local newspaper showed water over six inches deep flowing across a road along Sugar Run, which was heavily swollen with runoff from the heavy rain. Some damage occurred to roads along this stream.

The New River at Radford (RDFV2) crested at 16.48 feet late on April 13th. Moderate flood stage is 16 feet. The peak discharge of 60200 cfs was close to a 5-year annual recurrence interval event (0.20 annual chance flood) per USGS studies. Several roads close the river were flooded.

The New River at Glen Lyn (GLLV2) crested at 15.24 feet, just above the Minor flood stage of 15 feet very early in the morning of April 14th. The peak discharge at this gage of 76800 cfs was very close to a 5-year recurrence interval (0.20 annual chance flood) according to USGS data. Several roads near the river were flooded and closed.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree in the 900 block of Old U.S. Highway 421.
Mudslides and debris blocked portions of Highway 220 near Hot Springs closing the road for several miles.
Power outages occurred from downed trees in Ferrum.
Trees were downed along Route 220 South.
Power lines were downed in the Bassett Forks area on Crestridge Road.
Thunderstorm winds brought down several pine trees and caused minor roof damage to a house.
Several trees were downed by thunderstorm winds.
A grocery store sign was blown over and damaged by thunderstorm winds.
Trees were downed across northern Amherst county.
Bath County High School measured a 61 mph gust.
One tree was downed on the south end of the City of Danville. Power lines were downed in the city with nearly 2,000 people losing power.
A large tree was downed by a thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph.
Trees and power lines were downed by thunderstorm winds.
Tree was downed at Mountain Road in Oak Level.
A tree was blown down along Volens Road, or Highway 603.
A tree was downed by thunderstorm winds near River Road.
Thunderstorm winds brought down a tree on State Highway 501.
Thunderstorm wind gust to 60 mph downed a tree in Scottsburg.
A tree was blown down on Buck Shoal Road.
A tree was blown down at the intersection of Highway 360 and Highway 626.
A tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Route 607.
A tree was blown down at Highway 501 and Horse Trail.
Trees and power lines were blown down at the intersection of Bowen Road and Hudson Road.
Trees were down on Highway 360 near Public Fork.
Trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds along Sharon Church Road off Route 20.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree along Virgilina Road.
Portions of downtown Hot Springs near the Bath House were flooded and parts of U.S. 220 flooded for several miles to the south, leaving the road impassable for a period.
Trees were blown down along Old Tower Hill Road.
A 180 foot shed was lifted and thrown by thunderstorm winds. Several slate shingles blown off a home on Route 656.
