Runoff due to heavy rain from thunderstorms caused Foster Springs Branch to overflow its banks, closing Old Highway 16 due to flooding.  Radar-based rainfall estimates indicated the possibility of 3 to 4 inches having fallen in the nearby area, while a mesonet station 1.3 miles to the north-northeast recorded roughly 1.6 inches having fallen in a 45 minute period.

Runoff due to a thunderstorm producing heavy rain caused flooding along the Christiansburg Pike, temporarily making the road impassible. A landslide occurred from a roadside hill onto the pike, blocking the road. Radar rainfall estimates indicate that 2 to possibly 3 inches fell in the nearby area where the flooding and the landslide occurred.
Runoff due to heavy rain falling from a slow-moving thunderstorm caused Beaver Creek to rise out of its banks, flooding onto adjacent Beaver Creek School Road.
A home mesonet station recorded 4.46 inches of rain which fell in a little over 2 hours.  This equated to roughly a 150-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point rainfall frequency analysis.
Runoff due to heavy rain from thunderstorms caused Railroad Grade Road to be flooded and impassible.  The road reopened during the evening after flood waters had receded.
A home mesonet station recorded 4.13 inches of rain which fell in a 2-hour period.  This equates to a roughly 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 rainfall frequency estimates.
A CoCoRaHS station recorded 2.48 inches of rain from a slow-moving thunderstorm, most of which fell between 2 pm and 5 pm on August 7th.

A slow-moving thunderstorm produced 4 to 5 inch rainfall amounts over a 2-hour period in the Fleetwood area.  CREST unit streamflow estimates put this event close to 1000 cfs/mi^2, or a 100-200 year rainfall event at both the 1- and 2-hour time intervals.  This resulted in several reports of flooding in the Fleetwood area, including at the intersection of Windy Hill Road and Highway 221, which made the intersection impassible.  The heavy rain caused a mudslide to occur along Paul Goodman Road.  Rock Quarry road was impassible where a tributary of the South Fork New River, the drainage area of which was completely within the area of heaviest rainfall, flooded out of its banks and over-topped the intersecting bridge.  The same tributary caused flooding along Dick Phillips Road further upstream where the two run adjacent to one another.

Doppler radar indicated rainfall amounts of 1.5 to 2 inches in the Stoney Fork area, with CREST unit streamflow indicating 550 cfs/mi^2.  FLASH data indicates this rainfall was roughly a 10-year event.  Runoff from this rainfall caused a creek running adjacent to Lawrence Greene Road to overflow its banks onto the roadway, making travel impossible until the water receded.
Heavy rain caused a debris flow near the 2500 block of Gladys Fork Road.
A home weather station recorded nearly 2.1 inches of rain within a 1-hour period.  This was a 25-year average return interval per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced 1.5 to 2 inches of rain within about an hour across the town of Tazewell. FLASH data indicates this amount to be 1.5 to 1.7 times greater than 1-hour flash flood guidance for this area. CREST unit streamflow for this event was 550 cfs/mi^2, while the 1-hour average return interval was around a 25-year event. Runoff from this rainfall caused flooding of several roads in the vicinity of Dogwood Road and Steeles Lane.

A home mesonet station recorded 1.42 inches of rain in an hour.  About 1.3 inches fell within a 30 minute period, which equates to between a 10- and 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point precipitation estimates.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced 1.5 to 2 inches of rain within about an hour in an urbanized/highly developed area within the town of Claymont Hill. FLASH data indicates this amount to be 1.5 to 1.7 times greater than 1-hour flash flood guidance for this area. CREST unit streamflow for this event was 600-650 cfs/mi^2, while the 1-hour average return interval was around a 25-year event. Runoff from this rainfall caused flooding of roads around the Claymont Hill Mall, which were closed off until the flooding receded.  Water from the area around the mall then channeled along an unnamed creek running north adjacent to Highway 460, where flooding occurred near the Bandy Auto Care Center.
A personal mesonet station recorded a storm total of 1.95 inches of rain.  1.89 inches fell within an hour, roughly a 5-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in North Wilkesboro, NC recorded a 2-day total, for thunderstorms occurring during the afternoons on the 13th (2.89) and 14th (2.20), of 5.09 inches of rain.  This was the 8th wettest 2-day period for this station during the month of August, with station records dating back to September 1921.

Runoff due to heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused an unnamed creek to overflow its banks, and cause flooding of buildings nearby the intersection of 2nd Street and Statesville Road (Highway 115) in the town of North Wilkesboro.  The road reopened after flood waters receded.

Between 3 and 5 inches of rain fell fell over a 2 to 3-hour period across nearly the entire drainage basin for Ramey Creek near the community of Lowgap.  Per FLASH data at the 3-hour period, these amounts were anywhere from 1.8 to 2.5 times flash flood guidance, or a 200+ year event.  CREST unit streamflows were over 1,000 cfs/mi^2, indicating a major flooding event was possible.  However, the area where the rain occurred is heavily wooded and very sparcely developed.  Given the late hour at which the rain occurred, there were very few eye witness accounts of what actually happened.  The only report received was early in the event, likely before maximum flooding was achieved, where over six inches of water was observed flowing across Ramey Creek Road due to flooding from Ramey Creek. This heavy rain also caused a small slide debris flow onto the road.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in Copper Hill, VA recorded a 2-day rainfall total of 6.46 inches from thunderstorms that occurred on the afternoons/evenings of the 12th (3.27) and the 13th (3.19).  This total is the 5th highest 2-day total to occur at this station anytime during the month of August, and the 20th highest 2-day total all-time.  Records for this station date back to April 1940.  The rainfall total of 6.46 inches represents between and 10- and 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates.

Two to three inches of rain fell across portions of Christiansburg during a roughly 2-hour period, which was between a 5- and 10-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates.  Runoff from this rainfall caused a roadside ditch running along Phlegar Street to overflow onto the road an estimated couple feet deep between 2nd and 3rd Streets.  2nd Street was also observed to be under water and impassible.  In addition, water several inches deep was observed flowing across nearby Radford Street.

Peak Creek was observed overflowing its banks, with flood waters several inches deep entering buildings across portions of downtown Pulaski. Several downtown roads were closed in the area, including a portion of U.S. Highway 11 and VA Highway 99.
A debris flow was observed along River Road near Interstate 81 in Chilhowie. A tree and other debris slid into the road off the side of a roadside hill, blocking the road.

The Wythe County 911 Operations Center reported multiple debris flows taking place along VA Highway 94 in and around the community of Ivanhoe.  Multiple rounds of thunderstorm activity, both on the 15th and in the days prior, resulted in saturated soil conditions.  The multiple rounds on the afternoon of the 15th reached up to 1.5 times the 6-hour flash flood guidance, roughly a 5-year rainfall event per FLASH estimates.

A partially blocked culvert caused Dalton Creek to rise out of its banks near the Fries School, flooding the parking lot up to the building.  Radar rainfall estimates of about 1.5 inches fell within the 0.54 mi^2 (USGS Stream Stats) Dalton Creek watershed, with a personal mesonet station in the town of Fries recorded 1.48 inches rainfall in a 30-minute period, roughly a 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas-14 point frequency estimates.

The Cooperative Weather Observer (COOP) at Stuart, VA recorded 2.06 inches of rainfall for the 24-hour period ending 7 am on September 1st.  Most of this rainfall fell during the morning and afternoon of August 31st.  This rainfall amount sets a new daily record for the Stuart COOP for September 1st, breaking the previous record of 2.05 inches set in 2007.  Records for this station date back to May 1913.

The Cooperative Weather Observer (COOP) at Meadows-of-Dan, VA recorded 2.31 inches of rainfall for the 24-hour period ending 7 am on September 1st. Most of this rainfall fell during the morning and afternoon of August 31st. This rainfall amount sets a new daily record for the Meadows-of-Dan COOP for September 1st, breaking the previous record of 1.96 inches set in 1959. Records for this station date back to December 1950.

The Patrick County 911 Center reported that Commerce Street in the Town of Stuart is closed off due to Campbell Branch overflowing its banks several inches deep across the roadway.  A personal mesonet station in Stuart recorded roughly 1.8 inches of rainfall between 1130 am and 1230 pm EDT, between a 2- and a 5-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas-14 point frequency estimates, though soils were becoming saturated from rainfall earlier in the day before this convective band moved through.

A personal mesonet station recorded 4.48��� for a storm-total, with about 3.4 of it falling during the period 7 am to 10 am. This amount represented around a 100-yr event for the 3-hour duration per NOAA Atlas-14 estimates.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in Martinsville, VA recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 2.54 inches from thunderstorms that occurred during late morning of the 21st. This total sets a new rainfall record for the 22nd August, breaking the previous record of 1.41 inches set in 1962. Records for this station date back to September 1930.

A home mesonet station near Reed Creek recorded a storm total of 5.67 inches of rainfall from training thunderstorms, the vast majority of which fell during a 6-hour period between 6 am and noon on the 21st.  This rainfall amount equates to roughly a 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates.

A home mesonet station near Bassett recorded a storm total of 3.39 inches of rainfall from training thunderstorms, the vast majority of which fell during a 6-hour period between 6 am and noon on the 21st.
A CoCoRaHS station recorded at 2-day total of 4.08 inches rainfall on the mornings of the 21st (2.31 inches) and the 22nd (1.77 inches).
Poor drainage issues caused Union Street to be closed due to standing water in the roadway.  The intersection of Jefferson Street and Pine Street was also closed by standing water.
Runoff from very 1.5 to 2 inches of rain within a 2-hour period caused Blackberry Creek to rise rapidly out of its banks and cause flooding on Blackberry Road.

Widespread flooding was observed in the Bassett and Stanleytown communities.  This includes flooding of Riverside Drive as Blackberry Creek rose out of its banks, as well as flooding at the intersection of Oakcrest Circle and Winnfield Road where a tributary of Little Reed Creek overflowed its banks.  Little Reed Creek also flooded out of its banks, overflowing onto Highway 220, including numerous businesses along the highway as far south as where the creek merges with Reed Creek and then empties into the Smith River.  There were reports that as many as 40 automobiles were trapped along Highway 220 by the flood, with a few occupants needing assistance to evacuate the vehicles.  Most people were able to leave the vehicles on their own.  Flood waters of Little Reed Creek were intense enough to damage the bridge that crosses the creek along Edgewood Drive. Portions of the Great Road were closed for several hours due to flooding, as was Daniels Creek Road near Reed Creek.  Numerous other roads and buildings were impacted as well to varying degrees.

Radar precipitation estimates and personal mesonet stations indicate that between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rain fell in the Chatmoss area, much of this rain falling in a 1-hour period across soils that were near saturation from recent rainfall.  These amounts were anywhere from an 8- to 15-year rainfall event per FLASH estimates.  Runoff from this rainfall caused flooding along Spruce Street, near Irisburg Road, making the road impassible until the floodwaters receded.

Radar rainfall estimates and nearby personal mesonet station indicated that 2 to 3 inches of rain fell across the Collinsville community in a 2 to 3 hour period of time.  This heavy rain caused a debris flow to occur along Figsboro Road near the intersection of Kings Mountain Road, causing the road to be blocked and impassible until maintenance crews could clear the debris.

Radar estimated that between 2 to 4 inches fell from a thundestorm across much of the West Prong of the Little Yadkin River basin, much of this within a 2-hour period. One personal mesonet station recorded 6.18 inches storm total (suspect data, but not impossible). CREST unit streamflow across the basin ranged from 400/ to 700 cfs/mi^2, with average return intervals ranging from 50- to nearly 200-year events. This basin is 8.3 mi^2 in size across rural, modestly hilly land.  The West Prong of the Little Yadkin River overflowed its banks and flooded both Volunteer Road and Tillotson Road, making the roads impassible until the floodwaters receded.

A personal mesonet station recorded a storm total of 3.49 inches of rainfall in a 2-hour period, with 3 of those inches falling inside a 1-hour period. This equates to roughly a 200-year rainfall event at the 1-hour interval and close to a 200-year event at the 2-hour interval, per NOAA Atlas-14 point precipitation frequency estimates.
A CoCoRaHS observer recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 3.68 inches of rainfall.

A personal mesonet station recorded a storm total of 2.62 inches of rainfall in a 2-hour period, with about 2 of those inches falling inside a 1-hour period. This equates to roughly a 25-year rainfall event at both the 1-hour interval and 2-hour intervals, per NOAA Atlas-14 point precipitation frequency estimates.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in Lexington recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 1.53 inches.  This is the 2nd highest rainfall total for August 23rd in the history of this station.  Records for this station date back to June 1889.

Slow-moving thunderstorms produced widespread 2 to 4 inch rainfall amounts across central Rockbridge County, more than double the 1-hour flash flood guidance in this area given moist soil conditions. Much of this rainfall fell in a 2-hour period, which equated to around a 100-year rainfall event for areas just west of the Kerrs Creek community.  Multiple roads were closed due to flooding of Kerrs Creek, including Big Spring Drive, West Midland Trail at Fredericksburg Road, and Muddy Lake at West Midland Trail.

Radar-estimated rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches were close to double that of the 1-hour flash flood guidance in the Joshua Creek basin.  The Wilkes County 911 Center reported that Joshua Creek washed out Long Bottom Road.

Widespread 3 to 5 inch rainfall amounts from slow moving thunderstorms across northern Surry and southern Carroll Counties, with locally higher totals, were roughly double that of the 3-hour flash flood guidance.  CREST unit streamflows were anywhere from 600 cfs/ to over 1000 cfs/mi^2 along the NC/VA state line, with widespread areas of 100 year to 200+ year rainfall events.  Runoff from this rainfall resulting in flooding along Greenhill Road as Schoolhouse Creek overflowed its banks.  Brushy Fork was observed overflowing its banks, flooding White Pines Country Club Road.  Pauls Creek flooded out of its banks and onto both Pipers Gap Road and Busick Lane.  Much of Cross Creek County Club was underwater as Cross Creek rose out of its banks, destroying a pedestrian bridge and heavily damaging the course fairways.

Widespread heavy rain upstream caused the Ararat River stream gauge at Ararat to rise from a stage of around 2 feet to a crest at around 11 feet in less than a 4-hour period, a within-bank rise to Action Stage for this gauge.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of NC Highway 119 North and Stephentown Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of Roxboro Lake Road and Ridgeville Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of Prospect Church Road and Hundley Road, and another tree down near the intersection of Prospect Church Road and Gunn Poole Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of NC Highway 119 North and Woody Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree near the intersection of NC Highway 119 North and NC Highway 57 North.

Gusty winds in the wake of a recent cold frontal passage blew down one tree near the intersection of Spencer Preston Road and Airview Drive.  Another tree was blown down near the intersection of Spencer Preston Road and Newberry Drive.
Heavy rain caused a small debris flow to occur from a hillside onto Highway 221 in the community of Jefferson.
A personal weather station reported a rainfall accumulation of 4.41 inches from 1:30 am through 6:30 am EDT on September 12th.
A personal weather station recorded 3.42 inches of rainfall between 1:30 am and 6:30 am on the morning of September 12th.

Multiple weather stations in the vicinity of the Blue Ridge in Carroll County indicate that between 1.5 and 2.5 inches of rain fell inside a two-hour period during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta at rates of one to two inches per hour in spots.  This rain caused multiple streams to flood out of their banks onto nearby roadways, making them impassible until the water receded, including across Spring Bud Road and Route 52 as Paul's Creek rose out of its banks.

A tributary of Daniels Creek overflowed its banks and flooded onto Oakland Drive, making it impassible until the water receded.  The flooding was the result of up to two inches of rain inside a two hour window, with one to 1.5 inch per hour rainfall rates per nearby personal weather station observations.

Bassett Branch overflowed its banks and flooded onto Meadowood Trail, making it impassible until the water receded. The flooding was the result of up to two inches of rain inside a two hour window, with one to 1.5 inch per hour rainfall rates per nearby personal weather station observations.

Multiple data sources across all of Patrick County, including trained spotters and personal automated weather stations, indicate that between two and locally three inches of rain fell during a two-hour period during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta from roughly 9 am to 11 am EDT.  Rainfall rates were observed at one to two inches per hour in spots.  This rain caused multiple streams to flood out of their banks onto nearby roadways, some up to 12 inches deep in the vicinity of Buffalo Creek, making them impassible until the water receded.  This included Egg Farm Road where it intersected Grassy Branch Creek, as water was estimated to be at least eight inches deep over the roadway.

Training thunderstorms formed along a boundary left in the wake of Tropical Storm Zeta, producing 2.5-4 inches of rain in a three to four hour period.  Rainfall rates were observed to be one to two inches per hour.  The Campbell County 911 Center reported that at least seven roads within the central part of the county were flooded and impassable.  This included Yellow Branch rising out of its banks near the intersection of Morman Mill Road and Patterson Road.

Multiple personal weather stations in the upper Falling River basin indicated three to four inches of rain fell during the late evening hours of the 29th into the early morning hours of the 30th.  Runoff from this rain collected in the Falling River, with the gauge at the Falling River near Naruna (FLRV2) rising to 20.39 feet (10600 cfs).  This is between a 5- and 10-year average return interval for this river gauge per USGS stream statistics.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Concord 4SSW (CONV2) recorded a 24-hour rainfall measurement ending at 7am EDT on October 30th of 3.80 inches. This was the third highest 1-day rainfall measurement during the month of October for this station since it was opened in September 1950. It is also the 13th highest 1-day measurement of any month for this station.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Appomattox (APXV2) recorded a 24-hour rainfall measurement ending at 7am EDT on October 30th of 3.99 inches. This was the second highest 1-day rainfall measurement during the month of October for this station since it was opened in November 1937.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Buckingham (BUKV2) recorded a 24-hour rainfall measurement ending at 7am EDT on October 30th of 3.54 inches. This was the fourth highest 1-day rainfall measurement during the month of October for this station since it was opened in May 1894.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Altavista (ALTV2) recorded a 24-hour rainfall measurement ending at 7am EDT on October 30th of 3.56 inches. This was the fourth highest 1-day rainfall measurement during the month of October for this station since it was opened in May 1945.

The Roanoke River at Brookneal (BROV2) crested above moderate flood stage at 27.74 feet, which is about 35,100 cfs.  This is between a two and five year average return interval per USGS analysis for this gauge.  Typical impacts at this stage are that the nearby low-lying fields and woods are flooded, though the Brookneal Fish Hatchery pond furthest downstream may begin to experience some flooding.

Multiple weather stations in the southeastern portion of Franklin County recorded between two to locally 3.5 inches of rainfall inside a three hour period during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.  Rainfall rates of one to two inches per hour were observed in some locations.  This rain caused multiple streams to flood out of their banks onto nearby roadways in the Snow Creek area, making them impassible until the water receded.  This includes Muddy Fork Road flooded by Reed Creek and Sutton Hollow Road closed due to flooding of Crawford Creek and Snow Creek. Fawndale Road and portions of the Virgil Goode Highway were also reported flooded and impassible for a few hours.
Around two inches of rain during a 2-hour period caused flooding of Powder Mill Creek onto both School Board Road, while flooding of Doe run closed both Doe Run Road and Ashpone Road.
Two roads flooded in the northern part of Pittsylvania county where up to three inches of rain fell from Tropical Cyclone Zeta. The roads were closed until the water receded.

A personal weather station in Wilkesboro recorded 4.92 inches of rainfall during a 24-hour period ending 10 am on the 29th. It was observed that 2.42 inches fell in a single hour on between 8:30 am and 9:30 am on the 29th.

The rain gauge at W. Kerr Scott Reservoir measured a 48-hour rainfall total ending 8 am on the 30th of 4.06 inches. This is the 9th highest 2-day total during the month of October for this station, with records dating back to 1965.

Privately-owned weather stations across northern Ashe County indicate that 1.5 to slightly over 2 inches of rain fell across soils already very moist from rainfall earlier in the past 24 hours.  This caused flooding of Helton Creek, overflowing across a bridge along Jim Duvall Road.

Multiple privately-owned weather stations indicate that between 2 and 2.5 inches of rain fell during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.  Soils were already very moist due to rounds of rain that passed across the region earlier in the night.  Runoff from the rain caused Cranberry Creek to overflow its banks across a bridge on Double Springs Church Road, making the bridge impassible for several hours.

Reports of 2 to 2.5 inches of rain caused rapid river rises along the South Fork of the New River.  At least one low bridge was flooded along Boggs Road, making the bridge impassible for several hours.

Extensive flooding took place along Cub Creek during the late morning and afternoon hours as two to three inches of rain fell across the basin with the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta, most of it within a one hour period, on top of an additional one to two inches that fell during the previous evening for a total of nearly five inches in 24 hours.  Virtually all of Cub Creek Park was flooded, and the bridge on South Bridge Street that crosses the creek was completely over-topped by the flooded creek.  Elsewhere, the dam of a 3.5 acre pond collapsed at around 1:40 pm EST, sending flood water that washed out at 20 foot section of Woodfield Way just downstream.  Concern for the bridge on Industrial Park Road that crosses the creek about one mile downstream prompted evacuations of multiple businesses and apartments that would be cut off if the that bridge too was washed out, though it did not. Country Club Extension Road along Little Cub Creek was flooded and closed, as was Westover Road, where storage buildings and nearby residences were also flooded.

Extensive flooding took place along Moravian Creek during the late morning and afternoon hours as 2 to 3 inches of rain fell across this basin with the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta, most of it within a 1-hour period.  This rain was in addition to another 1 to 2 inches that fell during the previous evening, for a total of nearly 5 inches in 24 hours.  Newspaper reports indicate that nearly all of Moravian Creek was out of its banks, causing flooding Wilkes Community College's lower campus.  School Street further downstream was also closed by the flood waters.

Numerous businesses along Wilkesboro Boulevard from the Yadkin River bridge to Memorial Park were flooded when the Yadkin River swiftly rose out of its banks, the result of 4 to 5 inches or rain within a 24-hour period both preceding and during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta. Multiple personal weather stations observed 2-3 inches of rain within a 1-hour period just before the onset of flooding. Flash flooding ended as the river crested during mid-afternoon, and roads were reopened during the evening once the river receded. Among the businesses flooded were Extreme Collision Auto Body, which had to move several vehicles to prevent them from being damaged by flood waters. Flood waters completely inundated Memorial Park as well as the Yadkin River Greenway.

The Reddies River at Wilkesboro (REDN7) crested at 11.79 feet (6760 cfs), which was between a 5- and 10-year Annual Return Interval per USGS StreamStats.  These rises were the result of 3-5 inches of rainfall within a 24-hour period, much of which fell within a 2-hour period during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.  The rapid rises resulted in the precautionary evacuation of residents from the Rose Glen Manor assisted living facility, though flooding did not enter the buildings.  Employees of other nearby businesses were evacuated as well out of precaution.

Widespread flooding took place along Fishing Creek during the late morning and afternoon hours as 2 to 3 inches of rain fell across this basin with the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta, most of it within a 1-hour period. This rain was in addition to another 1 to 2 inches that fell during the previous evening, for a total of nearly 5 inches in 24 hours. Newspaper reports indicate that Fishing Creek Arbor Road at Fishing Creek was washed out when the culvert running beneath the road failed.  Further downstream, flood waters from the creek carried away several dozen propane gas storage tanks.  It is unclear how many tanks were recovered and still functioning. In addition, high water rescues were conducted for cars that became stranded in the flood waters.  One rescue was conducted on Highway 115 near the intersection with Speedway Road, and the other was on Speedway Road near the Fishing Creek Road intersection.

Moravian Creek quickly rose out of its banks during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta, the result of three to five inches of rain within a 24-hour period.  This caused several roads intersecting the creek to be flooded and closed until the flood water receded, including Germantown Road and Falls Road near the Moravian Falls waterfall.

Heavy rain across central and western Wilkes County due to the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta caused rapid river rises along the Yadkin River.  The Yadkin River quickly rose out of its banks, flooding multiple roads in the Roaring River and Ronda communities, including Red, White and Blue Road, Roaring River Road and Clingman Road.
Flooding due to heavy rain caused by Tropical Storm Zeta resulted in flooding along the Middle Fork of the Reddies River.  Colvard Road was flooded and closed for several hours as a result.
Heavy rain during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta caused a debris flow along Highway 16.

The Yadkin River at Wilkesboro (WKSN7) crested within minor flood stage at 15.86 feet (13,100 cfs), resulting from heavy rain during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.  This crest is between a 2-year and a 5-year annual return interval per USGS StreamStats.  The crest would likely have been higher had W. Kerr Scott Reservoir not reduced its outflow by 500 cfs in response to the flooding at several points downstream.  By holding back outflow and combined with heavy inflow, W. Kerr Scott Reservoir had risen to a pool stage of 1044 feet by 9 pm on October 29th, up 14 feet from before the onset of rainfall during the day prior.
The Yadkin River at Elkin (ELKN7) crested at the moderate flood of 22.52 feet (27,300 cfs) due to heavy rain associated with the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.

Heavy rain from Tropical Storm Zeta caused Whittier Creek to overflow its banks and completely wash out Nurse Road, making the road impassible.  Water was estimated to be flowing about two feet over the bridge before it was destroyed.

Between two and four inches of rainfall occurred in the hours before and during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.  Multiple personal weather stations indicate that more than half of the rain fell within a 2-hour period as the center of the storm passed. The heavy rain caused widespread flooding of small creeks and streams, pushing many out of their banks.  Several roads, both within the Ararat community and the surrounding area, were flooded and impassible until flooding receded.  A few bridges were damaged or destroyed.
Heavy rain caused by Tropical Storm Zeta caused a debris flow across Highway 268, partially blocking the road.

Between two and four inches of rainfall occurred in the hours before and during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta. The heavy rain caused widespread flooding of small creeks and streams, pushing many out of their banks. Several roads, both within the Dobson community and the surrounding area, were flooded and impassible until flooding receded. A few bridges were damaged or destroyed. Highway 601 was impassible due to flooding of Bear Creek, where one swift water rescue was performed for an automobile that became stranded in the flood waters.  Fisher River Park was also closed due to flooding.

Two swift-water rescues were performed for the occupants of vehicles that became stranded where Hiatt Road passes across Stoney Creek.  The road was flooded and impassible for several hours.  This flooding was the result of heavy rain which occurred during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rainfall occurred in the hours before and during the passage of Tropical Storm Zeta. Multiple personal weather stations indicate that more than half of the rain fell within a 2-hour period as the center of the storm passed. The heavy rain caused widespread flooding of small creeks and streams, pushing many out of their banks. Several roads, both within the Elkin community and the surrounding area, were flooded and impassible until flooding receded, including Commerce Street, Pleasant Hill Road, and Memorial Park Drive. A debris flow was reported on Johnson Ridge Road.

Several roads were observed flooded and closed in and around the community of Jonesville. Among them, over six inches of water from the nearby Yadkin River was observed flowing rapidly over Fabric Lane.

Several trees were downed across Ashe County during Tropical Storm Zeta, with four completely or partially blocking roads, and at least one tree down on a utility line. Almost 500 households were without power at some point during the storm.

Approximately 100 tree damage reports were received countywide, in addition to a report of a shingle roof being blown off. About 40 homes in Rockingham were reported to have suffered damage from a fallen tree.
A few trees were blown down in Stokes County. One tree was uprooted causing damage to a carport, and two others blocked a roadway in Pinnacle, NC.
Numerous trees were downed across the county, causing power outages. Hundreds of customers in Surry County lost power during Tropical Storm Zeta.
Several trees were blown down countywide. Over 200 customers in Watauga County lost power during Tropical Storm Zeta. In addition, mesonet site KNCBANNE24 recorded a wind gust of 54 MPH.
Several trees were blown down across the county.
Several trees were downed across Yadkin County, bringing down power lines and blocking a few roadways. A particularly strong gust in Yadkinville brought down three large trees.
Five trees were reported down across Campbell County and the City of Lynchburg, with most of those blocking roadways. One tree brought down a power line as well.
Several trees were blown down across the county. A mesonet site in Huddleston recorded a wind gust of 40 MPH.
Several trees were blown down across Carroll County.
Numerous trees were blown down across Charlotte County, blocking several roadways. Several power lines were also brought down around the county.

Over 100 trees were blown down throughout Pittsylvania County and the city of Danville, with at least one tree falling on a house in Danville. In downtown Danville, a few trees brought down power lines and blocked large intersections. Over 20,000 customers were without power at the peak of the storm. In Chatham, a light pole was blown down onto a vehicle. Winds at the Danville Regional Airport gusted up to 40 miles per hour.
Two trees were blown down in Floyd County, one blocking Stagecoach Run Road south of Check, and another blocking Christiansburg Pike near Pilot.
A few trees were blown down across Franklin County, partially or totally blocking roadways.
A dozen trees were blown down across Halifax County, with a couple of those falling down on power lines as well.
Numerous trees were blown down across Henry County and the city of Martinsville. A few power lines were brought down as well, with one utility pole landing on a vehicle.
Two dozen trees were blown down across Patrick County.
A few trees were blown down near downtown Danville, with one blocking the intersection of Kirk and Seminole Drive, and another blocking the intersection of West Main Street and Virginia Avenue.
Two trees were brought down across a roadway in Pinnacle.
Two trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
A couple trees were uprooted or snapped near Eden. In addition, a roof was blown off of a building.

The Cooperative Weather Observer for Appomattox, VA (APXV2) recorded a storm-total rainfall amount of 9.20 inches rainfall during a 72-hour period ending 12Z on November 13th.  This is the highest 3-day total ever for November, and the 4th- highest ever for any month.  During the 24-hour period ending 12Z on the 12th, 7.28 inches fell, the highest 24-hour precipitation ever recorded during November, and 2nd-highest of any month for this station.  Both the 7.28 inch measurement for a 24-hour period, and 9.20 inch storm-total measurement over 72 hours are each around 50-year ARI events per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates. Records for this station date back to November 1937.
Thunderstorm winds brought down a tree.
Numerous 50 to 70 foot tall spruce pine trees were blown over or snapped at Beech Mountain Ski Resort. The window in one of the ski lifts was also blown out.

Personal weather station KNCHAMPT11 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 6.83 inches.  The station observed 4.56 inches within a 12-hour window on the morning of the 12th, between a 10- and 25-year Average Recurrence Interval per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.

Personal weather station KNCHAMPT3 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 5.98 inches.  The station observed 3.80 inches within a 12-hour window on the morning of the 12th, close to a 10-year Average Recurrence Interval per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.
Personal weather station KNCWILKE20 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 4.13 inches.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Yadkin 6 E observed a 72-hour storm total of 5.70 inches rainfall, ending 12Z on November 13th.  This is the highest 72-hour total for the month of November in the station's history, though only the 19th-highest of all months.  The station observed a 24-hour total of 4.08 inches ending on 12Z of the 12th, and a 48-hour total of 5.15 inches ending at 12Z on the 13th, all of which are new highest records for the month of November.  These amounts are in the 5- to 10-year ARI range per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.

Multiple personal weather stations observed that 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across the upper Logan Creek basin during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of it during a 90-minute period.  This resulted in flash flooding along Logan Creek.  The Cornelius Road bridge crossing the creek was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Multiple personal weather stations observed that 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across eastern Yadkin County during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of it during a 90-minute period for some of these stations. This resulted in flash flooding along Mill Branch. Bloomtown Road crossing the Mill Branch was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Personal weather station KNCEASTB20 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 7.43 inches.  The station observed 5.25 inches within an 8-hour window on the morning of the 12th, between a 25- and 50-year Average Recurrence Interval per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.

Multiple personal weather stations observed 3 to 5 inches of rain during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding of Forbush Creek, including along Lace Knoll Road where is crosses over the Creek. Lace Knoll Road was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Multiple personal weather stations observed that 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across eastern Yadkin County during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding of Forbush Creek, including along Hutchens Road where is crosses over the Creek. Hutchens Road was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Multiple personal weather stations observed 3 to 5 inches of rain during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding of Forbush Creek, including near the intersection of Griffin Road and Snider Road. Griffen Road was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Multiple personal weather stations observed 3 to 5 inches of rain during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding of Forbush Creek, including along Union Cross Church Road where is crosses over the Creek. This road was completely flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.  Residents along the creek were stranded inside their homes due to the flooding, and required rescue from the Yadkinville Fire Department.

Multiple personal weather stations observed 2 to 3 inches of rain during the early morning hours of November 12th across the upper Ararat River basin. This resulted in a rapid 8- foot rise above flood stage within a 3-hour period at the Ararat River.  Extensive flooding of Riverside Park was observed during late morning as a result of this flooding.

Personal weather station KNCMADIS16 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 6.33 inches, though most of the rain fell within 48 hours.  The station observed 4.6 inches within a 12-hour window on the morning of the 12th, between a 10- and 25-year Average Recurrence Interval per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.

Multiple personal weather stations observed 2 to 3 inches of rain during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding of Hogan Creek, including where the creek intersects Hogan Bridge Road, causing the bridge to be flooded and impassible until the flood waters receded.

Two to three inches of rain fell during the early morning hours of November 12th, about half of these amounts during a 90-minute period with the main convective band. This resulted in flash flooding along the Mitchell River, flooding over-passing bridges at several locations.  Among other roads, Zephyr Mountain Park Road became flooded and impassible where it crosses over the river.

Race Track Road was flooded and impassible during the afternoon of November 12th when backwater flooding from County Line Creek pushed a tributary (name unknown) out of its banks across the roadway surface.

Backwater flooding of the Dan River into Seven Island Creek caused Gentry Road to be flooded.  A car became stranded in the flood waters, requiring a the occupants to be rescued by emergency personnel.

Flooding was observed along the North Fork Reddies River and Darnell Creek due to 4 to 5 inches of rainfall on the 11th.  An additional inch of rain during the early morning hours of the 12th caused renewed flooding along these waterways, causing Vannoy Road and Sheets Gap Road to be flooded and impassible.

Several roads throughout Rockingham County were flooded and impassible as multiple rounds of heavy rain passed across the county.  One round in Reidsville produced 1 to 1.25 inches within a 40 minute period, with rainfall rates at times of 2 to 3 inches per hour.  Particularly affected was Scale Street in Reidsville.

Several rounds of heavy rain passed across Rockingham County on the evening of November 11th.  One round in passing across the community of Madison produced around 1 inch in less than an hour over saturated soil conditions, with rainfall rates at times of 2 to 3 inches per hour.  Multiple streets within the community were flooded and impassible.

With 1.5 to 2 inches of rain having already fallen earlier in the day, a band of fast-moving thunderstorms producing heavy rain moved across the community of Blacksburg.  Between 7:00 pm and 7:40 pm, a weather station in Blacksburg recorded about 1.25 inches of rain with this band.  Runoff from the rainfall push Stroubles Creek out of its banks near the Duck Pond on the Virginia Tech University campus, flooding Duck Pond Drive.  The road was impassible for several hours.

With about 2 inches of rain having already fallen earlier in the day across the Jacobs Creek watershed, a band of thunderstorms passed across the area during the evening.  Multiple personal weather stations observed 1.25 to 1.5 inches of rain during a 45-minute period between 6:30 pm and 7:15 pm, falling over saturated soils.  Runoff from this rain pushed Jacobs Creek out of its banks, which was then observed flowing across Red House Road. The road was impassible until the flood waters receded.  An automobile became stranded in the floodwaters and had to be towed out.

Personal weather station KVAAPPOM24 recorded a 72-hour storm-total rainfall amount, ending 12Z on November 13th, of 6.28 inches.  This is roughly a 10-year Average Recurrence Interval per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Frequency Estimates.

Local personal weather stations indicate that between 2 and 2.25 inches of rain fell between 6 am and noon on November 11th.  Around 1 inch of that amount fell between 10:30 am and 11:30 am.  Runoff from this rainfall caused a pond along Rock Fence Road to overflow across the road, blocking the roadway until the water receded.

Local personal weather stations indicate that nearly 3 inches of rain fell between 5:15 am and 11:15 am on November 11th, with 1.5 inches falling between 10 am and 11:15 am.  This caused Buck Creek to overflow its banks, flooding Snapps Mill Road and other nearby roads.

A little over 2.5 inches of rain fell across central Appomattox County during the morning of November 11th, with an inch falling during the 10 am to 11:15 am timeframe. Runoff from this rainfall pushed Big Cub Creek out of its banks, with flood waters observed flowing across Rock Spring Road.
Runoff from heavy rain was observed ponding across the roadway near the intersection of Stage Road and Stonewall Road, causing the road to be impassible.
Ponding of water due to heavy rain was observed across Oakleigh Avenue, causing the road to be impassible.
Runoff from heavy rain was observed ponding across Oakley Avenue, briefly closing the road until the water receded.

Runoff from heavy rain resulted in about six inches of standing water at the intersection of Badcock Place and Atlanta Avenue.  Poor drainage is suspected given the highly developed retail area surrounding the intersection.
Runoff from about 2.3 inches of rain during the previous 6-hour period was observed ponding across South Constitutional Route near the community of Scottsville.

Runoff from 2 to 2.5 inches or rain that fell between 4 am and 10 am in the vicinity of the City of Lynchburg caused Buffalo Creek to rise out of its banks.  About 4 inches of water from the creek was observed flowing across Whitestone Drive.

Runoff from 2 to 2.5 inches or rain that fell between 4 am and 10 am in the vicinity of the City of Lynchburg caused Buffalo Creek to rise out of its banks. Water from the creek was observed flowing across Homewood Drive.

Runoff from 2 to 2.5 inches of rainfall across portions of Buckingham County between 5:30 am and 11 am caused Walton Fork to rise out of its banks. Water from the fork was observed flowing across St. Andrews Road, but was less than 6 inches deep at the time.

Runoff from 2 to 2.5 inches of rain that fell between 5:30 am and 11 am caused Sharps Creek to flood out of its banks.  Water from the creek was observed flowing across Diana Mill Road, but less than 6 inches deep.
Poor drainage issues after 2+ inches of rain earlier in the morning caused Union Hill Road to be closed off due to standing water.

After 2 to 3 inches of rain fell across Appomattox county during the morning, an additional 1.75 to 2.25 inches of rain fell during the evening, most of it within a hour, as a line of slow-moving thunderstorms passed across the area.  This caused numerous creeks, already running high from the earlier rainfall, to flood out of their banks.  Notable among the flood reports was water about one foot deep running across Horseshoe Road. At least five water rescues were performed by emergency personnel, including one at North Creek Road where North Creek was observed flooding the roadway, and another at River Ridge Road at the Appomattox River.  Additional rounds of rain of weaker intensity persisted through the late evening hours, maintaining the flooding conditions, though flash flooding ended by 11:00 pm.

After 2 to 2.5 inches of rain fell during the morning across much of Buckingham County, a  band of slow-moving thunderstorms moved across the county during the evening.  Runoff from this heavy rain caused water to flow across the road near the intersection of Howardsville Road and Watoga Road.

After 2 to 2.5 inches of rain fell during the morning across much of Buckingham County, a  band of slow-moving thunderstorms moved across the county during the evening.  Runoff from this heavy rain caused water to flow across the road near the intersection of Twin Creek Road and West James Anderson Highway.

Runoff from 1 to 1.5 inches of rain in about a one-hour time period caused flooding several inches deep to flow across the intersection of Wilkerson Road and Kentuck Road. The road was reported impassible until after the water receded.

The Smith River rose out of its banks and flooded onto Appalachian Drive in the community of Fieldale during the afternoon of November 11th, after widespread rainfall amounts of 2 to 2.5 inches fell earlier in the day.  One car became stranded while trying to pass through the flood waters.  Emergency services successfully rescued the lone occupant of the vehicle.

Multiple personal weather stations indicated between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rain fell during the evening of November 11th across portions the Banister River basin.  Some of this rain fell inside a 2 hour period.  This caused flooding along the Banister River, which washed out the bridge along Meadville Road.  It was initially estimated that it would take 2 to 3 months to repair the bridge.  Outage of the bridge required a roughly 20-mile detour for motorists to go around.

The Dan River at South Boston (SBNV2) crested at 29.44 feet on November 15th at 1:15 am EST, which is the 14th-highest crest on record, but below two other crests that occurred earlier in 2020.  Flooding of this magnitude is between a 5- and 10-year event per USGS StreamStats.  Flooding from the Dan River caused water to flood the road and businesses along Highway 501 as far south as the intersection with Highway 58, about a half mile from the river.  The intersection was closed from late afternoon of the 14th until late afternoon of the 15th, when the river was around a stage of 28 feet.  Highway 501 remained closed until the morning of the 16th.

Trade Street was reported closed due to flooding from the Dan River when the river was above a stage of about 23.5 feet beginning around 3:00 pm on November 12th.  The river did not recede below this stage until late afternoon on the 14th.

Multiple weather stations across Franklin County recorded between 4 and locally-6 inches of rainfall occurring in multiple waves during the morning and again in the evening.  An additional 1.5 to 2.5 inches occurred during the morning and early afternoon on the 12th.  Runoff from this rainfall caused numerous roads across Franklin county to be covered with water and impassible until the water receded.  Some of these roads include Virgil Goode Road, Doe Run Road, School Board Road at Powder Creek, Franklin Street.  At least one road was reported washed out, which was Rock Lily Road.  Multiple minor debris flows were also reported on the roads, impeding traffic until they were cleared.

The Dan River at Danville (DVLV2) was in flood stage (21 feet) from November 12th through the 14th and crested at the moderate flood stage of 26.10 feet (40,100 cfs) at 11:30 PM EST on November 13th.  This was just under a 25-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Dan River at Paces, VA (PCEV2) was above flood stage (22 feet) from November 12th through the 15th and crested at the minor flood stage of 28.65 feet (47,000 cfs) at 4:15 PM EST on November 14th.  This was just over a 25-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Dan River at Wentworth, NC (WENN7) was above flood stage (19 feet) from November 12th through the 13th, and crested at the moderate flood stage of 27.62 feet (38,500 cfs) at 6:30 AM EST on November 13th, the 5th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was between a 25- and 50-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Yadkin River at Elkin, NC (ELKN7) was above flood stage (18 feet) on November 12th, and crested at the moderate flood stage of 21.81 feet (25,100 cfs) at 1:00 PM EST, the 8th highest crest on record for this gauge.

The Roanoke River at Roanoke, VA (RONV2) was above flood stage (10 feet) on November 12th, and crested at the moderate flood stage of 14.07 feet (14,000 cfs) at 12:35 PM EST on November 12th, the 13th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was between a 5- and 10-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Roanoke River at Brookneal, VA (BROV2) was above flood stage (23 feet) from November 11th through the 14th and crested at the major flood stage of 34.51 feet (59,800 cfs) at 7:00 PM EST on November 12th, the 5th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was between a 10- and 25-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Roanoke River at Randolph, VA (RNDV2) was above flood stage (24 feet) from November 12th through very early on the 17th and crested at the moderate flood stage of 31.97 feet (58,200 cfs) at 9:15 PM EST on November 13th, the 7th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was between a 5- and 10-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

Cub Creek at Phenix, VA (CUBV2) was above flood stage (12 feet) from November 12th through the 13th and crested at a stage of 16.93 feet (7,610 cfs) at 5:30 PM EST on November 12th, the 4th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was between a 10- and 25-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.

The Falling River near Naruna, VA (FLRV2) was above flood stage (15 feet) from November 11th through the 13th and crested at a stage of 27.97 feet (19,700 cfs) at 11:45 AM EST on November 12th, the 4th highest crest on record for this gauge.  This was a 25-year Average Return Interval event per the USGS StreamStats website.

Strong winds blew two trees down at the Craig County Water Treatment Plant. Damage values are estimated.

Two to three inches of rain fell across the upper Ararat River basin during the early morning hours of November 12th.  Soils were already saturated leading up to this rainfall, with vegetation having entered dormancy.  During a 3-hour time period, from 3:15 am to 6:15 am, the river rose about 8 feet and exceeded flood stage.  The river eventually crested at 15.75 feet during early afternoon, which is under a 10-year Average Return Interval per the USGS StreamStats website.
A 62 mph wind gust was measured by North Carolina's ECONet observing system at Mt. Jefferson. A 60 mph wind gust was measured by a personal weather station two miles East-Northeast of Baldwin.
A 61 MPH wind gust was measured in Boone.
The month began with most of Buckingham County having Severe Drought (D2) conditions.  On the 29th of the month the level of drought was improved to Moderate (D1) conditions.
The eastern half of Charlotte County began the month under Severe Drought (D2) conditions.  By the 15th of the month, the drought severity level was  improved to Moderate Drought (D1) conditions.
The southern half of Halifax County began the month under a Severe Drought (D2).  On the 22nd of the month, the drought category was improved to a Moderate Drought (D1) for the entire county.

A small portion of the southeast part of Pittsylvania county began the month under a Severe Drought (D2).  On the 8th of the month, the drought category was improved to Moderate Drought (D1) for the entire county.

The county began the month only at the Moderate (D1) category of drought severity, but increased the morning of the 1st to the Severe (D2) category in the southern part of the county.  It remained only at this level one week before falling again to the Moderate (D1) level on the 8th.
Most of the county began the month in a Severe Drought (D2).  On the morning of the 8th, the drought category was decreased to Moderate (D1).

The southern quarter of the county began the month in an Extreme (D3) drought with the remainder of the county under a Severe (D2) drought.  On April 8, drought conditions were improved so that now the southern half of the county was under a Severe (D2) drought while the rest of the county was under a Moderate (D1) drought.  On the 22nd, conditions were upgraded again so that now the entire county was under a Moderate (D1) drought.

The far southeast corner of the county began the month in an Extreme (D3) drought with the remainder of the county under a Severe (D2) drought.  On April 8, drought conditions were improved so that now the southeast part of the county was under a Severe (D2) drought while the rest of the county was under a Moderate (D1) drought.  On the 22nd, the entire county was under a Moderate (D1) drought.

Broadcast media, Skywarn-trained weather spotters and members of the general public observed ice accumulations ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 inches in thickness across Campbell County and the City of Lynchburg, including in the communities of Rustburg, Gladys and Altavista. Over 5,260 power outages were reported in the city and county combined because of the icing.  In addition, the icing caused a tree to fall onto a truck along Highway 460 near the Candlers Mountain Road exit.  It does not appear that the driver was injured.  Key impacts: power outages; hazardous to impossible travel conditions; automobile accidentz; widespread tree damage.

Virginia State Police responded to calls for nine disabled vehicles and at least 37 traffic crashes caused by the hazardous road conditions in Appomattox County and the surrounding region.  No fatalities were reported.  Key impacts: power outages; hazardous to impossible travel conditions; automobile accidents; widespread tree damage.

Skywarn-trained weather spotters and members of the general public observed ice accumulations from freezing rain ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 inches in thickness across nearly all of Charlotte County, including in the communities of Keysville, Madisonville, and Charlotte Court House.  Over 5,000 power outages were reported at one point.  It was estimated that as much as 88 percent of the county's residents were without power by the end of the storm, with around 154 power poles snapped and 221 power lines brought down due to the weight of the ice.  Some residents were without power for a week before it was restored.  As a result, each of the county's seven fire stations were set up as warming and charging stations for the local residents. Thousands of trees and tree limbs were also brought down by the icing.  Key impacts: power outages; hazardous to impossible travel conditions; widespread tree damage.

This rise caused Back Creek to rapidly flood across Virginia Route 39, closing the road until the flood waters receded. Key Impacts: flooded & impassible roadway; transportation delays.

The Greenbrier River at Ronceverte (RONW2) crested at a stage of 18.43 feet at 5:05 pm EST, resulting in extensive flooding of Island Park in the community of Ronceverte.  The floor of the concession stand at the park was destroyed. Repairs were also necessary to a railing at the community amphitheater, and several loads of gravel and dirt were needed to fill a hole next to the amphitheater formed by the flooding.  Flood waters over the park rose to within inches of entering the lowest level of homes along Monroe Avenue upstream of the gauge (would be around 19.0 ft), though there were no reports of water entering any homes.  Water covered the roads and entered the yards of homes downstream of the park on both Monroe Avenue (right bank) and River Road (left bank), but no damage was reported in these locations either.  There is no defined level for moderate flood stage at this gauge, so somewhere between 19.0 feet and 21.0 would seem appropriate.  There is no rating curve developed for this gauge at this time, and no defined ARI for flooding of this magnitude.

The Greenbrier River at Alderson (ALDV2) crested at the moderate flood stage of 17.53 feet (52,600 cfs) at 8:15 pm EST on March 1st.  This crest ranked between a 5- and 10-year average return interval per USGS StreamStats, and is the 11th highest crest for this gauge since 1960. Flooding within this stretch of the Greenbrier River caused Highway 3/12 to be covered by several feet of water and impassible at multiple locations downstream from the gauge between Alderson and Talcott.  It did not appear much flooding occurred within the town of Alderson itself and no buildings were reported to be impacted.  All damage was confined to the professional removal of fallen trees blocking stream channels within the area and other related repairs.

The Greenbrier River at Hilldale (HLLW2) crested at the minor flood stage of 21.38 feet (56,200 cfs) at 1:00 am EST on March 2nd. This crest ranked just under a 10-year average return interval per USGS StreamStats, and is the 9th highest crest for this gauge since 1936. Portions of Highway 12 were observed flooded within a quarter mile upstream from the gauge.  Multiple homes along the right bank just downstream of the gauge were surrounded by water, but are elevated/on stilts.  Flooded was limited to areas below the living space of these homes.

The Meadow River near Hines (HNEW2) crested at the moderate flood stage of 16.69 feet (52,600 cfs) at 3:25 pm EST on March 1st.  Highway 60 was flooded by multiple feet of water and impassible in several spots between the communities of Rupert and Rainelle, leaving mud and debris which required cleaning reopen the road.  Multiple homes along the river between these points were observed surrounded by flood waters, but it is unknown to what degree, if any, that water entered the homes.  This gauge does not currently have a rating curve.

Sewell Creek above Little Sewell Creek at Rainelle (RANW2) crested at the moderate flood stage of 14.58 feet at 12:15 pm EST on March 1st. The mayor of Rainelle reported that there was little damage caused by the flooding, with some side streets off of Horton Avenue and adjacent properties covered with water.  Kanawha Avenue was also closed due to flooding for a short time.  The Rainelle City Park was covered with several inches of water from Sewell Creek.  The mayor reported that there was little damage and that any city expenses would be related to cleanup of debris.  No evacuations were necessary.  The gauge was installed during September 2019, so has a short operational history.

Prolonged heavy rain atop saturated soils caused The Clinch River at Richlands to rise above the minor flood stage of 10 feet to crest at 10.91 feet at 12:45 pm on March 1st.  Basin average rainfall upstream of Richlands was 1.25 to 1.5 inches for the 24-hour period ending 8 am on the 1st, and 2.5 to 3 inches for the 72-hour period ending at 8 am on the 1st.  The river rose out of its banks into nearby Forth Street, impeding travel along the road.  The water rose into adjacent yards and threatened a few homes, but didn't rise high enough to enter the homes.  The Police Department was also surrounded by water, but water did not enter the building.  Flood waters receded during the afternoon as rain exited the region.  No damage was reported.

A trained CoCoRaHS observer recorded a 24-hour total rainfall amount of 11.00 inches. Most of this rain fell within a 3- to 4-hour period on the evening of the 24th.  This amount was well over a 1000-year rainfall event at the 6-hour duration per a NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Estimate.
The hail covered roofs and roadways.
Thunderstorm winds blew down trees across Highway 460.  Power lines were also blown down by the winds.  Damage values are estimates.

The combination of heavy rain and poor drainage resulted in flash flooding in the community of Appomattox, especially along Confederate Avenue where runoff became over 3 feet deep, with one witness observing water rising up to the hood of a stranded vehicle.  Nearby automated personal weather stations indicated about 1.5 inches of rain fell within a 30 to 40 minute period, with rainfall rates as high as 4 inches per hour.

A personal automated weather station recorded 2.28 inches of rainfall from a thunderstorm that occurred during a 60-minute period.  This is about a 10-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency Estimates.
The hail completely covered the ground.
Damage values are estimated.
Damage values are estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAMONTE15) recorded 3.20 inches or rainfall during a 2-hour period in the afternoon of June 13th.  Per radar estimates, this appeared to be outside of the area of heaviest rainfall across Highland County.  This location is also outside of the Back Creek basin, but close enough to be representative.  At this location, this was a 25-year event per a NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimate.

The stream gauge at Back Creek at Sunrise (SUNV2) crested at the Moderate Flood Stage of 10.01 feet (4,370 cfs) at 8:00 pm EST, the highest level observed at this gauge since 2008.  This crest was less than a 5-year event per USGS StreamStats estimates for this gauge.  No impacts of the flooding were reported, perhaps due to the rural nature of land use surrounding the gauge.

Nearly 3 inches of rain fell from a thunderstorm inside of a 1 hour period of time in the Big Island area, including along Camden Road.  Rainfall rates were observed to be as high as 5 inches per hour at times during the event.  Runoff from this rainfall caused Camden Road to become flooded by several inches of water and impassible.  Water was also reported by law enforcement entering a basement of a home.  FLASH (Flooded Locations and Simulated Hydrographs Project) estimated that 1-hour rainfall was about 2.5 times that of Flash Flood guidance and that this was a 25 to 50-year event per FLASH 1-Hour ARI estimates.

A personal weather station in the Big Island area (Weather Underground: KVABIGIS8) recorded a rainfall amount from a thunderstorm of 2.76 occurring in less than 1 hour.  This amount is between a 50 and 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused Indian Run to flood out of its banks and flow across Fontella Road, causing the road to become impassible.  The road was reopened after the flood waters receded.

Rainfall of between 2.5 and 3 inches fell within a 90-minute period near the community of Keeling, at times falling at rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour. This is estimated to be a 10- to 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency Estimates. The heavy rain caused a tributary of Birch Creek to overflow its banks across Richmond Highway, temporarily closing the highway until the water receded. No damage to the road was reported.

Between 2 and 2.5 inches of rain fell within a 90-minute period across the community of Boonsboro, at times falling at rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour. This is roughly a 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates. This rainfall caused flooding across Walnut Hollow Road at Indered Farm Road.  The road was reopened and passable after the water receded.  No damage was reported.
A trained weather spotter recorded 4.81 inches of rainfall within a nearly 1-hour period.  This amount would be over a 1,000-year event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.
Two to locally in excess of four inches of rain caused a mudslide along Highway 501.  The road was passable after the debris was cleared.

Water was observed flowing several inches deep across River Ridge Road as Plain Run Branch overflowed its banks.  Doppler radar indicated that between 2.5 and 3 inches of rain fell in the area during a 3-hour period from a slow-moving thunderstorm.  This amount was between a 10- and 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.
A drainage issue after more than 2 inches of rain fell caused several inches of standing water to back up across Whittle Street in the community of Chatham.

An automated personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVALYNCH81) recorded 3.21 inches of rain from a thunderstorm during a 90-minute period.  This is estimated to be around an 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

Between 2.5 and 3.5 inches of rain fell from a slow-moving thunderstorm across the Blackwater Creek watershed during a 90-minute period.  Rainfall rates were observed to 2 to 3 inches per hour during much of this event.  This caused flooding along Blackwater Creek, which caused water to enter apartments along Sandusky Drive.  Multiple residents of these apartments were forced to evacuate until the water receded.  In addition, an automobile became stranded in the flood water along Greenwood Drive where it crosses Blackwater Creek.  No injuries were reported and the occupants were able to escape the flooded vehicle and move to a safe location.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCSTONE2) recorded 2.82 inches of rain during a 60-minute period. This was a 50-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

Heavy rain, falling at rates of 2 to locally 5 inches per hour, caused the railroad underpass along Business Highway 220 to be flooded by several feet of standing water.  The underpass was reopened after the water receded.
Runoff from heavy rain caused by a thunderstorm was observed flowing across Stone Mountain Road at M. P. Drive.  No damage was reported and the road was reopened after the flood waters receded.

Runoff from heavy rain caused by a thunderstorm resulted in several inches of flowing water across S. Henry Street near the Adams Mart.  No damage was reported and the road was passable after the flood waters receded.

A poor drainage issue after up to an inch of rainfall across the community of Reidsville resulted in several inches of standing water along the 800 block of Scales Street.  The water receded once the drainage issue was resolved, with no damage reported.
Little Rock Creek was observed flowing out of its banks, with water a few inches deep across Sugar Shack Road.  The road was closed as a precaution for increased flooding.  No damage was reported.
A pond overflowed its banks due to heavy rainfall across Saddlebridge Road.  Water was only a few inches deep.  No damage was reported and the road was passable after the water receded.
Heavy rain caused Cabbage Creek to flood out of its banks up to the front porch of a home along Cabbage Creek Road.  No damage was reported to the home and the creek water receded soon afterward.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KNCVILAS25) recorded 2.10 inches of rain that fell from a thunderstorm during an 80-minute period.  Rainfall rates were observed to be as high as 3.5 inches per hour at one point during this storm.  This was between a 5- and 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A slow-moving thunderstorm produced a radar-estimated 3.5 inches or rain during a 90-minute period along Beaverdam Road, which fell at rates as high as 5 inches per hour at times.  This would be roughly a 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  Runoff from this heavy rain, possibly combined with a poor drainage issue, caused one lane of Beaverdam Road to buckle.  Numerous stones at least six inches in diameter were also washed across Beaverdam Road and Moody Boulevard.
A home caught fire from a lightning strike during a thunderstorm in the community of Altavista, Virginia.  The home sustained heavy fire and smoke damage, but no injuries were reported.
A few trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds in the community of Hurt, Virginia.

An estimated two inches of rain fell within an hour from a slow-moving thunderstorm across the Dry Creek drainage basin, between a 10- and 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  The rain was estimated to be falling at rates of three to four inches per hour per KFCX Doppler radar, and caused Dry Creek to overflow its banks and flow across Camp Road several inches deep.  No damage to the road was reported.

Runoff from roughly an inch of rainfall within an hour was observed flowing across Bee Tree Ridge Lane, when the culvert under the road was clogged. Part of the road was damaged by the runoff and required repair.
Crooked Creek briefly rose out of its banks up to Honeymoon Lane.  Up to an inch of rain fell within an hour across the headwaters of the Crooked Creek basin.  No damage was reported.

Doppler radar estimated that two to locally as much as four inches of rain from a series of thunderstorms fell across upper Moores Fork Creek basin (1.85 miles^2 per USGS Stream Stats), all within about a 2-hour period of time.  For this duration, most locations within this area experienced between a 5- and a 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.  If indeed four inches of rain fell, that would be around a 100-year rainfall event at the 2-hour duration.  Runoff from this rainfall caused Moores Fork Creek to rise out of its banks, flooding several inches deep across Kitty Hawk Lane and potentially other locations.  No damage was reported.

Runoff from several inches of rain caused Sycamore Creek to rise out of its banks and flow across Sycamore Creek Road near the intersection of Woodlawn Church Road.  At around 9:40 pm EST, the rainfall triggered at least one debris flow nearby.  The flooding left large amounts of debris along the bridge crossing the creek and across the roadway.  Structural damage to the road was also observed and required repair.

Portions of Salem Avenue and Campbell Avenue were flooded with up to 4 feet of standing water as heavy rain overwhelmed the storm sewer system.  Five water rescues were performed as cars drove into the flood waters, causing the vehicles to stall.  No injuries were reported.  Broadcast media reported that multiple cars parked along Salem Avenue experienced water intrusion into the vehicle passenger compartments and exhaust systems, with some of the vehicle needed to be towed.

Between 1.5 and 2.2 inches of rain (both a 5-10 event per NOAA Atlas-14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates) fell across the southern half of the Town of Blacksburg, including the headwaters of Cedar Run, within a 60-minute period.  Though not a particularly impressive rainfall event by most standards, flooding of Cedar Run along Cedar Run Road near Sweeny Road is known by locals to flood at times due to constricted culverts passing under the road.   Runoff from the rainfall was sufficient to overflow across Cedar Run Road several feet deep, with one automobile becoming stranded in the flood waters up to its headlights.  The occupant of the vehicle required the assistance of a swift-water rescue team, with no injuries reported.  The vehicle had to be towed out of the area.

An automated weather station in the community of Blowing Rock (KNCBLOWI61) observed 4.89 inches of rainfall for the calendar day of August 17th, including 2.1 inches during a 45 minute period between 9:00 and 9:45 pm EDT (5- and 10-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates). Rainfall rates during this time were measured to be as high as 6 inches per hour. The 24-hour amount is between a 2- and 5-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14.

The Watauga River at Sugar Grove crested at 10.61 feet at 12:00 am EST on August 18th due to 24-hour rainfall amounts ranging from 6 to 8 inches of rainfall across the headwaters of the Watauga River, tapering down to 2 to 4 inches near the stream gauge.  This is a little over a 2-year ARI event per USGS Stream Stats.

After several hours of steady rainfall through the day on the 17th, a band of heavy rain passing across the Town of Boone produced between 1.8 and 2.6 inches of rain in less than an 1-hour period, falling at rates of 4 to locally 6 inches per hour at times.  Runoff from this rain caused rapid rises along Winkler Creek and Hodges Creek, with quickly overflowed their banks and flooded over 3 feet deep in spots across the Boone Mall shopping complex.  No injuries were reported, however several cars were observed flooded, a few of which had water up to the windows.

The Rankin Science Building on the Appalachian State campus had about four to six inches of water from Boone Creek enter the first floor building.  Edwin Duncan Hall and Varsity Gym both had minimal flooding on portions of the lowest levels of each building.  Five vehicles were flooded to some degree in nearby parking lots.  One student sustained a minor injury after sliding in mud.

Four to locally eight inches of rain across the headwaters of the Watauga River caused the river to overflow its banks and flow across Shulls Mill Road near the intersection with Old Shulls Mill Road.  The road was reopened once flooding subsided, with no damage reported.

Four to six inches of rainfall, including 1.5 to 2.25 inches falling within a 1-hour period between 9:00 pm and 10:00 pm EST, caused numerous creeks and rivers to flood out of their banks, including the New River and its tributaries.  Flooding was observed along Deerfield Road near the Loyal Order of Moose lodge, Bamboo Road near Airport Road, along Elk Road, New River Hills Road, and Roby Green Road.  No damage to these roads was reported other than what was required to clear the roads of debris.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCMOUNT12) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 7.83 inches, which is between a 50- and 100-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration.  This event includes about five inches of rain which fell between 9 PM and midnight on the 21st, which is between a 200- and 500-year event per NOAA Atlas 14.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCARARA1) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 6.18 inches, which is about a 25-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration. This event includes 3.57 inches of rain which fell between 9 PM and midnight on the 21st, which is between a 25- and 50-year event per NOAA Atlas 14.

An automated weather station (Weather Underground: KNCMOUNT12) observed a 24-hour rainfall total, ending 8 AM EDT, of 6.73 inches, which is between a 25- and 50-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 point frequency estimates for this duration. This event includes about 4.47 inches of rain which fell between 9 PM and midnight on the 21st, which is between a 100- and 200-year event per NOAA Atlas 14.  Rainfall rates between this 3-hour period continuously ranged between 1.5 and 2.5 inches per hour.
